tracks.title: Start here (zero knowledge)
tracks.blurb: No finance background needed. Learn what a company and a share really are, then read your first statements using a corner shop.

tracks.title: Profit & Loss
tracks.blurb: The report card of a business: how much it sold, what it spent, and what was left for the owners.

tracks.title: Balance Sheet
tracks.blurb: A photograph of what the business owns and owes on one day, and who paid for it.

tracks.title: Cash Flow
tracks.blurb: Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact. See where money actually came from and went.

tracks.title: Connecting the statements
tracks.blurb: The three statements are one story told three ways. Learn to move between them.

tracks.title: Fundamental Ratios
tracks.blurb: Turn statements into simple, comparable numbers. Learn what each ratio means in plain words, with Ravi's shop as the example.

tracks.title: Putting it together
tracks.blurb: Use everything you have learned: judge businesses by their industry, estimate what they are worth, and spot trouble early.

tracks.title: Technical Analysis Foundations
tracks.blurb: What technical analysis does, how to read a chart, and the structure of price: trend, support, resistance and trendlines.

tracks.title: Candlestick Analysis
tracks.blurb: Read a single candle as a story of supply and demand, then learn why context matters more than the pattern name.

tracks.title: Moving Averages and Trend Systems
tracks.blurb: What a moving average measures, how to read alignment and crossovers, and why the 10-week average is a practical tool for managing winners.

tracks.title: Volume and Price-Volume Analysis
tracks.blurb: Volume shows how much conviction stands behind a move. Learn to read expansion, dry-up, breakout volume and accumulation.

tracks.title: Momentum Indicators
tracks.blurb: RSI, MACD and the stochastic oscillator: what each actually measures, when it helps, and why “overbought” is not a sell signal.

tracks.title: Relative Strength
tracks.blurb: Leaders outperform the market before they are obvious. Learn the RS line, RS rating, the Mansfield version and a leadership checklist.

tracks.title: Weinstein Stage Analysis
tracks.blurb: Every stock cycles through basing, advancing, topping and declining. Learn to identify the stage and to trade only where the odds are best.

tracks.title: Chart Patterns
tracks.blurb: Why bases form, and how to recognise cup and handle, flat base, high tight flag, VCP, double bottom, flags and failed patterns.

tracks.title: Breakouts and Entries
tracks.blurb: What a breakout is, how to define the pivot, what volume to expect, where to enter, and what to do when it fails.

tracks.title: Pullbacks and Continuation Entries
tracks.blurb: Buy constructive weakness in strong stocks: what a healthy pullback looks like, where it ends, and how to tell it from a trend break.

tracks.title: Market Regime and Market Breadth
tracks.blurb: A good setup works better in a good market. Learn to read the index, breadth, distribution, follow-through and sector rotation.

tracks.title: O’Neil and Minervini Framework
tracks.blurb: The technical side of CAN SLIM and Mark Minervini’s Trend Template, and how they combine with Weinstein’s stages and relative strength.

tracks.title: Risk Management
tracks.blurb: Stops that invalidate the idea, position sizing from rupee risk, reward-to-risk, expectancy and portfolio-level risk.

tracks.title: Trade Management
tracks.blurb: After entry: trailing stops, partial profits, when to sell, and how to add to and reduce positions.

tracks.title: Technical Screening
tracks.blurb: Turn chart observations into objective conditions that generate repeatable candidate lists, and learn what screens cannot do.

tracks.title: Building a Complete Trading Setup
tracks.blurb: Put everything together: a complete framework and three worked fictional examples, a breakout, a pullback and a failure.

tracks.title: Backtesting and Systematic Trading
tracks.blurb: Test an idea on history without fooling yourself: biases, overfitting, performance metrics and turning a trading idea into rules.

tracks.title: Trading Psychology and Execution
tracks.blurb: Why capable traders break their own rules, and the habits that keep decisions mechanical: accepting small losses and keeping a journal.

tracks.title: TradeEdge Technical Analysis Framework
tracks.blurb: A single synthesis: scorecard, screen-to-trade workflow, final checklist and your own written trading plan.

tracks.title: Privi Speciality Chemicals (FY26)

lessons.title: What is a company, a share and a stock price?
lessons.summary: Before any analysis: what you actually own when you buy a share, and why the price moves.

blocks.x: Imagine Ravi opens a kirana (corner) shop. He puts in ₹5 lakh of his own money. The shop earns profit, owns shelves and stock, and owes some money to a supplier. Now imagine Ravi splits ownership of the shop into **500,000 equal slices of ₹1 each** and sells some slices to friends. Each slice is a **share**. A friend holding 50,000 shares owns 10% of the shop and gets 10% of its profit.

blocks.title: In plain words
blocks.x: A share is a small slice of ownership in a real business. You are a part-owner, not a lender. If the business grows and earns more, your slice becomes more valuable. If it fails, you can lose your money.
From a corner shop to the stock market

A **listed company** is one whose shares can be bought and sold by anyone on a stock exchange (NSE or BSE in India). Instead of finding a friend, you place an order on your broker app and a buyer and seller are matched in seconds.

head: Term
Meaning
Shop example
rows: What one slice costs right now
Share price × number of shares. What the market says the whole company is worth
Part of profit paid out to shareholders in cash
₹2 lakh profit ÷ 5 lakh shares = ₹0.40 per share

blocks.x: Why does the price move every second?

The price is simply the last rate at which a buyer and seller agreed. If more people want to buy than sell, it rises. It reacts to results, news, interest rates, fear and greed. Over days, prices swing on **mood**. Over many years, they tend to follow **how much profit the business earns**.

blocks.title: The idea the whole course is built on
blocks.x: **Price is what you pay. Value is what you get.** Fundamental analysis is the skill of estimating the value of a business from its numbers, so you can tell whether today's price is cheap, fair or expensive.
How to use this course

items: Read **Start here** fully, in order. It teaches the language.
Then study Profit & Loss, Balance Sheet and Cash Flow, one at a time.
Move to Ratios, then Putting it together.
Use the **Glossary** whenever a word is unfamiliar. Nobody remembers every term on day one.

quiz.q: You buy 1,000 shares of a company. What do you own?
options: A small slice of the business
quiz.why: A share is part-ownership. Your return depends on how the business performs, and nothing is guaranteed.

quiz.q: A company has 10 crore shares priced at ₹50. What is its market cap?
quiz.why: Market cap = price × shares = 50 × 10 crore = ₹500 crore.

lessons.title: What is fundamental analysis?
lessons.summary: Studying the business behind the ticker, and the three questions it answers.

blocks.x: Suppose a stranger offers to sell you Ravi's kirana shop for ₹10 lakh. Would you just say yes? You would first ask: How much does it earn each year? Does it owe money? Is the location good? Will a big supermarket open next door? Those questions **are** fundamental analysis. You are studying the business before deciding if the price is sensible.
The three questions

items: **Is it a good business?** Does it earn a healthy profit on the money invested in it, year after year?
**Is it safe?** Can it survive a bad year without being crushed by debt?
**Is the price reasonable?** Are you paying a fair rate for what it earns and how fast it can grow?

blocks.x: A great business bought at a very high price can still be a poor investment. A mediocre business at a very low price can also disappoint. You are looking for **good business, safe finances, sensible price**.

head: Fundamental analysis
Technical analysis
rows: The business and its financial statements
Where might the price go next?

blocks.title: What it cannot do
blocks.x: Fundamental analysis does not tell you next week's price. Even good companies can fall in a bad market. It improves your chances over long holding periods. It never removes risk.

quiz.q: Which question belongs to fundamental analysis?
options: Did the price cross its 50-day average?
How much profit does the business earn on its capital?
quiz.why: Profit earned on invested capital describes the business itself, which is what fundamental analysis studies.

lessons.title: The three statements, explained with one shop
lessons.summary: Profit and loss, balance sheet and cash flow, built from Ravi's shop. Learn why a profitable business can run short of cash.

blocks.x: Every company reports three statements. Each answers a different question. We will build all three for Ravi's shop (amounts in ₹ lakh; 1 lakh = 100,000).

head: Statement
Think of it as
Question it answers
Covers
rows: Did the business earn a profit this year?
What does it own and owe, today?
Where did the cash come from and go?

blocks.x: Day one: the starting balance sheet
Ravi invests ₹5 lakh of his own money and borrows ₹3 lakh from a bank. He buys shelves and fittings for ₹3 lakh, stocks goods worth ₹4 lakh and keeps ₹1 lakh in cash.

blocks.title: The rule that never breaks
blocks.x: **What the business owns (assets) = what it owes (liabilities) + what belongs to the owners (equity).** Both sides are always equal because every rupee the business holds came from somewhere.
Statement 1: the year's profit and loss

head: Line
₹ lakh
Plain meaning
rows: What Ravi paid for the items he sold
Profit from the shop's day-to-day work
Fittings wear out: ₹3 lakh spread over 10 years. No cash leaves

blocks.x: The surprise: profit ₹2 lakh, but cash went down

During the year Ravi sold ₹2 lakh of goods on credit (customers promised to pay later), bought ₹1 lakh of extra stock, and his supplier gave him ₹0.5 lakh of goods on credit. See what that does to cash:
The year-end balance sheet

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.x: The shop made a profit but has less cash than before, because money got stuck in stock and unpaid bills. Many real companies get into trouble exactly like this. **Profit is an accounting opinion. Cash is a fact.** That is why we always read all three statements together.
How they connect

items: Net profit (P&L) is added to equity (balance sheet): 5.0 + 2.0 = 7.0.
Depreciation lowers the value of fittings (balance sheet) and is also a cost (P&L).
Closing cash on the cash flow statement equals cash on the balance sheet: 0.8.

quiz.q: A shop owns ₹12 lakh of assets and owes ₹5 lakh. What is the owner's equity?
quiz.why: Assets = liabilities + equity, so equity = 12 − 5 = ₹7 lakh.

quiz.q: Why did Ravi's cash fall even though he earned ₹2 lakh profit?
options: Cash got tied up in unpaid customer bills and extra stock
quiz.why: Credit sales and extra stock consumed cash. Profit counts a sale when made, but cash arrives only when customers pay.

lessons.title: Where the numbers come from, and Indian basics
lessons.summary: Financial year, units, consolidated vs standalone, and the documents companies file.

blocks.x: Everything on a stock website comes from documents a company must file with the exchanges. Knowing the basics prevents the most common beginner mistakes.

items: **Financial year (FY):** April to March. FY25 means April 2024 to March 2025.
**Quarterly results:** published every 3 months. The year is the sum of four quarters.
**TTM (trailing twelve months):** the latest four quarters added together, fresher than the last full year.
**Units:** usually ₹ crore. 1 crore = 100 lakh = 10 million. Always check before comparing.
**Consolidated:** the parent plus all its subsidiaries together. Use this by default.
**Standalone:** the parent company alone. A useful cross-check.

head: Document
What it tells you
How often
rows: Audited statements, management discussion, notes, auditor's opinion
Sales and profit for the quarter
Who owns the company: promoters, FIIs, DIIs, public

blocks.title: Promoters, FIIs and DIIs
blocks.x: **Promoters** founded or control the company. **FIIs/FPIs** are foreign investors. **DIIs** are Indian institutions such as mutual funds and insurers. Their stakes, and whether promoters have **pledged** shares as loan security, are often read as signals of confidence or stress.

blocks.title: On TradeEdge
blocks.x: Open any stock in FinSight to see the P&L, Balance Sheet, Cash Flow and Ratios tabs, plus Shareholding and Documents for the original filings.

quiz.q: A company reports FY26 results. Which months does that cover?
quiz.why: The Indian financial year runs April to March and is named after the year in which it ends.

lessons.title: The P&L, one line at a time
lessons.summary: Follow a rupee from sales down to net profit, and learn why there are five different 'profits'.

blocks.x: The Profit & Loss statement (P&L, also called the income statement) covers a **period**, such as a quarter or a year. It starts with total sales at the top and subtracts costs layer by layer until only the owners' profit remains. Each layer answers a different question, which is why you will meet several different profit numbers.

blocks.caption: Ravi's shop, year one, ₹ lakh
head: Line
₹ lakh
Plain meaning
rows: Everything customers bought, the top line
What Ravi paid for the items he sold
Left after paying for the goods
Fittings wearing out. No cash leaves
What is left before the taxman
The owners' profit, the bottom line

blocks.x: Why five profits instead of one?

head: Profit
Answers
If it is weak
rows: Does what I sell earn enough over its cost?
Pricing or buying costs are the problem
Does the core business earn money?
Is it still profitable after assets wear out?
Is it still profitable after paying lenders?
What is finally left for owners?
Tax or a combination of the above

blocks.label: How the lines connect
blocks.expr:
Gross profit = Sales − Cost of goods
EBITDA = Gross profit − Running costs
EBIT = EBITDA − Depreciation
PBT = EBIT − Interest
PAT = PBT − Tax
blocks.note: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset over its life. Ravi's ₹3 lakh fittings over 10 years is ₹0.30 lakh a year.

blocks.x: What a real company's P&L adds

items: **Revenue from operations** is sales. **Other income** is extra money such as interest on deposits or dividends. It is not from the main business.
**Raw material consumed**, **employee benefit expense**, **other expenses**, **finance costs** and **depreciation and amortisation** are the names you will see for costs.
**Exceptional items** are one-off gains or losses, such as selling a factory. They distort a single year's profit.
**Minority interest:** if the company owns only part of a subsidiary, the outside owners' share of profit is carved out. The rest belongs to the parent's shareholders.
**EPS (earnings per share)** is PAT divided by number of shares. Ravi: ₹2 lakh ÷ 5 lakh shares = ₹0.40 per share.

blocks.title: In plain words
blocks.x: The P&L tells you how much money a business keeps from each rupee of sales. Always ask two things: how big is each profit, and which line is moving it?

quiz.q: Ravi's EBIT is ₹2.70 lakh and interest is ₹0.36 lakh. What is profit before tax?
quiz.why: PBT = EBIT − interest = 2.70 − 0.36 = ₹2.34 lakh.

quiz.q: Which cost reduces profit but does not take cash out of the business this year?
quiz.why: Depreciation is the yearly share of an asset bought earlier. The cash left when the asset was bought.

lessons.title: Reading a P&L: growth, margins and quality
lessons.summary: Turn a table of numbers into a judgement: is this business growing, profitable and honest?

blocks.x: Reading a P&L means comparing numbers, not admiring them. Always compare **across years**, **across quarters** and **against similar companies**. Here is Ravi's second year next to the first:
1. Growth: how fast, and for how long?
One good year proves little. Look at 5 to 10 years of sales and profit. Prefer growth that comes from **selling more** over growth from only raising prices or a single big order.

blocks.label: CAGR (smoothed yearly growth)
blocks.expr: CAGR = (End value ÷ Start value)^(1 ÷ years) − 1
blocks.note: Sales grow from 600 to 1,200 in 5 years: 2^(0.2) − 1 = 14.9% a year.

blocks.x: 2. Margins: how much of each rupee is kept

items: Steady or rising margins suggest the business can hold its prices and control costs.
Falling margins while sales grow can mean growth is being bought with discounts.
Compare margins only with companies in the **same industry**.

blocks.x: 3. Operating leverage: why profit can grow faster than sales

Sales grew 25% but EBITDA grew 30%. Why? Running costs (rent, salaries) rose only 20% because a shop's rent does not rise with every extra sale. When costs are mostly fixed, extra sales fall through to profit. The reverse is also true: a small fall in sales can hit profit hard.
4. Quality of profit: is it real and repeatable?

items: **Other income** forming a big share of PBT means the main business is weaker than it looks.
**Exceptional items** inflate or hide the true earning power. Mentally strip them out.
A sudden fall in the **tax rate** can lift profit once. Ask if it will last.
Profit growth caused only by **cheaper debt** is fragile.
Check **cash flow**: profit that never arrives as cash is a warning.

blocks.x: 5. Quarterly results

items: Compare **YoY** (this quarter vs the same quarter last year). This removes festive or seasonal effects.
Use **QoQ** (vs the previous quarter) only for businesses without seasons.
**TTM** (last 4 quarters added up) gives a fresher view than the last full year.

blocks.title: P&L red flags
blocks.x: Sales growing while operating cash flow falls. Profit rising only because of other income or lower tax. Gross margin shrinking for several quarters. Frequent "one-time" items that keep recurring.

quiz.q: Sales rise 10% but profit rises 25%. What is the most likely reason?
options: Fixed costs did not rise, so extra sales fell through to profit
quiz.why: When many costs are fixed, extra sales add profit faster than sales grow. This is operating leverage.

quiz.q: Why prefer YoY to QoQ for a business that sells more during festivals?
options: YoY compares the same season, removing the festive effect
quiz.why: Comparing the same quarter across years keeps seasonality out of the comparison.

quiz.q: Sales rise from 500 to 800 in 4 years. About how much is CAGR?

lessons.title: Fixed and variable costs, and break-even
lessons.summary: Find the sales a business needs just to avoid a loss, and how far sales can fall before it hurts.

blocks.x: Some costs rise with every sale, such as the goods Ravi buys to resell. These are **variable costs**. Others stay the same whether he sells a little or a lot, such as rent, salaries, depreciation and loan interest. These are **fixed costs**. Splitting costs this way explains how a business really behaves when sales change.

blocks.label: Contribution margin and break-even sales
blocks.expr:
Contribution margin = Contribution ÷ Sales = 6.0 ÷ 24 = 25%
Fixed costs = 3.0 + 0.3 + 0.36 = 3.66
Break-even sales = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution margin
                 = 3.66 ÷ 0.25 = ₹14.64 lakh
blocks.note: Every ₹100 of sales leaves ₹25 to pay the fixed costs. Ravi must sell about ₹14.6 lakh just to cover them. Beyond that, each ₹100 adds ₹25 of profit.

blocks.label: Margin of safety: how far can sales fall?
blocks.expr:
(Actual sales − Break-even sales) ÷ Actual sales
= (24.0 − 14.64) ÷ 24 = 39%
blocks.note: Ravi's sales can fall by about 39% before he makes a loss. A thin margin of safety means a business is fragile.

blocks.title: In plain words
blocks.x: Break-even is the sales level where profit is exactly zero. The higher a company's fixed costs, the more it must sell before it earns anything. Airlines, hotels, steel plants and telecom firms carry large fixed costs, so their profits swing sharply with sales.

blocks.title: Limits
blocks.x: Costs are rarely perfectly fixed or variable. Over long periods, a business can add a shop or a factory and its fixed costs step up. Treat break-even as a good approximation for a normal range of sales.

quiz.q: Fixed costs are ₹40 lakh and the contribution margin is 20%. What are the break-even sales?
quiz.why: Break-even sales = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin = 40 ÷ 0.20 = ₹200 lakh.

quiz.q: Which cost is fixed for a shop?
quiz.why: Rent stays the same however much is sold. The other costs rise with sales.

lessons.title: How stock changes the profit you see
lessons.summary: The cost of goods sold depends on closing stock, so the stock count can raise or lower reported profit.

blocks.x: A shop does not charge all the goods it bought to the P&L. It charges only the goods it **sold**. The rest is still sitting on the shelf as stock, which is an asset. So the cost of goods sold depends on how the unsold stock is valued.

blocks.label: Cost of goods sold
blocks.expr:
COGS = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock
     = 4.0 + 19.0 − 5.0 = 18.0
blocks.note: Ravi began with 4.0 of stock, bought 19.0 during the year, and ended with 5.0 unsold. So 18.0 was the cost of what he sold.

blocks.x: Why the closing stock matters

Counting more stock, or valuing it at too high a price, raises profit without any extra sale. Slow-moving or damaged goods that should be written down are a common source of this. The reverse can also happen: a company may understate stock in a good year to push some profit into the next.
What to check as an analyst

items: **Inventory days** rising steadily for several years, especially while sales are flat.
Inventory growing **faster than sales**.
Gross margin that looks unusually good while cash from operations is weak.
Notes to accounts about **write-downs** or a change in how stock is valued.

blocks.title: Why this ties to cash
blocks.x: Money spent on stock that has not sold is gone from the bank but has not yet hit the P&L. So rising stock can raise profit and lower cash at the same time. Always read stock together with the cash flow statement.

quiz.q: Opening stock 10, purchases 50, closing stock 12. What is COGS?
If closing stock is overstated, what happens to reported profit?
quiz.why: Higher closing stock lowers COGS, so profit looks higher without any extra sale.

lessons.title: Operating leverage, financial leverage and borrowing
lessons.summary: How fixed costs and debt multiply the effect of a change in sales on profit, in both directions.

blocks.x: Fixed costs and borrowed money both act like a lever. A small push on sales moves profit by a much larger amount. A lever lifts when sales rise and drops just as hard when they fall.
1. Operating leverage: the effect of fixed operating costs

blocks.label: Degree of operating leverage (DOL)
blocks.expr: DOL = Contribution ÷ EBIT = 6.0 ÷ 2.7 = 2.2
blocks.note: If sales rise 10%, contribution rises 0.6 and EBIT goes from 2.7 to 3.3. That is a 22% rise. Sales up 10%, operating profit up about 22%.

blocks.x: 2. Financial leverage: the effect of interest

blocks.label: Degree of financial leverage (DFL)
blocks.expr: DFL = EBIT ÷ Profit before tax = 2.7 ÷ 2.34 = 1.15
blocks.note: Interest is a fixed charge paid before owners get anything. The more debt, the higher this number.

blocks.x: 3. Both together

blocks.label: Combined leverage
blocks.expr: DOL × DFL = 2.2 × 1.15 = about 2.6
blocks.note: Sales up 10% takes profit before tax from 2.34 to 2.94, which is up 25.6%. Sales down 10% would cut it by the same amount. Check: 2.34 − 0.6 = 1.74, a fall of 25.6%.

blocks.x: Why borrowing can help owners

Ravi borrows ₹3 lakh at 12% and the business earns 27% on all its capital (ROCE). He pays 12% on the loan but earns 27% on that borrowed money, and the 15-point gap goes to Ravi as extra profit. That lifts his return on equity. This is called **trading on equity**.

blocks.title: It cuts both ways
blocks.x: If the business earned only 8% while the loan costs 12%, borrowing would reduce the owners' return. Interest must be paid even in a bad year. Companies with high fixed costs **and** high debt are the most fragile. This is why analysts check interest cover and debt levels beside margins.

quiz.q: Contribution is ₹8 crore and EBIT is ₹2 crore. What is the degree of operating leverage?
quiz.why: DOL = 8 ÷ 2 = 4. A 10% rise in sales lifts operating profit by about 40%.

quiz.q: Why can heavy borrowing be dangerous in a downturn?
options: Interest must be paid even when profit falls
quiz.why: Interest is a fixed charge. When profit shrinks, the fixed interest takes a bigger bite out of what is left.

lessons.title: The balance sheet, line by line
lessons.summary: Every line explained in plain words, using Ravi's shop at the end of year one.

blocks.x: A balance sheet is a photograph taken on one day (usually 31 March). It lists everything the business **owns** (assets) on one side, and on the other side **where the money to buy those things came from**: from lenders (liabilities) or from the owners (equity).

blocks.label: The one rule
blocks.expr: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
blocks.note: Both sides always match, because every rupee the business holds came from someone. If you know any two, you can find the third.

blocks.x: What each line means

head: Line
Plain meaning
What to notice
rows: Things used for years: machinery, buildings, fittings (shown after depreciation)
Big for factories, small for software firms
A factory or project still being built
If it stays high for years, the project may be stuck
Shares or deposits the company holds in other entities
Growing faster than sales is a warning
Owner's money plus profits kept in the business
Should grow steadily if profits are retained
Free credit, up to a point

blocks.x: Current and non-current

**Current** means due or turning into cash within 12 months (stock, receivables, cash, payables). **Non-current** means longer-lasting (fittings, long-term loans). This split tells you whether the company can pay its near-term bills.

blocks.title: In plain words
blocks.x: Equity is the part of the business that truly belongs to the owners. Equity = assets − liabilities. For Ravi: 10.5 − 3.5 = **7.0**.

quiz.q: A company has assets of ₹20 crore and liabilities of ₹12 crore. What is equity?
quiz.why: Equity = assets − liabilities = 20 − 12 = ₹8 crore.

quiz.q: Which item is a liability?
quiz.why: A loan is money the business owes. The others are things it owns.

lessons.title: How to judge a balance sheet
lessons.summary: Five simple questions that reveal whether a company is strong, stretched or hiding trouble.

blocks.x: You do not need advanced maths. Ask five questions and use Ravi's shop to see how each answer is worked out.
1. Is the owners' money growing?

Equity should rise roughly by the profit kept each year. Ravi's equity went from 5.0 to 7.0 because he kept the whole ₹2 lakh profit. If profit is high but equity barely moves, ask where the money went: dividends, buybacks, or losses elsewhere.
2. How much debt, compared with owners' money?

blocks.label: Debt to equity
blocks.expr: Debt ÷ Equity = 3.0 ÷ 7.0 = 0.43
blocks.note: Below 1 is generally comfortable for most businesses, meaning owners fund more than lenders. Banks and NBFCs are different because lending with borrowed money is their business.

blocks.x: 3. Can it pay the bills due soon?

blocks.label: Current ratio
blocks.expr: Current assets ÷ Current liabilities
blocks.note: Ravi: current assets 7.8 (stock 5.0 + customers 2.0 + cash 0.8) against current liabilities 0.5 = 15.6. Very comfortable. Below 1 means short-term stress.

blocks.x: 4. How long is money stuck?
These "days" ratios show how many days of sales or costs are locked up.

head: Measure
Formula
Ravi's shop
Meaning
rows: Customers take a month to pay

blocks.x: Ravi could free up cash by selling stock faster and asking suppliers for longer credit. Falling days over time show good discipline. Rising days mean cash is getting stuck.
5. Anything hiding in the notes?

items: **Contingent liabilities:** possible future payments, such as tax disputes or guarantees, listed in the notes. Large ones compared with equity are risky.
**Loans to related companies:** money lent to the promoter's other businesses.
**Goodwill:** the premium paid when buying another company. It can be written off.

blocks.title: Red flags
blocks.x: Receivables growing much faster than sales. Inventory piling up. Borrowing heavily while holding lots of cash. Large loans to related parties. Contingent liabilities that rival equity.

quiz.q: Sales rise 10% but receivables rise 50%. What should you suspect?
options: Customers are paying slower, or sales were pushed on easy credit
quiz.why: Receivables outrunning sales means more money is owed and not yet collected, a classic warning sign.

quiz.q: Debt is ₹30 crore and equity is ₹60 crore. Debt to equity is?
quiz.why: 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5. Owners fund twice as much as lenders.

lessons.title: Who funded what, and what does the money cost?
lessons.summary: Every rupee on a balance sheet has a price. A business creates value only when its assets earn more than that price.

blocks.x: Money is never free. A bank wants interest. Owners expect a return too, or they would have kept their money elsewhere. The right-hand side of the balance sheet tells you where the money came from. The left-hand side tells you what it was used for. A healthy business earns more from its assets than it pays for the funds that bought them.

blocks.caption: Ravi's shop, year end, ₹ lakh
head: Source of funds
₹ lakh
Cost
Why
rows: The return Ravi expects for taking the risk

blocks.label: Average cost of the money used
blocks.note: This is called the weighted average cost of capital (WACC). The 15% for owners is an assumption: owners' cost is not written on any statement, it is the return they could reasonably expect for the risk.

blocks.x: The test: do the assets earn more than the money costs?

Ravi's shop earns 27% (ROCE) on money that costs about 14.1%. The gap of roughly 13 percentage points is the value he creates. If ROCE were 10%, the shop would be destroying value even though it shows a profit.
Idle assets: money that earns nothing

Some assets sit on the balance sheet but add no profit: dead stock nobody buys, old receivables that will never be collected, a half-built project, cash lying idle. Suppose ₹1 lakh of Ravi's stock is dead. That money costs about 14.1%, so the shop loses roughly ₹0.14 lakh a year for nothing.

blocks.label: Making assets work harder
blocks.expr: Asset turnover = Sales ÷ Total assets = 24 ÷ 10.5 = 2.29
blocks.note: Sell more using the same assets, or release money from idle assets, and returns rise without borrowing more.

blocks.title: In plain words
blocks.x: Ask two questions of any balance sheet: what is each rupee costing, and what is it earning? Growth only helps when the second answer is larger than the first.

quiz.q: A company earns 9% ROCE on funds that cost 12%. What does this mean?
options: It destroys value even if it shows a profit
quiz.why: Earning less than the cost of the money used means the owners would have done better elsewhere.

quiz.q: Which of these is an idle asset?
options: Dead stock that no one buys
A shop in a busy market
quiz.why: Dead stock ties up money but produces no sales or profit.

lessons.title: Working capital and the short-term funding trap
lessons.summary: How much money does daily operation need, and why long-term assets must be paid for with long-term money.

blocks.x: Working capital is the money that keeps daily business moving: stock on the shelf and bills customers owe, less the bills the shop owes its suppliers. It is a number you can compute straight from the balance sheet.

blocks.label: Net working capital
blocks.expr:
Current assets − Current liabilities
= (5.0 + 2.0 + 0.8) − 0.5 = 7.3 lakh
blocks.note: Ravi has ₹7.3 lakh working in daily operations. A larger number means more money is stuck in the cycle of buying, selling and collecting.

blocks.x: A second way to see the same number

blocks.label: Funding view
blocks.expr:
Net working capital = Long-term funds − Long-term assets
= (7.0 + 3.0) − 2.7 = 7.3 lakh
blocks.note: Same answer. Long-term money that is not locked in fittings and machines is what funds the day-to-day business.

blocks.x: The trap: short-term money in a long-term asset

Suppose Ravi buys a ₹2 lakh freezer using a 6-month loan. The freezer earns an extra ₹0.8 lakh a year, so it needs about 2.5 years to pay itself back. After 6 months the bank wants ₹2 lakh. Ravi must take it from other cash or borrow again. If he cannot, he has a crisis even though the freezer is a good purchase.

head: Match
Use
Why
rows: They repay slowly, so funding should last as long
Short-term bank credit and supplier credit
It turns into cash within months

blocks.x: Why paying suppliers late backfires

Delaying supplier payments looks like free money. But suppliers notice. They may cut credit, raise prices or demand cash upfront, and banks hear about it too. A business whose lenders and suppliers stop trusting it can run short of cash even if it is profitable. Rising payable days with a falling cash balance is worth investigating.

blocks.title: What to check
blocks.x: Short-term borrowings rising while fixed assets or CWIP also rise. Current ratio falling below 1. Payable days stretching year after year. A company that keeps refinancing short-term loans to fund long-term projects.

quiz.q: Current assets are ₹60 crore and current liabilities are ₹25 crore. What is net working capital?
Which funding fits a new factory best?
quiz.why: A factory pays back over many years, so it needs funds that stay for as long.

lessons.title: Owner or lender: the same balance sheet, two views
lessons.summary: A balance sheet that pleases a lender may bore an owner. Learn which numbers each one watches.

blocks.x: A bank that lends Ravi ₹3 lakh gets a fixed interest and the loan back. It does not share in extra profit. So it wants **safety**. An owner shares in the profit and also takes the first loss. So an owner wants **returns and growth**. They look at the same sheet but ask different questions.

head: Lender asks
Owner asks
rows: Will I be repaid in full and on time?
How much do I earn on my money, and will it grow?
Debt/equity, interest cover, asset cover, current ratio
ROE, ROCE, growth, free cash flow
Low debt, steady cash, strong assets
High returns, growth, sensible use of debt

blocks.label: Asset cover: how safe is the lender?
blocks.expr: Total assets ÷ Borrowings = 10.5 ÷ 3.0 = 3.5
blocks.note: The shop owns 3.5 times what it owes the bank. If the business failed and assets sold for even half their value, the loan would still be covered.

blocks.x: Ravi's numbers: debt/equity 0.43, interest cover 7.5, asset cover 3.5. A lender would be comfortable. An owner sees ROE of 28.6% and would be happy too, but would ask whether the ₹5 lakh stock and ₹2 lakh receivables could be turned into cash faster.
A well-built balance sheet looks like this

items: Equity growing from retained profit rather than shrinking.
Debt that is modest compared with equity and comfortably covered by profit.
Long-term assets funded by long-term money.
Stock and receivables growing no faster than sales.
Few idle or doubtful assets.
Cash flow from operations that supports repayment and dividends.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.x: Always ask whose view you are taking. A very safe company with low returns may suit a lender, not an investor who wants growth. A very aggressive one may thrill an owner, but terrify a lender.

quiz.q: Total assets are ₹90 crore and borrowings are ₹30 crore. What is asset cover?
quiz.why: 90 ÷ 30 = 3.0, so the lender's loan is covered three times over.

quiz.q: Which number matters most to a lender?
quiz.why: Interest cover shows how comfortably profit pays the interest on the loan.

lessons.title: The cash flow statement in three buckets
lessons.summary: Operating, investing and financing: where cash comes from and where it goes.

blocks.x: Remember Ravi: ₹2 lakh profit, yet cash fell. The cash flow statement explains why. It is like a bank passbook for the business and it sorts every movement of cash into three buckets.

head: Bucket
Question it answers
Examples
Healthy sign
rows: Does the main business make cash?
Cash from customers minus cash paid to suppliers, staff and tax
What is it spending on the future?
Usually negative for a growing firm
How is it funded and rewarded?
Taking or repaying loans, issuing shares, paying dividends and interest

blocks.x: Year one: why profit became less cash

head: Item
₹ lakh
Why
rows: Reduced profit but no cash left
Cash spent, not yet a cost

blocks.x: Year two: customers paid, Ravi invests

blocks.label: Free cash flow (FCF)
blocks.expr:
FCF = Cash from operations − Capex
      = 3.0 − 2.0 = 1.0
blocks.note: FCF is the cash left after keeping the business running and growing. It is what can safely go to lenders and owners. **Capex** means money spent on long-lasting assets.

blocks.title: In plain words
blocks.x: Profit says what the business earned. Cash flow says what actually landed in the bank. Over several years, a good business turns most of its profit into cash.

quiz.q: Cash from operations is ₹5 crore and capex is ₹3 crore. What is free cash flow?
quiz.why: FCF = CFO − capex = 5 − 3 = ₹2 crore.

quiz.q: Buying a new machine appears in which bucket?
quiz.why: Spending on long-lasting assets is an investing activity.

lessons.title: Reading cash flow: patterns and red flags
lessons.summary: Does profit become cash, and what do the three buckets say about the company's stage?

blocks.x: 1. Does profit become cash?

blocks.label: Cash conversion
blocks.expr: CFO ÷ Net profit   (and CFO ÷ EBITDA)
blocks.note: Look at the total of 4 to 5 years, not one year. Healthy businesses often show CFO near or above profit, and CFO/EBITDA of roughly 60 to 80% or more. A persistent big gap is the biggest red flag. Rules of thumb vary by industry.

blocks.x: 2. What the three buckets say together

head: CFO
CFI
CFF
Plain reading
rows: Mature and healthy: earns cash, invests, repays debt, pays dividends
Growing fast: also borrowing or raising money. Fine if returns justify it
Selling assets to repay debt. Check if it is sustainable
Burning cash and borrowing. Risky unless it is an early-stage business
Possible distress: selling assets and borrowing to run the business

blocks.x: 3. Is capex for growth or just upkeep?

items: Capex well above depreciation usually means expansion. Check that sales and returns rise afterwards.
Capex far below depreciation for years can mean machines are ageing and under-investment.

blocks.x: 4. How good is free cash flow?

items: Add up FCF over 5 years. Mostly positive is a good sign.
**FCF yield** = FCF ÷ market cap. It shows cash earned per rupee you pay for the company.
See how FCF is used: repaying debt, dividends, or smart investments are better than idle cash or wasteful acquisitions.

blocks.title: Cash flow red flags
blocks.x: Profit rising while cash from operations falls. CFO far below profit for many years. Dividends paid with borrowed money. Large unexplained "other" adjustments. Negative free cash flow year after year in a mature business.

quiz.q: Positive CFO, negative CFI and negative CFF most likely describes…
quiz.why: It earns cash, invests in growth, and repays debt or pays owners.

quiz.q: Why can profit rise while CFO falls?
options: Money got stuck in receivables and stock
quiz.why: If customers pay slowly or stock piles up, profit is recorded but cash has not arrived.

lessons.title: Sources and uses: reading the year as a story
lessons.summary: Compare two balance sheets to see where the year's money came from and where it went.

blocks.x: Put Ravi's opening balance sheet next to his closing one. Every change tells you something. A rise in a liability or in equity means money **came in** (a source). A rise in an asset means money **was used** (a use). A fall works the other way round.

The story is clear. Ravi earned and kept ₹2 lakh. That plus supplier credit and a little spare cash was swallowed by stock and unpaid customer bills. Nothing was spent on new assets and no new loan was taken.
What to ask of any sources-and-uses picture

items: Is the main source **profit and cash from operations**, or fresh borrowing and share issues?
Are the uses **productive** (assets that earn) or a drain (unpaid bills, piling stock)?
Is **short-term money** financing **long-term uses**? That is a warning sign.
Is the business **using up its cash balance** to survive?

blocks.title: In plain words
blocks.x: A rise in an asset eats cash. A rise in a liability or equity brings cash. If you can classify each change, you can reconstruct the cash flow statement from two balance sheets and one P&L.

quiz.q: Receivables rise by ₹5 crore during the year. In the sources-and-uses view, this is a…
quiz.why: Money owed by customers is cash not yet received, so it uses up funds.

quiz.q: Supplier credit rises by ₹2 crore. This is a…
quiz.why: The company got goods without paying yet, so supplier credit is a source of funds.

lessons.title: Two ways to build operating cash flow
lessons.summary: Start from profit (indirect) or from cash actually collected and paid (direct). Both give the same answer.

blocks.x: You have seen the **indirect method**: start with profit, add back non-cash costs and adjust for working capital. There is also a **direct method**: simply add up cash actually received and cash actually paid. Most companies publish the indirect version, but the direct one is easier to picture.

blocks.caption: Ravi's year one, direct method, ₹ lakh
head: Item
How it is worked out
₹ lakh

blocks.x: It matches the indirect method exactly: −0.2. Two roads, one destination. Both show that Ravi's customers had not paid ₹2 lakh and he had not yet paid ₹0.5 lakh, which together with the extra stock turned profit into negative cash.

blocks.title: The cash trail to remember
blocks.x: Cash collected = Sales − increase in receivables. Cash paid to suppliers = Purchases − increase in payables. Purchases = COGS + increase in stock (here 18.0 + 1.0 = 19.0).

blocks.title: Where interest sits
blocks.x: Some Indian companies report interest paid under financing rather than operating activities. Ravi's table puts it in operating, matching his profit-based version. Check the policy when comparing two companies' operating cash flow.

quiz.q: Sales are ₹100 crore and receivables rose by ₹15 crore. How much cash was collected from customers?
quiz.why: Cash collected = sales − rise in receivables = 100 − 15 = ₹85 crore.

quiz.q: COGS is 60 and stock rose by 5. What were the purchases?
quiz.why: Purchases = COGS + rise in stock = 60 + 5 = 65.

lessons.title: Free cash flow, dividends and the cash cost of growth
lessons.summary: Growth uses cash before it earns any. See what a business can afford to pay out and how fast it can grow.

blocks.x: Year two for Ravi: customers paid, so cash from operations was ₹3.0 lakh. He spent ₹2.0 lakh on a freezer, repaid ₹0.5 lakh of the loan, and paid ₹0.5 lakh as dividend.

blocks.label: Free cash flow and how it was used
blocks.expr:
FCF = CFO − Capex = 3.0 − 2.0 = 1.0
Used: loan repayment 0.5 + dividend 0.5 = 1.0
blocks.note: Everything he paid out came from the business itself, with no fresh borrowing. That is a sign of comfort.

blocks.x: A dividend test

head: Situation
Reading
rows: Dividend smaller than free cash flow
Comfortable. Cash is left over to repay debt or reinvest
Dividend about equal to free cash flow
Fine if steady. Little room for surprises
Dividend larger than free cash flow for years
Funded by borrowing or past cash. Not sustainable

blocks.x: Growth needs cash before it earns cash

Ravi's money tied up in daily operations is about 30% of sales (7.3 ÷ 24). If sales grow by ₹6 lakh, he needs roughly ₹1.8 lakh more working capital before he sees any benefit. That is on top of any new shop or freezer. A fast-growing business can be profitable and still run short of cash.

head: Growth funded by
Meaning
Risk
rows: Repeated new debt or share issues

blocks.label: A quick check
blocks.expr: Cumulative FCF over 5 years vs dividends and buybacks paid
blocks.note: If dividends and buybacks regularly exceed free cash flow, the company is paying out money it does not have.

blocks.title: Red flags
blocks.x: Profit and sales surging while cash from operations lags. Dividends paid while borrowing rises. Free cash flow negative year after year with no clear payoff in sales or returns.

quiz.q: CFO is ₹50 crore, capex is ₹30 crore and dividends are ₹25 crore. What does this suggest?
options: Dividends exceed free cash flow, so the gap needs outside money
quiz.why: FCF = 50 − 30 = 20, but dividends are 25. The ₹5 crore gap must come from cash reserves or borrowing.

quiz.q: Why can a fast-growing profitable company still run short of cash?
options: Growth needs working capital before it brings cash
Banks stop lending to profitable firms
quiz.why: More sales mean more stock and receivables, which absorb cash before customers pay.

lessons.title: How the three statements link
lessons.summary: Follow one sale through the P&L, the balance sheet and the cash flow.

blocks.x: The P&L shows performance over a period, the balance sheet shows position on a date, and the cash flow statement explains how cash moved between two balance sheets. They must agree with each other.
Follow a ₹100 credit sale

items: **P&L:** sales rise by 100. If the goods cost 60, profit rises by 40 (before other costs).
**Balance sheet:** receivables rise by 100 (customer owes) and stock falls by 60.
**Cash flow:** no cash has arrived, so cash from operations is lower than profit.
**Later:** the customer pays. Receivables fall by 100, cash rises by 100, and cash flow catches up.

head: Link
How it connects
Ravi's shop
rows: Profit kept (after dividends) is added to equity
Capex adds assets, depreciation reduces them and hits profit
Credit sales sit as receivables until paid
More debt means more interest in the P&L
Opening cash + net change = closing cash

blocks.title: A habit worth building
blocks.x: When a profit number surprises you, check the other two statements. Receivables, stock, capex, debt and other income usually explain it.
Next, in the Ratios track, we turn these statements into comparable numbers like margins, ROE and P/E, so you can compare companies of any size.

quiz.q: Where does profit that is kept in the business appear on the balance sheet?
quiz.why: Retained profit is added to the owners' money, which is equity.

quiz.q: Opening cash is 4, net cash flow is −1. What is closing cash?
quiz.why: Closing cash = opening cash + net change = 4 − 1 = 3.

lessons.title: Year two, end to end: all three statements tied out
lessons.summary: Build Ravi's second year across the P&L, cash flow and balance sheet, and prove they agree.

blocks.x: Time to put everything together. In year two Ravi repays ₹0.5 lakh of the loan at the start (so interest falls to 12% on ₹2.5 lakh), buys a ₹2 lakh freezer, collects some of his old bills, builds more stock to support higher sales, and pays a ₹0.5 lakh dividend. All amounts are in ₹ lakh.

Step 2: how the working capital moved
Step 3: the cash flow statement
Step 4: the closing balance sheet

head: Check
Result
rows: Both sides of the balance sheet match
Cash flow's closing cash = balance sheet cash

blocks.x: What the year adds up to

blocks.title: The story
blocks.x: Year one: profitable but cash-poor, because money was stuck in stock and bills. Year two: collections improved, the shop grew, invested in a freezer, cut debt, paid a dividend, and held its cash. The three statements told one consistent story.

quiz.q: Opening equity 7.0, profit 2.65, dividend 0.5. What is closing equity?
Why is cash from operations (3.00) higher than a plain look at profit might suggest?
options: Depreciation is added back and working capital changed only slightly
quiz.why: Profit 2.65 plus depreciation 0.50 less a small working capital outflow of 0.15 gives 3.00.

lessons.title: The statement detective: spotting errors and trouble
lessons.summary: Use the links between statements to catch mistakes, odd numbers and early warnings.

blocks.x: Because the three statements are linked, a lie or a mistake in one usually shows up as a mismatch in another. Good analysts use this like a detective uses a timeline: the pieces must fit together.

head: What you notice
Where to look
What it may mean
rows: Profit up, cash from operations down
Cash is stuck, or revenue was booked early
Fixed assets up, but capex in the cash flow is much lower
Notes on acquisitions, leases, capitalised costs
Costs were moved from the P&L into assets

blocks.x: A short routine for any company

items: Do the balance sheet sides match, and does equity move by profit less payouts?
Does cash from operations come close to profit over 3 to 5 years?
Do capex and the rise in fixed assets agree with each other?
Do stock and receivables grow no faster than sales?
Is borrowing rising while interest cover falls?
Are there large items in the notes that the headline numbers do not show?

blocks.title: A mismatch is a question, not a verdict
blocks.x: Many gaps have innocent explanations such as acquisitions, currency changes or reclassifications. Treat them as prompts to read the notes and the management discussion. Never assume wrongdoing from numbers alone.

quiz.q: A company's profit rose 30%, but its cash from operations fell for the third year. Where do you look first?
quiz.why: A growing gap between profit and cash is most often explained by money stuck in working capital.

quiz.q: Opening equity 50, profit 10, dividend 4, closing equity 70. What should you ask?
options: Why is closing equity 14 higher than profit less dividends explain?
quiz.why: Expected closing equity = 50 + 10 − 4 = 56. The extra 14 needs an explanation, such as new shares issued or revaluation.

quiz.q: Fixed assets rose by ₹80 crore but cash flow shows capex of only ₹20 crore. What might explain this?
options: Assets bought through acquisitions, leases or costs moved into assets
quiz.why: Assets can enter the balance sheet without cash capex, through acquisitions, leases or capitalised costs. Check the notes.

lessons.title: What is a ratio, and why use it?
lessons.summary: Ratios let you compare a tiny shop with a giant company on equal terms.

blocks.x: Student A scores 450 marks. Student B scores 90%. Who did better? You cannot tell until you know the total marks. Dividing one number by another, to make things comparable, is what a **ratio** does. In investing, a profit of ₹500 crore means little until you divide it by the sales, the capital or the price paid.

Ravi's shop earns ₹2 lakh. A large company earns ₹2,000 crore. Which is better run? Compare **profit ÷ sales**: Ravi keeps 8.3 paise per rupee of sales. If the large company keeps 12 paise, it is the stronger earner, whatever the size.

head: Family
Question in plain words
Examples
rows: What am I paying for it?
Can it pay bills and use money well?

blocks.x: Five rules for using ratios

items: **Compare with similar companies.** A bank and a software firm are not comparable.
**Look at 5 to 10 years**, not one year.
**Know the definition.** Websites calculate some ratios slightly differently.
**Combine ratios.** A low P/E on falling profits is a trap. A high ROE built on heavy debt is fragile.
**Treat thresholds as rough guides.** They are starting points for questions, not verdicts.

blocks.title: Ravi's numbers used in this track
blocks.x: Sales 24.0, cost of goods 18.0, EBITDA 3.0, EBIT 2.7, interest 0.36, profit 2.0, equity 7.0, loan 3.0, total assets 10.5, cash 0.8 (all ₹ lakh). Shares: 5 lakh, price ₹8.

quiz.q: Why divide profit by sales before comparing two companies?
options: To remove the effect of size so they can be compared
quiz.why: A ratio puts different-sized companies on the same scale.

lessons.title: Return ratios: ROE, ROCE and ROA
lessons.summary: How much profit each rupee of capital earns, the heart of judging a good business.

blocks.x: Imagine two shops. Both earn ₹2 lakh. One needed ₹7 lakh of capital and the other ₹20 lakh. The first is clearly the better business. **Return ratios** measure profit per rupee of money put in. Businesses that earn high returns and can reinvest at those returns grow wealth over time.

blocks.label: Return on equity (ROE): profit per rupee of owners' money
blocks.expr: ROE = Net profit ÷ Equity = 2.0 ÷ 7.0 = 28.6%
blocks.note: Many investors look for ROE that stays above about 15% for years.

blocks.label: Return on capital employed (ROCE): profit per rupee of all money used
blocks.expr: ROCE = EBIT ÷ (Equity + Borrowings) = 2.7 ÷ 10.0 = 27%
blocks.note: It ignores how the business is funded, so it compares debt-heavy and debt-free firms fairly.

blocks.label: Return on assets (ROA)
blocks.expr: ROA = Net profit ÷ Total assets = 2.0 ÷ 10.5 = 19.0%
blocks.note: The key measure for banks.

blocks.x: DuPont: why is ROE high?

blocks.label: Three ingredients of ROE
blocks.expr:
ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier
    = 8.3% × 2.29 × 1.5 = 28.6%
blocks.note: Net margin = profit ÷ sales. Asset turnover = sales ÷ assets. Equity multiplier = assets ÷ equity (how much debt is used).

head: Ingredient
High means
Be careful of
rows: High ROE from debt is riskier

blocks.title: ROCE vs the cost of money
blocks.x: Growth only creates value when ROCE is **higher than the cost of the money used**. If Ravi borrows at 12% and earns 27%, growing is smart. If he earned only 8%, borrowing to grow would hurt him.

quiz.q: Two firms both have ROE of 20%. Firm A has equity multiplier 1.2, Firm B has 4. Which depends more on debt?
quiz.why: A higher equity multiplier means more assets per rupee of equity, so more borrowed money drives the return.

quiz.q: Profit is ₹30 crore and equity is ₹150 crore. ROE is?

lessons.title: Growth ratios
lessons.summary: How fast the business is growing and whether that growth is healthy.

items: **Sales growth** shows whether customers keep coming. Use CAGR over 5 to 10 years.
**EPS growth** shows growth that reaches shareholders. It can differ from profit growth if new shares are issued.
**Profit vs sales growth:** profit growing faster than sales usually means margins are widening.

blocks.label: How fast can a business grow on its own money?
blocks.expr:
Sustainable growth ≈ ROE × Retention
Retention = 1 − Dividend payout
blocks.note: ROE 20% and 25% paid as dividend: 20% × 75% = 15% a year, without borrowing or raising capital.

blocks.x: Is the growth good quality?

items: Growth with **stable or rising ROCE** is excellent.
Growth funded by rising debt with falling returns is poor quality.
A small base fools: 100% growth from ₹1 lakh is not like 20% from ₹100 crore.
Check whether growth is **organic** (own business) or **bought** through acquisitions.

blocks.label: PEG ratio: is the P/E fair for the growth?
blocks.expr: PEG = P/E ÷ Expected yearly EPS growth (%)
blocks.note: Ravi's shop: P/E 20 and 25% growth gives PEG 0.8. Near or below 1 is often seen as reasonable, but it depends on a forecast, so use it as a rough check.

quiz.q: ROE is 20% and the company pays out 25% as dividends. Roughly how fast can it grow without outside money?
quiz.why: Retention is 75%, so 20% × 0.75 = 15%.

lessons.title: Valuation ratios: what am I paying?
lessons.summary: P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA and friends, built on the idea of paying a price for a stream of profit.

blocks.x: Suppose the shop's owners value the whole business at ₹40 lakh: that is ₹8 per share across 5 lakh shares (its **market cap**). Is that cheap? Valuation ratios compare the price you pay with what you get: profit, book value, sales or cash. A great business can still be a bad purchase at too high a price.

blocks.label: Price to earnings (P/E): years of profit you pay for
blocks.expr:
P/E = Price ÷ EPS = 8 ÷ 0.40 = 20x
Earnings yield = 1 ÷ 20 = 5%
blocks.note: A P/E of 20 means you pay 20 times one year's profit. The earnings yield is the profit you get per rupee invested.

blocks.label: Price to book (P/B)
blocks.expr: P/B = Market cap ÷ Equity = 40 ÷ 7.0 = 5.7x
blocks.note: Compares the price with the owners' money on the balance sheet. Most useful for banks and asset-heavy companies.

blocks.label: Enterprise value (EV) and EV/EBITDA
blocks.expr:
EV = Market cap + Debt − Cash = 40 + 3.0 − 0.8 = 42.2
EV/EBITDA = 42.2 ÷ 3.0 = 14.1x
blocks.note: EV is the price of the whole business, including what you must also repay. It lets you compare companies with different debt.

blocks.label: Price to sales and cash yield
blocks.expr:
P/S = Market cap ÷ Sales = 40 ÷ 24 = 1.7x
FCF yield = Free cash flow ÷ Market cap = 1.0 ÷ 40 = 2.5%
blocks.note: P/S helps when profit is tiny or negative but ignores margins. FCF yield uses year two's free cash flow of 1.0.

blocks.x: Which ratio for which business?

head: Business
Best ratios
Why
rows: Peak-year P/E looks cheap, trough-year looks expensive

items: Compare with the company's **own history** and with **peers**.
A high P/E needs **high growth and returns** to be justified.
**Cheap is not undervalued.** A low P/E often reflects falling profits or poor governance (a value trap).
For cyclicals, a low P/E at peak profit can be the most dangerous time to buy.

blocks.title: On TradeEdge
blocks.x: The Nifty P/E heatmap on your dashboard shows how the market's overall P/E has moved over time. Use it to judge whether broad valuations look stretched.

quiz.q: Price is ₹300 and EPS is ₹15. What is the P/E?
Market cap 1,800, debt 250, cash 60. What is EV?
Which pair suits a private bank best?
quiz.why: A bank's value comes from the equity it holds and how much it earns on it.

lessons.title: Safety and efficiency ratios
lessons.summary: Can the company pay its debts and bills, and does it use money and assets well?

blocks.x: Leverage: how risky is the debt?

blocks.label: Debt to equity
blocks.expr: Debt ÷ Equity = 3.0 ÷ 7.0 = 0.43
blocks.note: Below 1 is usually comfortable for non-financial firms.

blocks.label: Net debt to EBITDA: years of operating profit needed to clear debt
blocks.note: Below 2 to 3 is generally comfortable. It varies by sector.

blocks.label: Interest cover: how easily profit pays the interest
blocks.expr: EBIT ÷ Interest = 2.7 ÷ 0.36 = 7.5
blocks.note: Below 2 is a warning. Ravi can pay interest 7.5 times over.

blocks.x: Liquidity: can it pay bills due soon?

blocks.label: Current and quick ratios
blocks.expr:
Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities
Quick ratio = (Current assets − Stock) ÷ Current liabilities
blocks.note: Ravi: current ratio 7.8 ÷ 0.5 = 15.6, quick ratio 2.8 ÷ 0.5 = 5.6. Below 1 means stress. Extremely high can mean idle money.

blocks.x: Efficiency: how well is money used?

blocks.label: Working-capital days
blocks.expr:
Receivable days = Receivables ÷ Sales × 365 = 30
Inventory days = Stock ÷ Cost of goods × 365 = 101
Payable days = Payables ÷ Cost of goods × 365 = 10
Cash conversion cycle = 30 + 101 − 10 = 121 days
blocks.note: Days of cash stuck in the business. Falling days over the years show better discipline.

blocks.label: Asset turnover
blocks.expr: Sales ÷ Total assets = 24 ÷ 10.5 = 2.29
blocks.note: Each rupee of assets produced ₹2.29 of sales.

blocks.x: Cash quality

blocks.label: Does profit become cash?
blocks.expr: CFO ÷ EBITDA   and   Capex ÷ Depreciation
blocks.note: Over several years, a CFO/EBITDA of roughly 60 to 80% or more shows earnings that turn into cash.

blocks.title: Banks and NBFCs
blocks.x: Skip debt/equity, current ratio and EBITDA for lenders. Use **net interest margin, gross and net NPA, capital adequacy, CASA ratio, cost-to-income, ROA and ROE** instead.

quiz.q: EBIT is ₹170 crore and interest is ₹25 crore. Interest cover is?
Which change shortens the cash conversion cycle?
quiz.why: Faster sales cut inventory days, which frees cash sooner.

lessons.title: Common-size statements: every line as a share of the whole
lessons.summary: Convert rupees into percentages to see which costs and which assets are really changing.

blocks.x: Looking at rupee amounts alone can mislead. Sales grew, so almost every cost grew too. A cleaner trick is to express each P&L line as a **percentage of sales**, and each balance sheet line as a **percentage of total assets**. This is called a common-size statement, and it makes two years or two companies directly comparable.

head: Line
Year 1

rows: Fixed costs spread over more sales
Gain came from running costs and interest

blocks.x: The percentages show why net margin rose. The cost of goods did not change as a share of sales. The gain came from fixed costs and interest taking a smaller bite.

head: Assets
Share
Funding
Share

blocks.x: Nearly half the shop's money sits in stock. That is the first place to look for improvement. Almost three-quarters of the funding is the owner's own, which signals safety.

blocks.title: Why analysts love this
blocks.x: A cost that is a rising share of sales is eating margin. An asset that is a rising share of total assets is absorbing money. Both show up in percentages long before they show up in a headline ratio.

quiz.q: Sales are ₹200 crore and raw material cost is ₹130 crore. Raw material as a percentage of sales is?
Net margin rose although cost of goods stayed 75% of sales. What most likely explained it?
options: Fixed costs and interest fell as a share of sales
quiz.why: With the largest cost fixed at 75%, the gain must have come from smaller shares of other costs such as running costs and interest.

lessons.title: Cash quality ratios: is the profit real?
lessons.summary: Turn the cash flow statement into ratios that test whether profit becomes cash and whether growth pays for itself.

blocks.x: Margins and returns can look wonderful while the bank balance shrinks. Cash quality ratios catch this. Here are Ravi's two years side by side.
How to read each one

items: **CFO ÷ EBITDA:** how much operating profit turns into cash. Roughly 60 to 80% or more over several years is healthy. Year one's negative figure was a warning, year two's 77% is good.
**CFO ÷ net profit:** near or above 1 means profit is backed by cash. A low figure for many years is a red flag.
**FCF yield:** cash left for owners per rupee of market value. Compare it with what a safe deposit would pay.
**Capex ÷ depreciation:** above 1 means the business is expanding or renewing assets. Far below 1 for years can mean it is starving the business of investment. Ravi's 4.0x reflects the freezer.
**Cash conversion cycle:** days from paying for stock to collecting from customers. Shorter is better. It fell from 121 to 102 days because customers paid faster.

blocks.label: Year-two cash conversion cycle
blocks.expr:
Receivable days = 1.5 ÷ 30 × 365 = 18
Inventory days = 5.9 ÷ 22.5 × 365 = 96
Payable days = 0.75 ÷ 22.5 × 365 = 12
Cycle = 18 + 96 − 12 = 102 days
blocks.note: Receivable days fell from 30 to 18, so the shop collects money sooner.

blocks.title: Use several years
blocks.x: One year can mislead. A big freezer purchase depresses free cash flow in one year and raises it later. Look at 5 years of cumulative free cash flow and cash conversion before drawing a conclusion.

quiz.q: EBITDA is ₹80 crore and cash from operations is ₹60 crore. What is CFO ÷ EBITDA?
quiz.why: 60 ÷ 80 = 75%, a healthy conversion.

quiz.q: A mature business shows capex far below depreciation for many years. What could this mean?
options: It may be under-investing and its assets ageing
quiz.why: Capex below depreciation for years means assets wear out faster than they are replaced.

lessons.title: Same return, different engine: comparing two companies
lessons.summary: Use margin, turnover and leverage to understand how two businesses earn similar returns in very different ways.

blocks.x: Meet Meena, who runs a discount supermarket next door to Ravi. Both shops sell ₹24 lakh a year. Meena's shop makes a thin margin on very fast-moving goods. Ravi's makes a fatter margin on slower-moving goods. Which is better?

Their returns are close, yet the engines differ. Ravi earns by **margin**: he keeps more of each rupee. Meena earns by **turnover**: she makes less per sale but sells her assets four times over. Using the DuPont split you can see both clearly. Neither is better in the abstract.
Questions to ask when comparing

items: **Which engine drives the return?** Margin-led businesses depend on pricing power. Turnover-led businesses depend on volume and efficiency.
**How much leverage is behind it?** Equal equity multipliers mean neither is borrowing more to flatter the return.
**Is the engine durable?** A margin can be competed away. A volume advantage needs scale and tight operations.
**What does the cash flow say?** Meena's quick stock turns usually mean fast cash. Ravi's slow stock, 101 days, could be a drag.
**What is each priced at?** A similar ROE does not justify the same P/E. Growth, safety and cash also matter.

blocks.title: The takeaway
blocks.x: Never judge a company by one ratio. Break returns into margin, turnover and leverage, check cash and debt, then compare with similar companies. Two different-looking businesses can be equally good, or one can hide a weakness behind a number that matches the other.

quiz.q: Two companies both earn 25% ROE. One has high margin and low turnover, the other low margin and high turnover. What does that tell you?
options: They earn the same return through different engines
Only the high margin one is good
quiz.why: DuPont shows ROE can come from different mixes of margin and turnover. You must judge each engine's durability.

quiz.q: Net margin 4%, asset turnover 5, equity multiplier 1.5. What is ROE?

lessons.summary: Why a bank, a software firm and a cement maker cannot be judged with the same numbers.

blocks.x: You would not judge a fast bowler by his batting average. In the same way, each industry earns money differently, so each has its own key numbers. The general ratios you have learned are the base. The sector numbers below are the extras.

quiz.q: Which number is most useful for judging a bank?
quiz.why: Gross NPA shows how many loans have gone bad, which is the central risk for any lender.

quiz.q: Why is a low P/E for a steel company at peak profits risky?
options: Profits peak and then fall, so the true P/E is higher
P/E is not used for steel
quiz.why: Cyclical profits swing. A low P/E at the top of the cycle may soon turn expensive as profit drops.

lessons.title: What is a business worth?
lessons.summary: Three practical ways to estimate value, and why a margin of safety protects you from being wrong.

blocks.x: Ratios tell you what you are paying. **Valuation** tries to answer: what is the business actually worth? Nobody can be exact, so think of it as estimating a sensible range.
1. Compare with similar businesses

If three similar shops on a street sell at about 4 times yearly profit, a fourth asking for 12 times needs a good reason. This is **relative valuation**: compare P/E, EV/EBITDA or P/B with peers and with the company's own history. It is fast, but if the whole sector is overpriced, you will not see it.
2. Add up the future cash (DCF)

A business is worth the cash it will give its owners in the future. But ₹100 received after 3 years is worth less today, because you could have earned interest on money received now. Bringing future money back to today is called **discounting**.

blocks.label: Present value
blocks.expr: Present value = Future cash ÷ (1 + r)^years
blocks.note: At r = 12%, ₹100 received in 3 years is worth 100 ÷ 1.12³ = about ₹71 today.

items: Estimate free cash flow for the next 5 to 10 years with careful growth assumptions.
Estimate what the business will be worth after that (terminal value).
Discount all of it to today using a rate that reflects the risk.
Add cash, subtract debt, divide by number of shares for a value per share.

blocks.title: Handle with care
blocks.x: Small changes in the growth or discount rate change the answer a lot. Use a DCF to understand what you must believe, not to get a precise price.
3. Reverse it: what is already priced in?

Instead of guessing the future, start from today's price and ask what growth it assumes. If the price needs 25% growth for ten years from a company that never grew above 12%, it is demanding. This is a **reverse DCF**.
Margin of safety
Because estimates can be wrong, buy only when the price is comfortably below your estimate of value. If you think the shop is worth ₹10 lakh, paying ₹7 lakh gives a 30% cushion against mistakes.

blocks.title: A simple shortcut
blocks.x: Compare a stock's earnings yield (profit ÷ price) with what a safe bank deposit earns today. Ravi's shop earns 5% on its price. If deposits pay more, you are counting on growth to make up the gap. Is that growth believable?

quiz.q: Why is ₹100 received in 3 years worth less than ₹100 today?
options: Money today can earn a return in the meantime
quiz.why: Money in hand can be invested, so money you receive later is worth less today.

quiz.q: You estimate a stock is worth ₹200. What price gives a 25% margin of safety?

lessons.title: Warning signs and your stock checklist
lessons.summary: How weak accounts and governance show up early, and a 12-point checklist you can reuse on any stock.

blocks.x: Most failures leave clues years earlier. The clues usually sit in the **gaps between statements**: profit vs cash, sales vs unpaid bills, borrowing vs cash.
Warning signs in the numbers

items: Cash from operations stays well below profit for many years.
Receivables or stock grow much faster than sales.
"One-time" items keep coming back.
Projects under construction (CWIP) never get completed.
Other income is a large share of profit.
Margins jump with no industry reason.

blocks.x: Warning signs in the people

items: A high or rising share of promoter holding **pledged** with lenders.
Promoter holding falling steadily without explanation.
Auditor resigns, gives a qualified opinion, or results are filed late.
Large loans or deals with companies owned by the promoter.
Repeated missed promises by management.

blocks.x: Warning signs in funding

items: Borrowing heavily while holding a lot of cash.
Short-term loans used to fund long-term assets.
Raising new shares again and again to survive.
Interest cover falling year after year.

blocks.x: A 12-point checklist

head: Check
Looking for
rows: You can explain how it earns in two sentences
Cash from operations close to profit over years
Clean audits, no opaque related deals
Sensible against history, peers and growth
A cushion if you are wrong

blocks.title: A final habit
blocks.x: Write down why you are buying and what would make you sell. Revisit it every quarter when results come out.

quiz.q: Which combination is the most worrying?
options: Rising profit and rising cash flow
Rising profit, falling cash flow, swelling receivables
quiz.why: Profit without cash, with unpaid bills piling up, suggests profit may be booked but not collected.

quiz.q: Why is a high pledge of promoter shares a risk?
options: If the price falls, lenders may sell the pledged shares and hurt the stock
quiz.why: A falling price can force lenders to sell pledged shares, pushing the price down further.

lessons.title: Case study: analysing a company from start to finish
lessons.summary: Apply the whole checklist to a fictional company, five years of numbers, and reach a reasoned view.

blocks.x: Meet Sundar Foods Ltd (fictional), a packaged-snacks company. Amounts are in ₹ crore. We will run our checklist on five years of data and see where it leads.
Step 1: growth and margins

Sales grew from 100 to 170 over four years, a CAGR of about 14.2%. Profit grew faster, about 15.0% a year. Net margin held between 8.0% and 8.5%. That is steady growth with stable margins, a good start.
Step 2: returns and debt
ROE hovers around 14%, close to but just below the 15% many investors look for. Debt jumped in year 3 to fund a large capex programme, then eased. Leverage is modest.
Step 3: is the profit real cash?

Over five years, profit totals 55 and cash from operations totals 40, so CFO ÷ profit is about 73%. Free cash flow (CFO minus capex) over the five years sums to about −1. The company spent almost all its operating cash on growth.
Receivable days climbed from 55 to 78 while sales grew only 70%. Customers are paying more slowly, so some profit is stuck in unpaid bills. This is the main warning sign.
Step 4: draw the picture

head: Question
Finding
Verdict
rows: Steady growth, stable margins, ROE about 14%
CFO about 73% of profit, FCF near zero, receivable days rising
Not shown here. Check pledge, auditor, related deals

blocks.title: What a careful analyst concludes
blocks.x: A decent growing business whose profit is not yet turning into free cash, partly because customers pay slowly. It is neither a clear buy nor a clear reject. The next step is to find out **why** receivable days are rising, then decide what price makes the risk worthwhile.

quiz.q: Sales grew 70% over four years, while receivable days rose from 55 to 78. What does this suggest?
options: Customers take longer to pay, so receivables grew faster than sales
quiz.why: Receivable days measure how long customers take. A rise means more profit sits in unpaid bills.

quiz.q: Why is a CFO ÷ profit of 73% a point to investigate rather than an automatic reject?
options: It may be growth-related working capital, so you need to find the cause
quiz.why: Fast-growing businesses often absorb cash in working capital. You must check if it is temporary or a sign of weak collections.

lessons.title: Valuation in practice: thinking in scenarios
lessons.summary: Instead of one fair value, estimate what you might earn if growth and valuation turn out well, average or badly.

blocks.x: Suppose Sundar Foods has 5 crore shares and a net profit of ₹14 crore, so EPS is ₹2.80. The price is ₹70, a P/E of 25. Over five years, your return depends on two things: how much profit grows, and what P/E the market pays at the end. Scenarios turn this into numbers.

blocks.label: Price in five years, and yearly return
blocks.expr:
Future price = EPS in year 5 × P/E in year 5
Yearly return = (Future price ÷ ₹70)^(1/5) − 1
blocks.note: This ignores dividends, which add a little. It keeps the idea simple.

blocks.x: What the table teaches

items: At a P/E of 25 you are already paying for strong growth. If growth is merely decent and the P/E drifts to 20, the yearly return is only about 7%, near what a safe deposit pays.
The **range** is wide: from a loss to 15% a year. The price you pay decides how much room you have for disappointment.
At a lower purchase price, say ₹50, the same Base scenario gives about 14.6% a year, a far better bargain for the same business. Check: (₹99 ÷ ₹50)^(0.2) − 1 = 14.6%.

blocks.title: Make it a habit
blocks.x: Before buying, write three scenarios and the probability you give each. Ask: if the Bad case happens, can I live with it? If your answer is that you need the Good case to be satisfied, the price is too high.

blocks.title: Estimates, not promises
blocks.x: These are made-up numbers to teach a method. Real growth rates and future P/E levels are uncertain, and no scenario table removes risk.

quiz.q: EPS is ₹5 and the P/E is 20 in year five. What is the price?
quiz.why: Price = EPS × P/E = 5 × 20 = ₹100.

quiz.q: Why does buying at a lower price improve the same scenario's return?
options: The same future value is divided by a smaller starting price
quiz.why: A smaller price paid for the same future value means a higher yearly return and a bigger safety cushion.

lessons.title: Common mistakes and a research routine you can repeat
lessons.summary: The errors that trip up most beginners, and a simple one-page routine for every stock you study.

blocks.x: Ten common mistakes

items: **Trusting one ratio.** A low P/E, a high ROE or a big dividend can each hide a problem.
**Looking at one year.** Cycles and one-offs fool you. Use 5 to 10 years.
**Ignoring cash flow.** Profit without cash is an opinion.
**Comparing across industries.** A bank and a software firm need different yardsticks.
**Skipping the notes.** Contingent liabilities and related deals hide there.
**Falling for stories.** A great story at a high price can still be a poor investment.
**Buying cheap, ignoring why.** Low prices often reflect real problems.
**Ignoring governance.** Pledged shares and unclear deals have sunk many good-looking companies.
**Putting too much in one stock.** Even careful analysis can be wrong.
**Never writing the reason.** Without a written thesis you cannot tell if you were right or lucky.

What to write down

blocks.x: Analysing ten companies carefully with the same routine teaches you far more than skimming a hundred. Your notes become your own record of judgement, and judgement is the skill this course is meant to build.

blocks.title: Education, not advice
blocks.x: This course teaches how to analyse businesses. It does not recommend any stock. Investing involves risk, and you should consider your own goals or speak to a qualified adviser before making decisions.

options: So you can later judge whether your thinking was right or just lucky
Because it is required by law
quiz.why: A written thesis lets you learn from outcomes and decide objectively when to hold or sell.

quiz.q: Which is the biggest risk of using only one ratio?
options: It can hide a serious problem that another number would reveal

lessons.title: What technical analysis actually does
lessons.summary: Technical analysis is a way of reading what buyers and sellers are doing, and turning it into probabilities. It is not a crystal ball.

blocks.x: **Technical analysis (TA)** is the study of price and volume to judge what buyers and sellers are doing and where the odds look better or worse. It starts from a simple observation: every trade on the NSE is two real people agreeing on a price with real money. The chart is the record of all those agreements.
What it is, and what it is not

items: **It is** a framework for reading supply and demand, trend, and risk from price and volume.
**It is** a way to decide where to enter, where you are wrong, and how much to risk.
**It is not** a method that predicts the future with certainty.
**It is not** a collection of indicators to be stacked until one says buy.
**It is not** the opposite of fundamentals. It answers a different question: when and at what risk, rather than what and why.

blocks.x: Why price is the primary evidence

Price is where opinion meets money. News, earnings, rumours, fear and greed all end up in the price, sometimes before the public story is clear. A stock that keeps making new highs on rising volume is telling you that large buyers are willing to pay up. A stock that cannot rally even on good news is telling you that supply is heavy. Indicators such as RSI or MACD are not independent evidence. They are arithmetic done on price and volume, so they can only rearrange what price has already said.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.x: Price is the primary evidence. Indicators are secondary measurements derived from price and volume.
Prediction versus probability
