A forecaster says “this stock will go to ₹600”. A technical analyst says “if this stock closes above ₹500 on strong volume, the odds of a further advance are better than usual, and if it falls below ₹470 the idea is wrong”. The second statement has a trigger, an invalidation point, and no promise.

blocks.title: Probability, not certainty
blocks.x: Technical analysis does not predict the future with certainty. It identifies situations where the probability distribution may be favourable.
The idea of an edge
An **edge** is a situation that, repeated many times, pays more than it costs. You do not need to win most trades. You need the average winner to be large enough compared with the average loser.

blocks.label: Edge in one line
blocks.expr:
Edge exists when:
(Win rate × Average win) > (Loss rate × Average loss) + costs
blocks.note: Costs include brokerage, taxes and slippage. Lessons later in this course turn this into the expectancy formula.

blocks.caption: Three ways of looking at a stock
head: Approach
Main question
Main inputs
Typical output
rows: Is this a good business at a sensible price?
A view on value and quality
What are buyers and sellers doing, and where is the risk?
Does a precisely defined rule have a positive edge in past data?

blocks.title: How the three fit together
blocks.x: Many practitioners use fundamentals to build a list of good businesses and technicals to time and size the position. Systematic trading takes a technical idea and tests it with rules. This course moves in that direction, from reading charts to rule-based plans.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating a setup that worked three times as a law. Any setup has a failure rate. A trader who ignores this risks too much on one trade, and one failure erases weeks of progress.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Technical analysis reads price and volume to find favourable odds, defines where the idea fails, and manages risk when it does. It works in probabilities, so risk management is part of the method, not an add-on.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of technical analysis?
options: To forecast the exact price a stock will reach on a given date
To identify situations where the odds and payoff look favourable, using price and volume, and to define risk
To calculate the intrinsic value of a company from its financial statements
To find setups that cannot fail so that stop losses are unnecessary
quiz.why: TA is a decision framework: it reads supply and demand from price and volume to find better-than-average situations and to say where the idea is wrong. It does not give exact forecasts, intrinsic value (that is fundamental analysis), or certainty.

quiz.q: Why is probability a more appropriate frame than certainty for chart-based decisions?
options: Because every individual setup can fail, so only the long-run mix of win rate and payoff can be favourable
Because charts are random, so no analysis has value
Because probabilities guarantee a profit once you take ten trades
Because certainty is only possible on weekly charts
quiz.why: A single trade outcome is uncertain even for a good setup. What can be favourable is the distribution of many outcomes: how often you win and how much you make or lose when you do. Probabilities do not guarantee anything over a small number of trades either.

quiz.q: A setup has won 4 of its last 10 trades. The average winner was 2.5R and the average loser 1R. Which reading is most reasonable?
options: It is failing, because its win rate is below 50%
Expectancy is (0.4 × 2.5) − (0.6 × 1) = +0.4R per trade, so it may have an edge, but 10 trades is a small sample
It is guaranteed to be profitable from now on
Win rate alone should decide whether to continue
quiz.why: Win rate on its own is misleading. With 2.5R winners, a 40% win rate gives positive expectancy. But ten trades is too few to be confident, so the result should be treated as encouraging, not proven.

lessons.title: Reading a stock chart
lessons.summary: OHLC, candlesticks, timeframes, scales, gaps and volume: the vocabulary you need before any analysis makes sense.

blocks.x: A chart is a compressed record of trading. Each bar or candle covers one time period and summarises it in four prices and one volume figure.
OHLC and volume

items: **Open**: the first traded price of the period. On NSE, the daily open comes from the pre-open session auction at 9:00 to 9:15.
**High** and **Low**: the highest and lowest prices traded.
**Close**: the last price, based on a weighted average of the final minutes of trading. Most analysis uses the close because it is the market’s settled opinion for that period.
**Volume**: how many shares changed hands. It shows how much participation stood behind the price move.

blocks.x: A **candlestick** draws the open and close as a body and the high and low as thin lines called wicks. A close above the open is usually drawn as a green (hollow) body and a close below the open as a red (solid) body, though colour conventions vary by platform. The next track covers candles in depth.
Timeframes
The same stock looks different on every timeframe, and each answers a different question. A stock can be in a strong weekly uptrend while a 5-minute chart shows a messy decline that afternoon.

blocks.caption: ABC Industries (fictional) on three timeframes
head: Timeframe
What one candle shows
What you see
Best used for
rows: Intraday noise, opening drive, lunchtime lull, closing push
Swings, support and resistance, breakouts, base building
Swing and positional trading, most setups in this course
The primary trend, major bases, long-term averages
Trend context, stage analysis, position management

blocks.title: Start with the weekly chart
blocks.x: Look at the weekly chart first to see the primary trend and the major levels. Then move to the daily chart to time the entry. A daily buy signal in a weekly downtrend is working against the bigger current.
Linear versus log scale

On a **linear** scale, equal rupee moves look equal. On a **log** (percentage) scale, equal percentage moves look equal. A move from ₹100 to ₹200 is +100% and from ₹200 to ₹300 is +50%, but a linear chart draws them the same height. For stocks that have moved a lot, use log scale so that trendlines and pullback depth are comparable across the chart.
Adjusted versus unadjusted prices

When a company does a split or a bonus, the price drops mechanically without any loss for shareholders. A 1:1 bonus halves the price. If the chart does not adjust for this, it shows a fake crash that can trigger false stops and false signals. Use **adjusted** price history for analysis. Dividends can also be adjusted, though most Indian charting platforms adjust for splits and bonuses by default.

blocks.title: NSE specifics
blocks.x: Regular trading runs 9:15 to 15:30 IST. Most stocks carry daily price bands (for example 5%, 10% or 20%), so a stock can hit a circuit and be unable to trade further in that direction. Small and mid caps can also be thinly traded, so the chart looks cleaner than the real ability to enter or exit. Always check liquidity.
Gaps

A **gap** appears when a period opens above the prior high or below the prior low, leaving empty space on the chart. Gaps usually follow overnight news such as results or global moves. A gap up on heavy volume out of a base shows urgent demand. A gap that gets filled in a day or two shows the demand was not durable.
Volume bars

The volume bars under the price chart show participation. A move on high volume carries more information than the same move on thin volume. Compare each bar with the stock’s own average (for example 50-day average volume), not with other stocks.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Analysing an unadjusted chart after a split or bonus, or drawing levels on a linear chart of a stock that has tripled. Both produce levels and signals that do not mean what you think.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Use the weekly chart for context, the daily chart for decisions, log scale for big moves, adjusted prices always, and volume relative to the stock’s own average.

quiz.q: A stock’s daily chart shows a bullish breakout, but its weekly chart is in a clear downtrend below a falling 30-week average. What does the weekly chart add?
options: Nothing; the daily chart is always more accurate
Context: the breakout is going against the primary trend, so it needs more caution or a smaller position
Proof that the breakout will fail
A guaranteed signal to short the stock
quiz.why: Higher timeframes show the dominant trend. A daily signal against it is not automatically wrong, but the odds are less favourable and the risk is higher. Weekly context does not guarantee a failure either.

quiz.q: A stock did a 1:1 bonus issue, halving its price overnight. The chart you use is unadjusted. What is the likely problem?
options: The volume will look too high
It will show a false 50% crash that can trigger false stops and distort every indicator
Nothing, because bonus issues do not affect price
The chart will be on log scale automatically
quiz.why: A bonus lowers the price mechanically with no loss to shareholders. Unadjusted data records a fake collapse that can break averages and trendlines. Use adjusted data.

quiz.q: Why use a log scale for a stock that has gone from ₹100 to ₹600 over three years?
options: Log scale makes the stock look cheaper
Equal percentage moves occupy equal vertical distances, so trends and pullbacks stay comparable
Log charts remove the need for volume
Log scale predicts when the trend will end
quiz.why: On a linear chart, early moves look tiny and recent moves look huge, although the percentage moves may be similar. A log scale shows proportional change, which is what matters for returns.

lessons.title: Market structure: highs, lows and trend
lessons.summary: Trend is not an opinion. It is a sequence of swing highs and swing lows. Learn to read it, and to tell a trend from a range.

blocks.x: Before any indicator, ask one question: **what is price doing with its swings?** A chart moves in waves. Each wave leaves a **swing high** (a peak with lower highs on both sides) and a **swing low** (a trough with higher lows on both sides). The order of these swings defines the trend.
The four building blocks

blocks.caption: Swing relationships
head: Term
Meaning
What it suggests
rows: A rally peaks above the previous swing high
Buyers can push past earlier supply
A pullback ends above the previous swing low
Buyers step in earlier, at higher prices
A rally peaks below the previous swing high
A decline ends below the previous swing low

blocks.label: Structure rules
blocks.expr:
Uptrend:   HH + HL  (bullish structure)
Downtrend: LH + LL  (bearish structure)
Range:     roughly flat highs and lows
blocks.note: A trend is defined by the sequence of swings. A single new high does not make an uptrend.

blocks.x: Trend, range and consolidation

items: **Uptrend**: a series of HH and HL. Pullbacks are shallow compared with advances, and each pullback holds above the last low.
**Downtrend**: a series of LH and LL. Rallies fail below the previous peak.
**Range**: price moves between a ceiling and a floor without making progress. Buyers and sellers are balanced.
**Consolidation**: a tighter pause inside a trend or after a move. It can resolve in either direction, and the earlier trend gives it a tilt, not a promise.

blocks.title: Do not call every sideways move a trend
blocks.x: A stock bouncing between ₹180 and ₹210 for four months is in a range, not an uptrend because it made one slightly higher high. Many bad trades come from forcing a trend label on a range.
How structure evolves
Structure changes in steps, not at once. Take a stock in an uptrend with a last higher low at ₹250.

items: **Healthy uptrend:** price keeps making HH and HL.
**First warning:** a rally fails to make a new high, forming a lower high, while the last higher low at ₹250 still holds.
**Break of structure (BOS):** price closes below ₹250, the last higher low. The pattern of HL has broken.
**Change of character (CHoCH):** the first clear sign that the dominant behaviour has changed, for example the first lower high followed by a break of the last higher low in an advance.
**New regime:** if later rallies stay below the new lower high and lows keep falling, a downtrend has replaced the uptrend. If price instead stabilises and forms a range, it is basing.

blocks.x: Break of structure and change of character are useful names for the same idea: **the sequence that defined the trend has stopped repeating**. Neither is a signal to sell on its own. They are a signal to reassess risk.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Mark the last two swing highs and lows on the daily chart. Ask: is each swing higher than the last? If the answer is not clearly yes or no, the chart is a range, and trend-following setups should be treated with caution.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Using tiny swings on a 5-minute chart to call a daily trend, or ignoring that a higher low can fail the moment price closes below it. Define swings on the timeframe you trade.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: HH + HL is bullish structure, LH + LL is bearish structure, and flat swings are a range. Trends end in steps, and the break of the last higher low is the first hard evidence.

quiz.q: A stock rises to ₹320, pulls back to ₹290, rallies to ₹315, then closes at ₹285. The earlier swing low was ₹290. What has happened to its structure?
options: It made a higher high, so the uptrend is stronger
It made a lower high (₹315 below ₹320) and then broke the last swing low (₹290), a break of structure
Nothing has changed because prices are still above where the rally began
It is now certain to continue falling
quiz.why: ₹315 is a lower high and the close at ₹285 is below the last swing low of ₹290. That is a break of structure and a warning that the uptrend’s pattern has failed. It does not guarantee a decline, but risk has risen.

quiz.q: A stock oscillated between ₹180 and ₹210 for four months. Which label is the most accurate?
options: Downtrend, because it has not made progress
Range, because highs and lows are not progressing
quiz.why: Roughly flat highs and lows indicate balance between buyers and sellers. Trend-following setups are lower probability inside a range until it resolves.

quiz.q: What does a change of character mean in practical terms?
options: The first clear evidence that the behaviour that defined the trend has stopped repeating, so risk should be reassessed
A change of the stock’s ticker
A candle with a long upper wick
quiz.why: It is an early structural clue, not a prediction. It tells you the old pattern of higher lows (or lower highs) is no longer reliable and that position size or stops may need review.

lessons.title: Support and resistance
lessons.summary: Where price has stopped or turned before is where it may stop or turn again. Think of zones, not exact lines.

blocks.x: **Support** is a price area where demand has been strong enough to stop a decline. **Resistance** is a price area where supply has been strong enough to stop an advance. They exist because traders remember: buyers who missed a bounce want to buy there again, and holders who were stuck at a peak sell when they get back to even.
Where levels come from

items: **Previous swing highs and lows**: the most common and most reliable source.
**Multiple-touch levels**: an area tested three or four times shows that many participants care about it.
**Demand and supply zones**: ranges where price moved away fast, suggesting large orders were filled there.
**Moving averages**: dynamic levels such as the 50-day or 200-day average that leading stocks often respect during pullbacks.
**Trendlines**: sloped support or resistance (covered in the next lesson).
**Round numbers and 52-week highs/lows**: psychological anchors, especially for retail participants.

blocks.x: Zones, not exact prices

Prices rarely reverse at the exact same rupee. A stock may peak at ₹498, ₹502 and ₹495 on three tests. Treat ₹495 to ₹505 as the resistance zone. Drawing a razor-thin line at ₹502 and calling every move to ₹503 a breakout leads to false signals. Zones also help you size stops sensibly: place them beyond the zone, not inside it.
Role reversal

When price breaks above resistance and then pulls back to that level, the old ceiling often becomes the new floor. The logic: sellers who sold there are gone, and holders who were trapped got out. New buyers see the old level as value. The same works in reverse when broken support becomes resistance.

blocks.title: Role reversal
blocks.x: Resistance becoming support after a breakout is one of the most important ideas in technical analysis. A breakout that retests the old resistance and holds above it confirms that supply there has been absorbed.
Strength of a level

blocks.caption: What makes a level more significant
head: Factor
Stronger level
Weaker level

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Mark only the levels you can see at a glance on the weekly and daily charts. If you have to zoom and squint to justify a level, it is probably not significant.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Drawing too many levels. A chart with ten lines gives a reason to justify any trade. Choose two or three that matter near the current price, and treat the rest as noise.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Support and resistance are zones where supply and demand have shown up before. More touches, more time, and higher timeframes make a level matter more. A breakout that turns old resistance into support is a sign the supply has been absorbed.

quiz.q: ABC Industries peaked at ₹498, ₹502 and ₹495 on three tests over four months. How should you treat resistance?
options: As a single line at ₹502 exactly
As a zone of roughly ₹495 to ₹505
As irrelevant because the highs differ
As support, because it was tested three times
quiz.why: Real trading produces slightly different peaks. A zone captures the area where supply has repeatedly appeared and avoids false breakout calls on a ₹1 or ₹2 move.

quiz.q: A stock breaks above ₹500 resistance, pulls back to ₹501 on low volume, and bounces. What does this suggest?
options: Old resistance is acting as new support, which supports the view that supply at that level was absorbed
quiz.why: A successful retest of the broken level, especially on lower volume, is the role-reversal pattern. It strengthens the case that the breakout was genuine, though no pattern guarantees continuation.

quiz.q: Which level is most likely to matter?
options: A level touched once on a 5-minute chart last Tuesday
A zone tested four times over six months on the weekly chart
A level you only see after zooming into a 1-minute chart
quiz.why: Levels that are visible on higher timeframes, tested multiple times, and held over longer periods represent more participants and more capital.

lessons.title: Trendlines and channels
lessons.summary: Trendlines add a sloped view of support and resistance. Use them as helpers, never as overrides of price structure.

blocks.x: A **trendline** connects swing points to show the slope along which price is moving. In an uptrend you draw it under the rising lows. In a downtrend you draw it over the falling highs.
How to draw a valid trendline

items: Use a **log scale** if the stock has moved a lot, so the line reflects percentage growth.
Connect **two clear swing lows** (uptrend) or swing highs (downtrend). Two points define the line; the third touch is what **validates** it.
Draw from wick to wick or body to body, but be consistent. Slight imperfections are normal.
A line with three or more touches, spread across time, carries more weight than one with two touches close together.
Very steep lines break quickly. A slope that fits the stock’s normal pace is more durable.

blocks.x: Trendline violations

A decisive close below an uptrend line suggests the pace of advance is changing, but it is **not** necessarily a reversal. Often price breaks the line and then moves sideways, forming a new base, or even resumes up with a shallower line. The break tells you to look at structure: is the last higher low still intact?
Channels
A **channel** adds a parallel line on the other side of the trend. Price oscillates between the two.

blocks.caption: Channel types
head: Channel
Description
Typical use
rows: Rising lows and rising highs, parallel
Trend following: buying near the lower line in an intact uptrend, with a stop below it
Recognising a downtrend; avoiding longs against it
Range trading or waiting for a breakout

blocks.x: A **channel breakout** upward from a descending channel can mark the end of a decline, but it needs confirmation: volume, a close beyond the line, and ideally a higher low afterwards. A **false trendline break** is a quick poke through the line that reverses within a day or two. Waiting for a close and a bit of follow-through filters many of them.

blocks.title: Trendlines are subjective
blocks.x: Two analysts can draw different lines on the same chart. That is why trendlines should support, never override, price structure. If a stock breaks its trendline but holds the last higher low and its moving averages, the structure is still intact.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Draw one trendline you believe in, on the weekly or daily chart. If you need three different lines to explain the same move, the chart is not giving you a clear trendline.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A trendline is a sloped support or resistance helper. Three touches validate it, a close through it asks you to reassess structure, and no line should override HH/HL or LH/LL.

quiz.q: What validates a trendline?
options: Two points joined, because any two points make a line
A third touch, ideally spaced over time, after the line was drawn from two swing points
Drawing it as steeply as possible
quiz.why: Two points always define a line, which proves nothing. A subsequent touch that respects the line is evidence that others see it too.

quiz.q: A stock closes below its ascending trendline, but the last higher low is intact and it holds the 50-day average. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: The uptrend is over and the stock should be sold at any price
The pace of the advance may be slowing, but the structure is still bullish, so the line break alone is not decisive
The trendline break proves a downtrend has started
quiz.why: Structure (HH/HL) and key averages matter more than a subjective line. A line break is a reason to watch closely, not an automatic exit.

quiz.q: Why wait for a close beyond a channel line and some follow-through before trusting a breakout from a descending channel?
options: Because intraday pokes through lines often reverse and become false breaks
Because channels only work after 3 pm
quiz.why: Intraday spikes through a line are common and often reverse. A close beyond it and some follow-through filter noise, though they cannot eliminate failures.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a candlestick
lessons.summary: One candle is a summary of a tug-of-war between buyers and sellers. Learn to read the body, the wicks and where it closed.

blocks.x: Every candle is built from the same four prices: open, high, low and close. What matters is the **relationship** between them.

blocks.caption: Parts of a candle
head: Part
What it is
What it tells you
rows: Who won the session and by how much
High to the top of the body
How far buyers pushed before sellers rejected the price
Low to the bottom of the body
How far sellers pushed before buyers rejected the price
How much price moved; compare with recent ranges
Where the close sits inside the range
Strong close near the high, weak close near the low

blocks.x: Bullish and bearish candles

items: A **bullish candle** closes above its open. Buyers ended the session in control.
A **bearish candle** closes below its open. Sellers ended in control.
A long body means one side dominated. A short body means indecision or balance.
Long wicks mean price was pushed and then rejected.

blocks.x: What a candle says about supply and demand

Imagine ABC Industries opens at ₹500, falls to ₹488 in the morning as sellers push, then buyers absorb the supply and lift the price to close at ₹509 with a high of ₹510. The candle has a long lower wick (the rejected low), a bullish body (₹500 to ₹509) and a close near the high. The message: sellers tried and failed, and buyers finished in control.

Now compare an identical range with a close at ₹489. The long upper wick says buyers pushed to ₹510 but were rejected, and the weak close shows sellers finished in control. The same high and low can tell opposite stories depending on **where the close lands**.

blocks.title: The close is the most important price
blocks.x: The close is the last agreement of the session and the price most holders use to judge gain or loss. A strong close near the high suggests demand at the end of the day. A weak close near the low suggests the opposite.
Range and volume

Compare each candle’s range with the previous ten to twenty sessions. A candle with a much bigger range than normal on strong volume matters more than a normal-sized candle. A tiny-range candle after a big move shows that activity is drying up.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Reading one candle in isolation. A long lower wick means very different things after a 30% fall into a major support zone than in the middle of a quiet range.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Read each candle as a battle: the body shows who won, the wicks show what was rejected, and the close shows who was in control at the end. Compare it with its recent neighbours and its location on the chart.

quiz.q: A candle opens at ₹500, drops to ₹488, then closes at ₹509 near its ₹510 high. What does the long lower wick tell you?
options: Buyers pushed the price down to ₹488
Sellers pushed the price down but buyers absorbed the supply and rejected the lows
quiz.why: A long lower wick means price traded much lower but was rejected, and a close near the high shows buyers finished in control.

quiz.q: Two candles have the same ₹488 to ₹510 range. One closes at ₹509 and the other at ₹489. Why do they differ?
options: They do not; the range is all that matters
The close shows who controlled the end of the session: demand in the first case, supply in the second
The first candle must have higher volume
quiz.why: The same range can be a strong or a weak session depending on where it closes. The close reflects the final balance of supply and demand.

quiz.q: Why compare a candle’s range with recent sessions?
options: A range that is unusually large (or small) relative to recent history carries more information about participation
Ranges are always equal across stocks
quiz.why: Candles are relative. A large range on strong volume signals unusual activity, and a very small range after a big move signals a pause or dry-up.

lessons.title: Important candlestick patterns
lessons.summary: Eleven patterns, each with its structure, meaning, the place where it matters, the volume you want to see, and how it fails.

blocks.x: Candlestick patterns are shorthand for a short sequence of supply and demand events. For each one below, ask five questions: what is the **structure**, what does it **mean**, **where** does it matter, what **volume** helps, and how does it **fail**.

blocks.caption: Single-candle patterns
head: Pattern
Structure
Meaning
Where it matters
Failure
rows: Open and close nearly equal; wicks on both sides
Indecision, balance of buyers and sellers
After a long move, at a key level
Next candle resumes the prior direction with a strong close
Small body at the top, lower wick at least twice the body, little upper wick
Sellers pushed down, buyers rejected the lows
Price closes below the hammer’s low
Small body at the bottom, long upper wick
Buyers tried, partial rejection; needs confirmation
Next candle closes below the low
Small body at the bottom, long upper wick, after a rally
Buyers pushed up and were rejected by supply
Price closes above the star’s high
Hammer shape, but after an advance
Warning that sellers appeared; needs confirmation
After an extended rise near resistance
Price makes new highs on strength

blocks.caption: Two- and three-candle patterns
head: Pattern
Structure
Meaning
Where it matters
Failure
rows: Bullish body that fully covers the previous bearish body
Demand overwhelms the previous session’s supply
Price falls below the engulfing candle’s low
Bearish body that fully covers the previous bullish body
Supply overwhelms the previous session’s demand
Price closes above the engulfing candle’s high
Long bearish candle, small-bodied candle, then a bullish candle closing well into the first body
Price falls below the middle candle’s low
Long bullish candle, small-bodied candle, then a bearish candle closing well into the first body
Price rises above the middle candle’s high
Entire range within the prior candle’s range
Compression and a pause; energy is building
In a trend or at a key level
Direction of the break against the prior trend is a warning
Range extends beyond both the prior high and low
Expansion; the close shows who won
A weak close nullifies the signal

blocks.x: Volume confirmation

Reversal patterns gain weight when they appear on higher-than-average volume, because more participants took part in the rejection. An engulfing candle on volume twice the average says far more than one on a quiet day. Inside bars usually come with falling volume, so look for the **expansion** when price leaves the mother bar.
Failure conditions matter more than the name

Every pattern comes with a built-in stop: the other end of the pattern. A hammer is invalid if price closes below its low. A shooting star is invalid if price closes above its high. Knowing this makes the pattern tradable, because the risk is defined before you act.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Memorising names without asking where the pattern appeared. A hammer printed in the middle of a quiet range is noise. The same candle after a 25% decline into a long-standing support zone on strong volume may be meaningful.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Give yourself a short filter: Is there a clear prior move? Is the pattern at a level that matters? Is volume supportive? Is there a logical stop at the pattern’s edge? If fewer than three answers are yes, skip.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Patterns are tools for reading a short battle between buyers and sellers. They are only worth acting on at meaningful locations, with volume support and a clear failure point.

quiz.q: A hammer forms after a 25% decline, right at a multi-month support zone, on 1.8 times average volume. What strengthens the signal?
options: Location at a meaningful support, prior decline, and volume above average
quiz.why: Context creates the edge: a prior move to reverse, a level where buyers have stepped in before, and heavy participation that shows the rejection was real.

quiz.q: Where does a hammer become invalid?
options: When price closes below the hammer’s low
When the next candle is green
quiz.why: A close below the hammer’s low means the rejection of the lows failed. That level is the natural stop for the idea.

quiz.q: A hammer-shaped candle appears after a long advance, near resistance. How is it named and how should it be treated?
options: It is a hammer and is strongly bullish
It is a hanging man: a warning that sellers appeared, which needs confirmation by a weak next candle
It is a bullish engulfing candle
quiz.why: The same shape means different things depending on where it appears. After an advance, the shape may show that sellers are testing the market, but a confirming weak close is needed.

quiz.q: What does an inside bar usually represent?
options: Compression and a pause; the break of the mother bar’s range shows where the market resolves
quiz.why: An inside bar shows reduced range and balance. The direction of the break from the mother bar, ideally with volume, is the information.

lessons.title: Candlesticks in context
lessons.summary: The same candle means different things in different places. Context beats pattern recognition.

blocks.x: A candle is a sentence, and the chart is the paragraph. Reading the sentence without the paragraph produces confident mistakes. Three comparisons show why.

blocks.caption: Same pattern, different value
head: Situation
Weaker reading
Stronger reading
rows: A hammer in the middle of a sideways range, on low volume
A hammer at a multi-touch support zone after a sharp decline, on high volume
Inside a strong uptrend after a tiny pullback
After a decline into support, closing near the high
In random price action with no nearby resistance
At a major resistance or after an extended run, on rising volume

blocks.title: The rule of context
blocks.x: A hammer at support is not the same as a hammer anywhere. A bullish engulfing after a decline is not the same as a bullish engulfing inside a strong uptrend. A shooting star near major resistance carries more information than one in random price action.
The four context filters

items: **Trend:** what was the prior move? Reversal patterns need something to reverse.
**Location:** is the candle at support, resistance, a moving average, or in empty space?
**Volume:** is participation above average at the key candle?
**Confirmation:** did the next one or two sessions follow through?

blocks.x: Worked example

PQR Engineering (fictional) has fallen from ₹420 to ₹310 over eight weeks and is approaching ₹300, a level that held in two earlier declines. On Tuesday it forms a bullish engulfing candle: open ₹304, close ₹322, covering Monday’s bearish body, on 2.1 times average volume. On Wednesday it holds above Tuesday’s midpoint and closes at ₹326.

items: Prior move: a steep decline gives the pattern something to reverse.
Location: the engulfing happens at a known support.
Volume: more than twice the average.
Confirmation: the next day holds and closes higher.
Failure point: a close below ₹304 (the engulfing candle’s low area) would invalidate it.

blocks.x: Now take the same engulfing candle in a stock that has risen 20% in two weeks with no pullback. The pattern is still a bullish candle, but it is not a reversal signal. It is just another up day, and the location suggests the risk of buying after an extended move.

blocks.title: Combine, do not stack
blocks.x: Use a candlestick pattern as a timing detail inside a bigger idea (for example a pullback to a rising 50-day average in a Stage 2 stock). It should not be the entire idea.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Trading every pattern that appears. A large share of candlestick signals have no follow-through. Selectivity comes from location, volume and trend, not from knowing more pattern names.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Read a candle after reading the chart around it. Trend, location, volume and confirmation turn a pattern from a coincidence into evidence.

quiz.q: A bullish engulfing candle appears in a stock that has risen 20% in two weeks without a pullback. How should you view it?
options: As a strong reversal signal because engulfing candles are bullish
As just another up day with no reversal to confirm, and a location that carries extension risk
As a signal to short immediately
As evidence of a Stage 4 decline
quiz.why: Reversal patterns need a decline to reverse. Inside a strong run, an engulfing candle adds little, and buying after an extended move increases risk.

quiz.q: Which one is the best example of using candlesticks properly?
options: Treating a hammer at a rising 50-day average in a stock with strong structure as a timing clue, with a stop below the hammer’s low
Ignoring volume because candles are enough
quiz.why: The candle gives timing inside a bigger idea (trend, support) and defines a stop. It is not the whole thesis.

quiz.q: A bullish engulfing candle forms at support on 2.1× volume. The next session closes below its low. What is the right conclusion?
options: The signal failed; the pattern’s low was the invalidation point, so the idea is wrong and exit rules apply
Hold, because engulfing candles never fail
Add to the position, because price is cheaper
Ignore the stop because the volume was high
quiz.why: Every pattern has a failure condition. Respecting it limits the loss and keeps the probabilities honest.

lessons.title: Moving average fundamentals
lessons.summary: A moving average smooths price to show direction. Understand how it is calculated, why it lags, and what the common periods are used for.

blocks.x: A **moving average (MA)** is the average of the last N closing prices, recalculated every period. As a new price arrives, the oldest price drops out, so the line “moves”. It filters noise and shows the direction and slope of the trend.
Simple moving average (SMA)

blocks.label: SMA
blocks.expr: SMA(N) = (Close₁ + Close₂ + … + Close_N) ÷ N
blocks.note: Every price in the window has equal weight.

blocks.x: Example: ABC Industries closes at ₹102, ₹104, ₹103, ₹106 and ₹110 over five sessions. The 5-day SMA is (102 + 104 + 103 + 106 + 110) ÷ 5 = 525 ÷ 5 = **₹105**. Tomorrow, if it closes at ₹108, the oldest close (₹102) drops out: (104 + 103 + 106 + 110 + 108) ÷ 5 = **₹106.2**.
Exponential moving average (EMA)

blocks.label: EMA
blocks.expr:
Multiplier = 2 ÷ (N + 1)
EMA today = (Close today − EMA yesterday) × Multiplier + EMA yesterday
blocks.note: Recent prices carry more weight, so the EMA reacts faster than the SMA of the same length.

blocks.x: Example: for a 10-period EMA, the multiplier is 2 ÷ 11 = 0.1818. If yesterday’s EMA was ₹100 and today closes at ₹110, EMA today = (110 − 100) × 0.1818 + 100 = **₹101.82**. A 10-day SMA would respond slower on a day like this, or faster depending on which old price drops out, so the two lines differ.
Smoothing and lag

The more days you average, the smoother the line and the later it turns. Every moving average **lags** because it is built from past prices. That is not a defect to be fixed. It is the trade-off: smoother lines give fewer false signals but later ones.

blocks.caption: Common moving averages
head: MA
Typical use
Advantage
Limitation
rows: Intermediate trend; common pullback support for leaders
About 30 weeks; part of trend-template and stage analysis
Widely followed; separates long-term bull and bear
A major trend can be well advanced before it turns

blocks.x: There is nothing magical about these numbers. They matter partly because many participants watch them, which makes them practical reference levels. A stock that repeatedly bounces from its rising 50-day average is telling you that buyers defend that area.
SMA or EMA?

Pick one convention and stay consistent. Trend templates and stage analysis traditionally use simple averages (50, 150, 200 days or 30 weeks). Many swing traders use EMAs such as 10 and 21 for shorter-term trends. The difference matters less than the discipline of using the same tool the same way.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating a moving average as a precise level. It is a zone and a slope indicator. A stock closing ₹1 below its 50-day average in an otherwise strong trend is not a trend break.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Look at two things on any average: the **slope** (rising, flat, falling) and the **location of price** relative to it. Both tell you more than any crossover.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A moving average is smoothed price. Longer averages are slower and more reliable but later. Use slope and price location, and use one convention consistently.

quiz.q: Five closes: ₹102, ₹104, ₹103, ₹106, ₹110. What is the 5-day SMA?
quiz.why: Sum = 525, divided by 5 = ₹105. The SMA gives each close equal weight.

quiz.q: Why does an EMA react faster than an SMA of the same length?
options: It gives more weight to recent prices
It is calculated on weekly data
quiz.why: The EMA’s multiplier puts greater weight on the latest closes, so it turns sooner than an SMA of the same period, at the cost of more false signals.

quiz.q: A trader complains that the 200-day average only turns after a big move has already happened. What is the right response?
options: Lag is inherent: it is the price paid for smoothness, so use it for context rather than precise timing
Use a 2-day average instead for all decisions
quiz.why: Moving averages are built from past prices. Longer averages filter noise but lag more. They are better for classifying the trend than for pinpointing turns.

lessons.title: Moving average alignment
lessons.summary: When short, medium and long averages stack in order and all slope the same way, the trend has a clear shape. Compression and expansion show how it is changing.

blocks.x: A single average tells you about direction. **Several averages together** tell you about the quality and maturity of the trend. The classic bullish arrangement is:

blocks.label: Bullish alignment
blocks.expr:
Price > 50 SMA > 150 SMA > 200 SMA
all three averages sloping upwards
blocks.note: Faster averages sit above slower ones because recent prices are higher than older prices. Slope shows the trend is still being fed.

blocks.x: What alignment tells us

items: **Bullish alignment:** over every horizon, recent average prices are higher than older ones. Pullbacks tend to find support at the 50-day or 150-day.
**Bearish alignment:** price < 50 < 150 < 200 with all sloping down. Rallies tend to stall at the averages above.
**Mixed or tangled averages:** the lines cross, flatten and overlap. Typical of ranges and transitions between trends.

blocks.x: Compression and expansion

**Compression** is when averages bunch together and flatten. It signals a pause or balance, such as the base before a new advance. **Expansion** is when averages fan out as an advance builds, with price pulling away from the longer lines. Neither is a signal on its own.

blocks.caption: Reading the arrangement
head: Arrangement
Typical meaning
How a trader may respond
rows: Look for pullbacks and breakouts; hold winners
Averages flat and bunched, price oscillating around them
Wait; watch for a break above the group on volume
50 below 150, price below both, all falling
Avoid long setups; rallies are for lightening up
Price well above a flat 200 with the 50 flattening

blocks.x: Slope and location

Slope matters as much as order. A 200-day average that is rising for at least a month shows that the long-term trend is turning up or intact. A price **far above** its 50-day average (say 30% to 40%) is extended and carries more pullback risk even in a healthy trend. A price **near** a rising 50-day average is closer to where buyers have defended before and often offers a better risk-to-reward.

blocks.title: Small and mid caps
blocks.x: Indian small and mid caps can stretch far above their averages in strong phases and fall sharply when momentum fades. Distance from the 50-day average is a useful risk gauge.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating alignment as a buy signal. It describes the **current trend**; it does not say whether this is a good moment to enter, where to put the stop, or whether the move is already extended.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Alignment and slope describe trend quality. Stacked, rising averages mean a mature uptrend, bunched flat averages mean a pause, and price distance from the averages is a gauge of extension.

quiz.q: What does 50 SMA > 150 SMA > 200 SMA, all rising, describe?
options: A healthy, mature uptrend over several horizons
quiz.why: Recent average prices exceeding older ones at every horizon is what uptrend means in averages. It is a description of trend quality, not a timing signal.

quiz.q: Averages are bunched, flat and tangled while price weaves through them. This most likely indicates:
options: A pause, base or range with no clear trend
quiz.why: Compression with price crossing the lines suggests balance. Direction will come from the resolution, ideally on volume.

quiz.q: A stock in a healthy uptrend is 40% above its 50-day average. What is the sensible conclusion?
options: It is a great entry because the trend is strong
Extension risk is high: a normal pullback toward the average would be large relative to a sensible stop
quiz.why: A strong trend can run further, but buying far from support makes the stop distant and the risk/reward poor.

lessons.title: Moving average crossovers
lessons.summary: Golden cross and death cross are famous, and mostly late. Learn what crossovers really say and where they fail.

blocks.x: A **crossover** happens when a faster average crosses a slower one. It is a rule that turns the alignment idea into an event.

items: **Golden cross:** the 50-day average crosses above the 200-day average.
**Death cross:** the 50-day average crosses below the 200-day average.
Shorter versions exist, such as 10 over 20, or 20 over 50, with the same logic and more frequent signals.

blocks.x: Why crossovers lag

The 50-day average can only cross above the 200-day after prices have been higher for a while. By the time the cross occurs, a large part of the move may already be done. For example, a stock that bottoms at ₹200 and rallies to ₹290 might only produce the golden cross at ₹290. A trader waiting for that signal pays 45% more than the low and can still be right.
Where they work and where they fail

blocks.caption: Crossover behaviour
head: Market type
What happens
Result
rows: Cross occurs once and price continues in the same direction
Crossover system captures a large portion of the move
Price oscillates around the averages and keeps crossing back
Repeated false signals (whipsaws) and small losses
Price changes direction faster than the averages
Signal arrives late, often near the turning point

blocks.title: Crossovers confirm; they do not forecast
blocks.x: A crossover is a trend-following confirmation. It says the trend has already changed, not that it will continue. That is useful for a long-term filter, but it is a poor entry timing tool.

blocks.title: Crossover systems are not magic
blocks.x: A golden cross does not guarantee an uptrend and a death cross does not guarantee a decline. In range markets, crossovers lose money repeatedly. If you use them, combine them with structure, volume and market regime, and expect false signals.
A better use of crossovers

items: As a **filter**: only look for long setups when the 50 is above the 200.
As a **context** statement: the long-term trend has turned up or down.
As a **warning**: a death cross after a long decline tells you the long-term trend is deteriorating, not that the bottom is in.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Ask “what is the average telling me that price structure has not already told me?” Usually the answer is that the structure came first.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Crossovers are late, trend-following confirmations that work in sustained trends and fail in ranges. Use them as filters and context, not as standalone buy and sell triggers.

quiz.q: Why do moving average crossovers lag?
options: Because they are calculated from past prices, so price must already have moved before the averages cross
Because only weekly charts can show them
quiz.why: An average of past prices can only cross after prices have changed for a while. That makes crossovers confirmations rather than predictions.

quiz.q: A stock oscillates between ₹95 and ₹105 for months. A 20/50 crossover system keeps flipping between buy and sell. What is happening?
options: Whipsaws: in a range, price repeatedly crosses the averages and the signals produce small losses
quiz.why: Trend-following tools do well in trends and poorly in ranges. Using a market-regime or structure filter can reduce this problem.

quiz.q: Which is the most sensible use of the golden cross?
options: A guaranteed buy at any price
A context filter: long setups are more interesting when the 50-day is above a rising 200-day
A signal to ignore stop losses
quiz.why: The cross says the long-term trend has improved. It narrows the list of candidates but does not provide entry, stop or size.

lessons.title: The 10-week average and position management
lessons.summary: Weekly charts remove noise. The 10-week and 30-week averages give practical rules for staying with winners and exiting broken trends.

blocks.x: Daily charts are noisy. A single bad session can look dramatic and still mean nothing. The **weekly chart** compresses five sessions into one candle, so it shows the trend that really matters for positions held for weeks or months.
Why weekly averages

items: A **10-week SMA** is about the same as a 50-day average. It tracks the intermediate trend.
A **30-week SMA** is about the same as a 150-day average. It tracks the primary trend and is the main line in stage analysis (covered later).
Weekly lines are slower and smoother, so a close below them is more meaningful than a daily dip below the 50-day.

blocks.x: Price versus the 10-week average
In a strong advance, leading stocks often hold above their rising 10-week average for months, and pullbacks end near it. That behaviour makes it a practical **trailing guide**.

blocks.caption: Reading price against the 10-week average
head: Observation
Likely meaning
Possible response
rows: Price holds above a rising 10-week average, with pullbacks to it bouncing
Hold; trail stop below the average or the last higher low
One weekly close slightly below it, then recovery next week
Check structure, volume and market before reacting
Two or more weekly closes below it, on rising volume, with the average flattening
Reduce or exit according to your plan
Price decisively below a falling 10-week average and the 30-week
Do not hold hoping; exit rules apply

blocks.x: Violation versus normal pullback
The difficulty is telling a **violation** from a **normal pullback**. Use evidence in combination.

items: **Close, not intraday:** a weekly close below the average, not just a wick.
**Depth:** how far did it close below? A few percent is different from 8%.
**Volume:** a break on heavy weekly volume is more serious than one on declining volume.
**Slope:** is the average still rising or has it flattened?
**Context:** is the stock’s relative strength holding, and is the broad market still healthy?

blocks.x: Selling rules in strong trends

A common approach for a stock you bought on a breakout: keep the initial stop below the base. Once the stock advances, move the stop up. When the stock is working well, trail below the 10-week average, and exit on a weekly close below it, particularly when volume is high and the average is turning. If the stock is a slower, steadier compounder, the 30-week average is a wider, more patient guide.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Choose one rule before entering (for example “exit on a weekly close below the 10-week average with heavier-than-average volume”) and write it into your plan. Deciding during the drawdown is where emotion enters.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Using the 10-week average on stocks that are not trending, or on illiquid names where one week can be distorted by a single large order. The rule belongs with leaders in clear uptrends.

blocks.title: Corporate actions
blocks.x: Check that weekly data is adjusted for splits and bonuses. A fake gap can push the stock below its average on paper.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: The weekly 10-week average is a practical trailing guide for strong stocks, and the 30-week is the primary trend line. A violation is judged by close, depth, volume, slope and context, not by a single wick.

quiz.q: Why is a weekly close below the 10-week average more meaningful than a daily dip below the 50-day average?
options: It is not; daily dips are always more important
Weekly data filters out noise from five sessions, so a weekly close below the line is a more established signal
quiz.why: A weekly candle summarises five sessions. A close beyond the average at that scale reflects a more durable change in the balance of buyers and sellers.

quiz.q: A stock in a strong uptrend closes one week 1.5% below its rising 10-week average on lighter-than-average volume, then recovers the next week. How should this be read?
options: As a likely normal pullback or shakeout; it needs evidence like more closes below, heavier volume and a flattening average to become a violation
As a signal to double the position at once
As proof the stock will not rise again
quiz.why: Shallow, low-volume dips that recover quickly are typical of healthy trends. A true violation is shown by more evidence, not one close.

quiz.q: Which exit rule is best defined?
options: Exit on a weekly close below the 10-week average on above-average volume while the average is flattening
Sell as soon as the stock falls 1%
quiz.why: A written, objective rule with confirmation filters prevents emotional decisions and reduces premature exits from ordinary pullbacks.

lessons.title: Understanding volume
lessons.summary: Volume is participation. It is not direction by itself, but it tells you how seriously to take a price move.

blocks.x: **Volume** is the number of shares traded in a period. Every share traded has a buyer and a seller, so volume does not say who was more aggressive. It says **how many people cared**. Price tells you what happened and volume tells you how much weight to give it.
Key terms

blocks.caption: Volume vocabulary
head: Term
Meaning
Why it matters
rows: Mean volume over a period, usually 50 days
Shows how unusual today’s participation is
Many participants acting; institutions often involved
Interest fading; often during orderly pullbacks and bases
Volume at or near its lowest levels in the pattern
Sellers have run out, supply is thin

blocks.label: Relative volume
blocks.expr: Relative volume = Today’s volume ÷ 50-day average volume
blocks.note: Example: average 4,00,000 shares and today 10,00,000 shares gives 2.5x. Compare a stock only with its own history.

blocks.x: Why volume matters

A stock moves 4% on 1.2 times average volume in a quiet week. A different stock moves 4% on 4 times average volume right after results. The percentage is the same, but the second move involved far more capital and probably large institutions, which can sustain a move. Large funds cannot buy or sell in one day, so their activity shows up as unusual volume spread over days or weeks.

blocks.title: Delivery and liquidity
blocks.x: In India, many traders also look at delivery percentage (the share of volume that is actually delivered rather than squared off intraday). It can help judge the quality of a volume spike. Also check absolute liquidity: a ₹2 Cr daily turnover small cap can show dramatic volume changes from a few large orders.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Comparing volume across stocks, or treating high volume as bullish by definition. High volume on a decline is selling pressure, and high volume near a top can be distribution. Direction comes from price; volume adds weight.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Volume tells you how much participation stands behind a price move. Measure it against the stock’s own average, and read it together with price, never alone.

quiz.q: A stock’s 50-day average volume is 4,00,000 shares. Today it traded 10,00,000 shares. What is its relative volume?
quiz.why: 10,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 2.5. Relative volume compares today’s participation with the stock’s own baseline.

quiz.q: Why is relative volume better than raw volume for comparing today’s activity?
options: Different stocks have very different normal volumes, so only a comparison with the stock’s own average is meaningful
quiz.why: A million shares is quiet for one stock and extreme for another. Relative volume normalises for that.

lessons.title: Price and volume together
lessons.summary: Four combinations of price and volume form the core vocabulary of price-volume analysis. They are tendencies, not laws.

blocks.x: Reading price and volume together gives four basic combinations. Each one tells you about the balance between buyers and sellers, subject to context.

blocks.caption: Price and volume combinations
head: Price
Volume
Typical interpretation
Caveat
rows: Demand confirmation: buyers are willing to pay higher prices in size
A late-stage spike can also be a climax
Weaker confirmation: the rise lacks broad participation
Fine during an orderly rebound in a healthy trend
Selling pressure or distribution: sellers are active in size
May also be a final shakeout or capitulation low
Potentially normal correction: sellers are not pressing
Persistent low-volume decline in a weak trend is still a decline

blocks.title: Tendencies, not laws
blocks.x: These combinations are contextual. High volume at a decline into major support can be capitulation, which marks a low. High volume at the end of a long advance can mean exhaustion. The same combination means different things at different places in the trend.
What to look for in a healthy advance

items: Up days with higher volume than down days.
Pullbacks with contracting volume that stop near support or a rising average.
Breakouts and new highs accompanied by above-average volume.
Few or no high-volume down days that close near their lows.

blocks.x: Warning patterns

items: **Churning:** unusually heavy volume with little price progress. Large sellers may be absorbing the demand.
**Heavy down days:** a day with the biggest volume in months on a sharp decline is a serious message, particularly after an advance.
**Rising prices on shrinking volume at highs:** fewer participants are chasing.

blocks.x: An example

XYZ Technologies (fictional) rises from ₹300 to ₹360 over six weeks. Weekly volume on up weeks averages 12 lakh shares and on down weeks 6 lakh. It then falls 6% on 20 lakh shares, the heaviest week in a year, and closes at the low. Compare: if that same 6% pullback had come on 5 lakh shares and bounced from the rising 50-day average, it would read as ordinary profit-taking. The price move is the same; the volume changes the story.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Count the number of high-volume up days versus high-volume down days over the last 15 to 20 sessions. A healthy stock usually shows more of the former.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Price up with volume up confirms demand, price down with volume up warns of supply. Always ask where in the trend you are, because the same combination can signal either strength or exhaustion.

quiz.q: A stock rises 3% on volume 40% below its average at the top of a long advance. What is the most careful reading?
options: Weaker confirmation: participation is thinner, so the rise deserves less trust
quiz.why: Price rising on fading volume suggests fewer buyers. It is a caution, not a sell signal in itself.

quiz.q: After a long advance, a stock falls sharply on the heaviest volume in a year and closes at its low. What does it most likely show?
options: Heavy selling by large holders, a serious warning that supply is overwhelming demand
A buy signal because price is cheaper
Nothing, because it was one day
quiz.why: A big decline on unusual volume at the end of an advance often reflects institutional distribution. It does not predict the outcome but warrants risk reduction.

quiz.q: Why are price-volume relationships called tendencies rather than laws?
options: Because their meaning depends on context such as where in the trend they occur
Because they only work on Fridays
Because they are exact on daily charts
quiz.why: High volume on a fall can be capitulation near a low or distribution near a high. Location and trend context decide.

lessons.title: Breakout volume
lessons.summary: A breakout without participation is a rumour. Learn what breakout volume should look like, and what a failed breakout looks like.

blocks.x: When price moves above a resistance zone, it must absorb all the shares that holders want to sell there. That takes demand, and demand shows up as volume.
What good breakout volume looks like

items: A **volume surge** on the breakout day, often 1.5 to 3 times the 50-day average or more. There is no magic number. Compare with how the stock usually behaves on strong days.
The surge comes after a period of **quiet volume** during the base, so the contrast is clear.
A strong close near the day’s high, showing buyers held the move.
**Follow-through:** the next several sessions hold above the breakout level, ideally with decent volume on up days and lighter volume on pullbacks.

blocks.label: Breakout volume check
blocks.expr: Relative volume on breakout day = Breakout day volume ÷ 50-day average volume
blocks.note: Example: 12,50,000 ÷ 5,00,000 = 2.5x. A reading above roughly 1.5x is commonly considered supportive, but the stock’s own history matters.

blocks.x: Low-volume breakouts

A breakout on average or below-average volume often fails to attract follow-through. Price pushed above the level but not enough shares were absorbed. Not every low-volume breakout fails, particularly in thin stocks or in a strongly rising market, but the odds are less favourable and the risk is higher.
Failed breakouts

A failed breakout happens when price moves above resistance and then falls back below it, usually on the same volume that looked promising or on heavy selling. This is a **bull trap**: late buyers are caught above the level.

blocks.caption: Breakout quality
head: Feature
Higher quality
Lower quality
rows: Near the low, long upper wick
Holds above the level for days

blocks.title: Intraday volume
blocks.x: Volume builds through the NSE session, so a stock showing 60% of its average volume by noon may finish well above average. When judging an intraday breakout, compare volume with the typical volume by that time of day, or wait for the close.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Write down the volume ratio of every breakout you take and what happened afterwards. After 30 trades you will have your own data on how much volume tends to matter for the stocks you trade.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Breakouts need demand to absorb supply. Look for a clear volume surge after a quiet base, a strong close, and follow-through. Without them the breakout is more likely to fail, and a quick exit is part of the plan.

quiz.q: A stock breaks out of a base on 2.5 times average volume after a quiet, low-volume base and closes near its high. What does this combination suggest?
options: Strong demand absorbed the supply at resistance, which raises the odds of follow-through
quiz.why: Volume expansion against a quiet backdrop plus a strong close is the footprint of real demand. It improves odds but nothing is guaranteed.

quiz.q: What is a bull trap?
options: A rise on very high volume
A breakout above resistance that falls back below it, trapping buyers who bought the move
A gap down on bad news
quiz.why: The breakout fails to hold, so buyers are caught above the level. This is why stops and a rule about closing back below the pivot exist.

quiz.q: Why can a stock that has 60% of its average volume by noon still be a valid high-volume breakout day?
options: Volume accumulates through the session, so it may finish well above average
Noon volume is the only volume that counts
quiz.why: Judging intraday needs time-of-day awareness. Many traders use the close or compare with typical volume by that hour.

lessons.title: Accumulation and distribution
lessons.summary: Large investors cannot buy or sell in a day. Their footprints show up as accumulation and distribution. Indicators like OBV try to measure it.

blocks.x: Mutual funds, insurers and foreign portfolio investors take days or weeks to build a position without moving the price too far. That process is **accumulation**. When they exit, it is **distribution**. Neither is announced, but both leave footprints in price and volume.

blocks.caption: Accumulation versus distribution
head: Feature
Accumulation
Distribution
rows: Bases, quiet pullbacks, early in an advance
Near highs, in extended or topping stocks
Higher volume but weak closes, stalling

blocks.x: Up-volume and down-volume

A simple measure is to add the volume on up days and compare it with the volume on down days over a period (for example 50 days). A ratio above 1 means more volume came on up days. It is crude but intuitive.
On-Balance Volume (OBV)

blocks.label: OBV
blocks.expr:
If today’s close > yesterday’s: OBV = previous OBV + today’s volume
If today’s close < yesterday’s: OBV = previous OBV − today’s volume
If unchanged: OBV = previous OBV
blocks.note: OBV is a running total. The absolute value means nothing. The direction and divergences from price are what you read.

blocks.x: If price is flat in a base while OBV rises to a new high, it can suggest buyers are quietly absorbing supply. If price makes a new high while OBV fails to, it suggests the rise has less volume behind it.
Accumulation/Distribution line and similar tools

The Accumulation/Distribution (A/D) line and Chaikin money flow use **where the close sits in the day’s range** to weigh the volume. A close near the high counts as more accumulation and a close near the low as more distribution. They add detail beyond OBV, which only checks whether the close was up or down.
Limitations

items: These indicators assume volume reflects institutional behaviour. It also contains retail and intraday trading.
A single huge block trade can distort the line for months.
They are derived from price and volume, so they cannot show new information. Use them to confirm what price and volume visually suggest.
On illiquid small caps, volume is erratic and these tools are less reliable.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Buying only because OBV is rising. An indicator can improve confidence in a setup that already looks good on the chart. It does not replace the setup.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Accumulation shows demand quietly absorbing supply, distribution shows supply overwhelming demand. Up-volume versus down-volume, OBV and A/D lines can help, but they are secondary to the price and volume bars themselves.

quiz.q: Price is flat in a six-week base while OBV climbs to a new high. What might this suggest?
options: Buyers may be quietly absorbing supply, a possible sign of accumulation, which still needs confirmation from price
quiz.why: OBV rising while price is flat means more volume is trading on up days than down days. It is a clue, not a signal.

quiz.q: Which pattern is more consistent with distribution?
options: Heavy volume on up days that close strong
Repeated heavy-volume days near highs with weak closes and stalling price
Light volume pullbacks that hold support
quiz.why: Stalling price with heavy volume and weak closes suggests supply is meeting demand at those levels.

quiz.q: What is a limitation of OBV?
options: It only uses whether the close was up or down, and one very large block of volume can distort it for a long time
It works only on weekly charts
quiz.why: OBV treats all volume on an up day as buying, which is crude. Large single-day volume can dominate the running total.

lessons.title: RSI: what it measures and what it does not
lessons.summary: RSI compares recent gains with recent losses. In strong trends it can stay high for a long time, so its value lies in ranges and divergences, not in 70/30 rules.

blocks.x: The **Relative Strength Index (RSI)**, created by J. Welles Wilder, measures the **speed and size of recent price changes** on a 0 to 100 scale. It is a momentum oscillator: it asks whether recent gains have been larger than recent losses.

blocks.title: RSI is not Relative Strength
blocks.x: RSI measures a stock’s own momentum. **Relative strength** compares a stock with an index or other stocks. They are different tools with similar names. The Relative Strength track covers the second.
The calculation idea

blocks.label: RSI (14 periods)
blocks.expr:
RS  = Average gain over 14 periods ÷ Average loss over 14 periods
RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ (1 + RS)
blocks.note: Wilder smooths the averages rather than taking a plain mean. If average gain is 1.2 and average loss is 0.6, RS = 2 and RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ 3 = 66.7.

blocks.x: If a stock has only gained, RSI approaches 100. If it has only lost, RSI approaches 0. A value near 50 means gains and losses have been balanced.
Why 70 and 30 do not mean sell and buy

The textbook rule says above 70 is overbought and below 30 is oversold. That is true for **ranging** markets and often fails in trends. A stock in a powerful advance can stay above 70 for weeks because strong momentum is exactly what produces high RSI. Selling every reading above 70 means selling the best stocks early.

blocks.title: Overbought is not automatically bearish
blocks.x: A high RSI shows strong momentum, not a reversal. In a downtrend, an RSI below 30 can persist while the stock keeps falling. Oversold is not automatically bullish.
RSI ranges during trends

blocks.caption: RSI behaviour by regime
head: Regime
Typical RSI zone
How to use it
rows: Often 40 to 80; dips to roughly 40 to 50 tend to attract buyers
Use pullbacks to the 40 to 50 area as potential entry context, with price confirming
Often 20 to 60; rallies to roughly 50 to 60 tend to stall
Treat 50 to 60 as resistance on rallies; avoid catching knives at 30
Classic overbought/oversold readings are more reliable here

blocks.x: Divergence

A **bearish divergence** occurs when price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high, showing the push has less momentum. A **bullish divergence** is a lower low in price with a higher low in RSI. Divergences warn that momentum is changing, but they can persist while price keeps trending, so they are best used with structure: a divergence plus a break of the last higher low is far stronger than a divergence alone.
Failure swings and RSI levels

items: **Failure swing (top):** RSI rises above 70, pulls back, rallies but fails to exceed its previous peak, then breaks below the pullback low. It suggests momentum cannot make a new push.
**RSI support and resistance:** RSI itself can break trendlines and hold levels. A move above 60 after a base can signal that momentum has shifted bullish.

blocks.title: When RSI helps
blocks.x: In ranges, for finding exhaustion near boundaries. In trends, for spotting the zone where pullbacks tend to end, and for detecting divergence at structural turning points.

blocks.title: When to ignore it
blocks.x: As a stand-alone sell signal for a leading stock above 70, or as a stand-alone buy signal for a stock falling in a weak structure at 30.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: RSI measures momentum. Use its regime-based ranges and divergences with price structure. The 70/30 rule is a range-market tool, not a universal signal.

quiz.q: A stock has average gains of 1.2 and average losses of 0.6 over 14 periods. What is RSI?
A leading stock in a strong uptrend shows RSI above 70 for six weeks. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: It must be sold immediately because it is overbought
Strong momentum can keep RSI elevated; the reading alone is not a reversal signal, and structure and volume should decide
It will fall to 30 next week
quiz.why: High RSI in a strong trend is a feature of momentum, not a flaw. Exits should rely on structure, risk rules and evidence of distribution.

quiz.q: Price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high. What is it called, and how should it be used?
options: A bearish divergence: a warning of weakening momentum, best combined with a break of structure
quiz.why: Divergences warn that the push is weaker. They can persist for long periods, so acting only on the divergence leads to early exits.

lessons.title: MACD
lessons.summary: MACD measures the gap between two moving averages. Learn to read the line, the signal, the histogram and the zero line.

blocks.x: **MACD** (Moving Average Convergence Divergence) shows how far a fast EMA has moved from a slow EMA, and whether that gap is widening or shrinking. In other words, it measures **trend and momentum together**.

blocks.label: Standard MACD (12, 26, 9)
blocks.expr:
MACD line   = EMA(12) − EMA(26)
Signal line = EMA(9) of the MACD line
Histogram   = MACD line − Signal line
blocks.note: When the fast EMA is above the slow one, MACD is positive. Its distance from zero reflects how strong the trend is.

blocks.x: The three components

items: **MACD line:** the gap between the fast and slow EMA. Rising means the trend is accelerating, falling means decelerating.
**Signal line:** a smoothed MACD. When MACD crosses it, momentum has shifted a notch.
**Histogram:** the gap between them. It is the earliest component to show acceleration or deceleration, because it turns before the lines cross.

blocks.x: Crossovers and the zero line

blocks.caption: Reading MACD
head: Event
What it says
Caveat
rows: MACD crosses above the signal line
Frequent in ranges; many false signals
MACD crosses below the signal line
In a strong trend this often marks only a pause
Fast EMA moved above slow EMA: an upward shift in trend
Histogram shrinking while price still rises
Can precede a pause or just consolidation
Momentum no longer confirming the new high or low
Can persist for long; use with structure

blocks.x: Momentum acceleration and deceleration

A rising histogram means momentum is accelerating. A histogram that peaks and starts shrinking, even while still positive, means the pace is slowing. That is information about **speed**, not about direction reversing. A car decelerating from 120 to 90 km/h is still moving forward.
Trend versus range behaviour

MACD is built from moving averages, so it behaves like them. In trends it gives useful context. In ranges it crosses back and forth constantly and produces many small losses if traded as a system. Use it after you know the regime.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: In a stock with strong structure, MACD staying above zero supports the view that the primary trend is up. A first dip of MACD toward zero followed by a turn back up often accompanies healthy pullbacks.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Selling every bearish signal-line cross in a strong uptrend. These crosses are common in healthy pauses and would cut your winners short.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: MACD is the gap between two EMAs plus a smoothed version. It helps judge whether trend momentum is accelerating or fading, works best in trending markets, and lags like any average-based tool.

quiz.q: What does the standard MACD line represent?
quiz.why: MACD is the difference between a fast and a slow exponential moving average, so it measures the gap between short-term and longer-term trend.

quiz.q: The histogram is shrinking while price is still rising. What does this show?
options: Acceleration is slowing; the advance is losing speed but not necessarily direction
quiz.why: The histogram measures the gap between MACD and signal. A shrinking gap means momentum is slowing. That can precede a pause or a reversal.

quiz.q: Why does MACD generate many false crossover signals in a sideways market?
options: It is built from moving averages, which cross back and forth when price has no sustained direction
It only works in bear markets
quiz.why: Averages need a trend to stay separated. In a range, the fast average repeatedly crosses the slow one.

lessons.title: The stochastic oscillator
lessons.summary: The stochastic shows where the close sits within its recent range. Useful in ranges, misleading in strong trends.

blocks.x: The **stochastic oscillator** asks a simple question: in the last N periods, is the close near the top of the range or near the bottom? In strong rising markets, closes tend to be near the highs of the range. In weak markets, they tend to be near the lows.

blocks.label: Stochastic %K (14)
blocks.expr:
%K = (Close − Lowest Low over 14) ÷ (Highest High over 14 − Lowest Low over 14) × 100
%D = 3-period average of %K
blocks.note: Example: the 14-day low is ₹90, the high is ₹110 and the close is ₹107. %K = (107 − 90) ÷ 20 × 100 = 85.

blocks.x: **Fast stochastic** uses the raw %K. **Slow stochastic** first smooths %K with a 3-period average, so its %K equals the fast %D. Slow is more common because it has fewer false flickers.
Overbought and oversold

Readings above 80 are called overbought and below 20 oversold. In a range, price tends to turn at the edges, so crossing back below 80 or above 20 gives timing clues. In a strong trend, the stochastic can sit above 80 for weeks because the close keeps landing near the top of the range. Treating that as a sell is a classic mistake.

blocks.title: Why it fails in trends
blocks.x: The stochastic measures position within a **recent range**, not trend strength. A stock grinding up with closes near the highs keeps reading overbought while price keeps rising.
Where it helps

items: **Range-bound markets:** boundaries at roughly 20 and 80 can time bounces within a known support/resistance box.
**Pullback timing in a trend:** a dip below 20 and a turn back above it in a stock with a strong, rising structure can add timing detail to an entry near support.
**Divergence:** like RSI, a lower stochastic high at a price high can warn of fading momentum.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Decide the regime first. If the stock is in a trend, ignore overbought readings and use dips to the low zone for timing. If in a range, treat the extremes as meaningful.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: The stochastic shows where the close is within its recent range. It is a range-market tool, can stay overbought in strong trends, and is best used for timing after the regime is identified.

quiz.q: The 14-day low is ₹90, the high is ₹110 and today’s close is ₹107. What is %K?
Why can the stochastic stay above 80 for many weeks in a strong uptrend?
options: Because it measures where the close sits within its recent range, and in strong trends closes cluster near the highs
Because it only works on weekly data
quiz.why: In a steady advance, each close is near the top of the lookback range, so the oscillator stays high. That reflects strength, not a certain top.

lessons.title: Choosing between momentum indicators
lessons.summary: Three indicators answer slightly different questions. Pick one with a purpose, not one of each by habit.

blocks.x: RSI, MACD and the stochastic all summarise momentum, so they are strongly correlated. Using all three at once usually repeats the same information three times and creates false confidence. The goal is to know when each is the right tool.

blocks.caption: Indicator comparison
head: Indicator
Measures
Best use
Major weakness
rows: Speed of recent gains versus losses
Momentum regime (40 to 80 vs 20 to 60 zones), divergence
Can stay extreme in strong trends
Gap between fast and slow EMA
Lags; many false crosses in ranges
Range markets and timing dips within a range
Overbought for long in strong trends

blocks.x: Matching tool to question

items: “Is momentum still healthy in this uptrend?” → RSI zone behaviour or MACD above zero.
“Is acceleration fading?” → MACD histogram.
“Is this a range, and where in the range are we?” → Stochastic with support and resistance.
“Is a new high being confirmed?” → Compare price with RSI or MACD highs for divergence.

blocks.title: Indicators support price
blocks.x: Structure, trend, volume and relative strength come first. A momentum indicator is a measuring tool for the push behind price. If price structure says wait, no indicator reading should override it.
The danger of indicator stacking
