Adding indicators until they agree is a form of confirmation bias. You will almost always find one that supports the trade you already want. A better approach: choose one momentum tool, learn its behaviour on your stocks, and write down what it must show for a setup to qualify.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating a bearish MACD cross, an RSI above 70 and a stochastic above 80 as three independent warnings. They all derive from the same price series and often react together.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: For trend-following setups in this course, a simple filter is enough: relative strength and price structure first, and RSI or MACD only for timing and for detecting divergence at key levels.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Momentum indicators are correlated views of the same data. Choose one for a defined purpose, learn its behaviour by regime, and keep price structure, volume and relative strength as the decision core.

quiz.q: Which pairing of tool and question is best?
options: Stochastic to decide whether a strong stock is in a long-term uptrend
MACD histogram to see whether trend momentum is accelerating or fading
OBV to find the exact top
quiz.why: The histogram measures the change in gap between MACD and its signal line, which describes acceleration. The other pairings use the wrong tool for the question.

quiz.q: A trader waits until RSI, MACD and the stochastic all agree before buying. What is the risk?
options: None; more indicators always mean better odds
They are correlated views of the same price data, so agreement adds little new information and can create false confidence
quiz.why: Momentum indicators are derived from the same prices. Agreement among them is largely redundant, and selecting for agreement can be confirmation bias.

lessons.title: Relative strength versus RSI
lessons.summary: Relative strength compares one stock with something else. It is the single most useful filter for finding leaders.

blocks.x: **Relative strength (RS)** compares the performance of a stock with a benchmark such as the NIFTY 50, or with its sector or peers. It asks: **is this stock doing better or worse than the market?**

blocks.title: RS is not RSI
blocks.x: RSI is an oscillator built from a single stock’s own price changes. Relative strength is a comparison between two price series. A stock can have a low RSI and strong relative strength (it is falling less than the market), or a high RSI and weak relative strength (it is rising less than the market).
Relative performance

Suppose over six months the NIFTY 50 is up 8%. ABC Industries is up 24% and PQR Engineering is up 3%. ABC outperformed the market by a wide margin and PQR underperformed, even though both rose. A stock that rises less than the market in a rally is lagging and usually attracts less institutional buying.
The relative strength line

blocks.label: RS line
blocks.expr: RS line = Stock price ÷ Benchmark price
blocks.note: Plot this ratio over time. A rising line means the stock is outperforming the benchmark. A falling line means it is underperforming. Direction matters more than the level.

items: **Stock versus NIFTY:** shows market leadership.
**Stock versus its sector index:** shows whether it is a leader within its group.
**RS line making new highs before price:** an early sign of leadership. Many leaders show this before they break out.

blocks.x: Why leaders outperform before they become obvious

Institutions build positions over weeks. Their buying lifts a stock relative to the index even before the price breaks a visible level, and that shows up in the RS line. By the time headlines and screens highlight the stock, it may already be well ahead. Watching the RS line lets you see the lead earlier.

blocks.title: TradeEdge
blocks.x: TradeEdge’s chart previews show Mansfield relative strength, and its screens use RS Rating and RS-based columns. The next lessons explain what those represent.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Relative strength compares a stock with a benchmark. A rising RS line shows outperformance, and leaders often show strong RS before their breakout. It is different from RSI.

quiz.q: The NIFTY 50 is up 8% over six months. ABC is up 24% and PQR is up 3%. Which statement is correct?
options: Both have strong relative strength because both rose
ABC has strong relative strength; PQR has weak relative strength despite rising
Relative strength cannot be negative if price rose
quiz.why: Relative strength is about performance versus the benchmark. PQR rose but underperformed the market.

quiz.q: How is a basic RS line calculated?
options: Stock price divided by benchmark price
quiz.why: The ratio of a stock to its benchmark rises when the stock outperforms and falls when it lags.

quiz.q: A stock’s price is still in a base but its RS line has just made a new high. What might this suggest?
options: Possible early leadership: the stock is outperforming even before a price breakout
quiz.why: An RS line at new highs ahead of price often appears before breakouts in leaders. It is a positive clue, not a trigger.

lessons.title: Relative strength rating and ranking
lessons.summary: An RS rating ranks a stock against all others over multiple horizons. It condenses leadership into a number you can screen on.

blocks.x: The RS line shows one stock against one benchmark. An **RS rating** ranks one stock against **all other stocks**. A rating of 90 means the stock’s weighted performance ranks in the top 10%, and one of 40 means it is below the median.
How ratings are typically built

items: Compute returns over several horizons: for example **3-month, 6-month and 12-month**.
Combine them into a composite score, often giving the most recent period more weight (for example heavier weight on the last 3 months).
Convert the composite score into a **percentile rank** across the universe, from 1 (weakest) to 99 (strongest).

blocks.caption: Horizon roles
head: Horizon
What it captures
Risk if used alone
rows: Can be noisy and chase short spikes
Late: may include a move that has already ended
A balance of all of them
Weights are a design choice, so ratings differ across providers

blocks.x: A **percentile ranking** is relative. If the whole market falls, a stock that falls less can still rank high. That is consistent with the idea of leadership: strong stocks resist declines and lead the rebound.
Why leadership matters

Studies of past big winners consistently find that they ranked high in relative strength before their major advances. A stock with a rating of 85 or above is already outperforming most of the market, which suggests institutions favour it. This does not guarantee future results, but it shifts the odds. Starting with strong stocks and waiting for a good entry beats starting with weak stocks and hoping they turn.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: Many TradeEdge screens use an RS Rating threshold, such as 70 or 80 and above, and RS improving screens look for stocks whose RS is rising versus one or two weeks earlier. Higher thresholds produce shorter lists of stronger names.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating a high rating as a buy signal. It is a **filter** for candidates. Entry, stop, volume and market conditions still decide the trade. Also remember a rating that is very high can mean the stock is already extended.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: An RS rating ranks a stock against the whole universe using weighted returns over several horizons. It is a leadership filter, not an entry signal.

quiz.q: What does an RS rating of 90 usually mean?
options: The stock’s weighted performance ranks in roughly the top 10% of the universe
quiz.why: RS ratings are percentile ranks. 90 means better than about 90% of stocks on the rating’s performance measure.

quiz.q: Why combine 3-, 6- and 12-month returns in a rating?
options: To balance recent momentum with established leadership and reduce the weakness of any single horizon
quiz.why: Each horizon has a bias: short is noisy, long is late. A composite balances them.

quiz.q: What is the right role of an RS rating in a trading process?
options: A filter that narrows the list to leaders, with entry, stop and market conditions still needed
quiz.why: A rating tells you which stocks lead. It does not tell you when to buy, where you are wrong, or how much to risk.

lessons.title: Mansfield relative strength
lessons.summary: Stan Weinstein’s version of the RS line puts a zero line on the chart, so outperformance and underperformance are visible at a glance.

blocks.x: **Mansfield relative strength** is a refinement of the RS line popularised by Stan Weinstein. The plain RS ratio has no natural reference, and you only see whether it is rising or falling. Mansfield RS normalises the ratio around a **zero line**, so you can immediately tell whether a stock has been outperforming or underperforming over the past year.

blocks.label: Mansfield RS (classic form)
blocks.expr:
RS ratio         = Stock close ÷ Benchmark close
Mansfield RS     = ( RS ratio ÷ 52-week average of RS ratio − 1 ) × 10
blocks.note: Above zero: the stock’s RS is above its own 52-week average. Below zero: below it. Implementations differ in scaling and smoothing, so check how your platform defines it.

blocks.x: Interpretation

blocks.caption: Reading Mansfield RS
head: Observation
Meaning
Use
rows: Crossing from below to above zero
RS has turned positive; leadership emerging
A positive sign when price is in a Stage 1 to 2 transition
Avoid for long setups unless a clear turn develops

blocks.x: Weekly interpretation

Weinstein applied it on **weekly** charts, aligned with the 30-week average. A stock breaking out of a long base into Stage 2 with Mansfield RS crossing above zero is a stronger case than one breaking out with RS still deep below zero. The latter is a breakout without leadership and, in his experience, was more likely to fail.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: TradeEdge computes Mansfield RS weekly in its database and shows it in chart preview popovers across dashboards. Use it as a quick leadership check when reviewing a screen result: is RS above zero and rising, or below zero and weak?

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Relying on a zero-line cross as a trigger. The line crossing zero says relative performance improved over the past year’s average. It does not say price is at a good entry, nor that the stock will keep outperforming.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Mansfield RS plots the RS ratio relative to its 52-week average around a zero line, making outperformance versus underperformance visible. Above zero and rising supports leadership; below zero is a caution.

quiz.q: What does Mansfield RS above zero tell you?
options: The stock price is above its 200-day average
The stock’s relative strength ratio is above its own 52-week average, so it has been outperforming the benchmark
quiz.why: Mansfield RS normalises the RS ratio against its 52-week average. Above zero means current relative performance is stronger than the past year’s typical level.

quiz.q: Why does Weinstein prefer Stage 2 breakouts with positive Mansfield RS?
options: Because positive RS shows the breakout has leadership behind it, which in his experience reduces failures
quiz.why: Breakouts in stocks that already lead the market tend to attract more sustained buying. It improves odds but does not remove risk.

lessons.title: Finding market leaders
lessons.summary: A practical checklist that combines price, relative strength, sector and structure to separate leaders from laggards.

blocks.x: Cheap stocks are not the best place to look for big winners. Historically, stocks that rose the most started their advance already **showing strength**. Finding leaders means stacking several pieces of evidence.

blocks.label: Leadership checklist
blocks.expr:
Price near 52-week high
+ Strong relative strength (RS line rising, high RS rating)
+ Strong sector
+ Positive trend (rising averages, price above them)
+ Constructive base
+ Volume confirmation
blocks.note: No single item is enough. Leaders usually satisfy most of these at the same time.

blocks.x: Why each item matters

blocks.caption: Leadership evidence
head: Item
What it shows
Failure signal
rows: No heavy overhead supply from trapped holders
Far below the high, with a long road back to breakeven for holders
Institutions prefer it to the market
RS line falling or making new lows
Orderly digestion of the prior advance
Accumulation on up days, dry-up on pullbacks

blocks.x: Leaders versus cheap stocks

A stock down 45% from its high may look attractive, but it carries a lot of supply: everyone who bought higher wants out near breakeven. A stock at a new high has no such overhead. Buying strength means paying a higher price per share but facing less resistance, and the odds of continuation have historically favoured the strong.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: Combine screens: a Stage 2 or Trend Template screen for the trend, an RS Rating threshold for leadership, and a check on sector strength in Sector Rotation. Then open the chart and judge the base and volume yourself.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Choosing the highest RS rating without looking at the chart. A stock that has gone up 300% in three months may have a top-tier rating and also be dangerously extended. Leadership and a good entry point are different questions.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.x: A leader is a stock that other stocks are measured against. You are not trying to buy the cheapest stock in a good sector; you are trying to buy the strongest while its risk is still low.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Leaders show strong relative strength, trend alignment, sector support, constructive bases and volume confirmation, near 52-week highs. Use RS as a filter, then judge the chart for a low-risk entry.

quiz.q: Why is a stock near its 52-week high often a better candidate than one 45% below its high?
options: Because it has less overhead supply from holders waiting to sell at breakeven, and it shows strength
Because 52-week highs are guaranteed to rise
quiz.why: Holders who bought higher create supply as price approaches their cost. Near highs, that overhead is largely absent.

quiz.q: A stock has an RS rating of 98 after rising 300% in three months and is 60% above its 50-day average. What is the sensible conclusion?
options: It is a perfect entry because the rating is the highest
It is a clear leader but may be extended, so the entry risk is a separate question
quiz.why: Leadership and entry quality are different. Even the strongest leader can offer poor risk/reward when far above its support.

quiz.q: Which is the best approach to build a leadership shortlist?
options: Combine trend, RS rating, sector strength and base quality, then review charts
Pick whatever is in the news
quiz.why: Leadership is multi-factor. A stack of evidence is more reliable than any single filter.

lessons.title: Stan Weinstein’s four stages
lessons.summary: A stock’s life cycle has four stages. The 30-week average, volume and relative strength decide which one you are in.

blocks.x: Stan Weinstein’s core idea is that **every stock is always in one of four stages**, and the single best decision is to avoid owning stocks in the wrong stages. He used weekly charts and the **30-week moving average** (roughly the 150-day) as the main reference.

blocks.caption: The four stages
head: Stage
Name
Price vs 30-week MA
30-week MA slope
Meaning
rows: Buyers and sellers balanced after a decline
Demand dominates; the trend is up
Supply dominates; the trend is down

blocks.x: What defines each stage

items: **The 30-week MA:** its slope and the position of price are the first test.
**Volume:** rises on advances in Stage 2 and on declines in Stage 4. Dries up during basing.
**Relative strength:** typically turns positive as Stage 1 ends and stays strong in Stage 2.
**Breakout or breakdown:** a move out of the base above resistance on volume starts Stage 2. A break below support starts Stage 4.

blocks.x: The transition between stages

Stage transitions are gradual. Stage 1 to 2 is confirmed by a breakout above the base’s resistance and the 30-week average, on strong volume, with the average flattening or turning up. Stage 2 to 3 shows as the average flattening, price chopping across it, and heavy volume with little progress. Stage 3 to 4 is a break below support and the average. Stage 4 to 1 is a long, quiet base after the decline.

blocks.title: The main idea
blocks.x: You do not need to buy at the bottom or sell at the top. You need to **own stocks in Stage 2 and avoid Stages 3 and 4**. Participating in the middle of the advance is enough.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: The Watchlist dashboard shows a Weinstein stage for each stock, and the Stage 2 Early screen under Market Leaders looks for stocks transitioning into Stage 2. Use the stage as a first filter, then confirm on the chart.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating stage as a precise label. Stages are an analytical framework, and stocks can sit on the boundary between two for weeks. When ambiguous, assume the less favourable stage.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: There are four stages: basing, advancing, topping and declining. The 30-week average slope, price location, volume and relative strength classify them. The goal is to participate in Stage 2 and avoid Stages 3 and 4.

quiz.q: Which description fits Stage 2?
options: Price below a falling 30-week MA with heavy volume on declines
Price above a rising 30-week MA, with strong relative strength and volume expanding on advances
Price oscillating around a flat 30-week MA with low volume
Price crossing a turning-down MA after a long run
quiz.why: Stage 2 is the advancing phase: price above a rising 30-week average with demand visible in volume and relative strength.

quiz.q: What is the practical goal of the stage framework?
options: To own stocks in Stage 2 and avoid Stages 3 and 4, rather than predicting tops and bottoms
quiz.why: The framework improves odds by avoiding stocks in unfavourable stages. It does not require perfect timing of turning points.

quiz.q: A stock sits right on the boundary between Stage 3 and Stage 4, with the 30-week MA falling. What is a sensible assumption?
options: When ambiguous, assume the less favourable stage until the chart proves otherwise
quiz.why: Capital preservation matters. A falling average with weak price action should be treated as Stage 4 risk until evidence improves.

lessons.title: Stage 1: the basing stage
lessons.summary: After a decline, a stock goes quiet. Learn the signs of accumulation, and why Stage 1 is a time to watch rather than buy.

blocks.x: Stage 1 follows a Stage 4 decline. Selling has exhausted itself, but buyers have not yet taken control. The stock moves sideways for months, sometimes years, in a base.
Characteristics

items: **Long consolidation:** often at least a few months, sometimes much longer. The longer the base, the greater the potential energy for the next move.
**Declining volatility:** the swings tighten compared with the earlier decline.
**Flattening 30-week MA:** the average stops falling and gradually levels off.
**Volume dry-up:** trading activity falls, and spikes tend to occur on up days.
**Failed breakouts:** brief pokes above resistance that reverse are common. They shake out weak hands.
**Accumulation:** large buyers gradually absorb supply at low prices.

blocks.caption: Late Stage 1 evidence
head: Evidence
Why it is encouraging
rows: Price holds above a prior low several times
Sellers can no longer push lower
Mansfield RS moves toward and across zero

blocks.x: Why not buy in Stage 1?

Because capital in a base is idle. A stock can trade sideways for a year, and then fall back into Stage 4. You gain only when it breaks out, and by then the breakout offers a higher-confidence entry with defined risk. Buying early means paying with time and uncertainty for a slightly lower price.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Keep a watchlist of late Stage 1 stocks with improving RS and tightening ranges. They are the pool from which Stage 2 breakouts emerge.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Calling every decline’s first bounce a Stage 1 base. A real base takes time, and the 30-week average must flatten. A short pause under a falling average is still Stage 4.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Stage 1 is a long, quiet base after a decline, with flattening averages and drying volume. Watch it and wait for a breakout rather than paying to be early.

quiz.q: Which sign most supports the end of a Stage 1 base?
options: A falling 30-week MA with heavy selling
Higher lows, tightening volatility, improving RS and volume spikes on up days
A single bounce lasting two weeks
quiz.why: A maturing base shows buyers becoming more aggressive, supply drying up and relative performance improving.

quiz.q: Why does Weinstein suggest not buying during Stage 1?
options: Because stocks in Stage 1 always fall
Because the capital may be idle for a long time and the stock can slip back to Stage 4, whereas a confirmed breakout provides better evidence and risk definition
Because volume is impossible to read
Because Stage 1 stocks cannot be traded
quiz.why: The cost of early entry is time and uncertainty. A breakout from the base gives a clearer entry, stop and confirmation.

lessons.title: Stage 2: the advancing stage
lessons.summary: Stage 2 is where most of the gains are made. Learn what a healthy advance looks like and why participating beats predicting.

blocks.x: Stage 2 begins when price breaks above the resistance of a Stage 1 base, on strong volume, and moves above a rising 30-week average. It is the phase when institutions have been buying, supply has been absorbed, and the stock trends up.
Characteristics

items: Price **above a rising 30-week MA**, with the average sloping up.
**Higher highs and higher lows.** Pullbacks are shallower than advances.
**Strong relative strength:** Mansfield RS above zero and often rising.
**Breakouts from successive bases** as the stock moves up in steps.
**Volume expansion on advances** and contraction on pullbacks.
**Pullbacks that hold the rising averages,** often the 10-week or the 30-week.

blocks.x: Breakouts, pullbacks and add-on opportunities

blocks.caption: Opportunities within Stage 2
head: Opportunity
What it looks like
Notes
rows: Initial breakout from a Stage 1 base
A move above resistance on heavy volume
A dip toward the breakout level on light volume
A second chance with a tight stop
A new breakout from a smaller base higher up
Needs RS and trend intact; extended entries carry more risk
A test of the 10-week or 30-week average
Works best in leaders with healthy volume patterns

blocks.x: Participate rather than predict

Weinstein’s main point is that you do not need to buy the exact low. The early part of Stage 2 provides a lot of the move. Aiming to buy the bottom exposes you to long waits and false starts. Waiting for Stage 2 means you buy at a higher price per share, but with confirmation, momentum and a clear risk level.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: The Stage 2 Early screen under Market Leaders targets stocks just entering Stage 2 (price above rising shorter averages and RS improving), and the Trend Template screens select established Stage 2 trends.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating Stage 2 as a promise. Many Stage 2 stocks fail at the first breakout, especially in a weak market. A stop is still essential.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Stage 2 is the advancing phase: price above a rising 30-week MA, strong RS and volume on advances. Participate on confirmation, add on constructive pullbacks, and keep stops.

quiz.q: Which is the best summary of how to approach Stage 2?
options: Predict the bottom and buy before the base ends
Participate after confirmation, using the breakout and healthy pullbacks, rather than predicting the low
Wait until the stock has doubled
Avoid all stocks above their averages
quiz.why: Stage 2 offers many entries with confirmation and defined risk. Predicting lows costs time and exposes you to false starts.

quiz.q: Which behaviour suggests a healthy Stage 2 advance?
options: Heavy volume on declines and light volume on advances
Higher highs and higher lows, volume expanding on advances and contracting on pullbacks, pullbacks holding rising averages
Price crossing a falling MA repeatedly
quiz.why: The Stage 2 footprint is trend, volume and relative strength all pointing the same way.

lessons.title: Stage 3 and Stage 4
lessons.summary: Stage 3 is the top, Stage 4 the decline. Learn the warning signs and why holding a declining stock is a cost, not a strategy.

blocks.x: Every advance ends. The goal is to notice **before** a large part of the gain is lost, and to avoid owning stocks that are falling.
Stage 3: distribution

items: **The 30-week MA flattens** and may begin to turn down.
**Price chops back and forth across the average** rather than staying above it.
**Failed rallies:** advances stall below the prior high.
**Churning volume:** heavy trading with little price progress, as large holders sell into strength.
**Relative strength weakens**, often before price.
**Lower highs** form, and then support breaks.

blocks.x: Stage 4: decline

items: Price **below a falling 30-week MA.** Rallies fail at or below the average.
**Lower highs and lower lows.**
**Heavy volume on declines,** though breakdowns can also happen on moderate volume.
**Negative Mansfield RS.**
**Bounces that look attractive** because the stock is “cheap”, but supply from trapped holders caps them.

blocks.caption: Stage 3 versus Stage 4
head: Feature
Stage 3
Stage 4
rows: Flat or beginning to roll over
Reduce, tighten stops, avoid new buys
Avoid longs; exit remaining holdings by plan

blocks.x: The risk of holding declining stocks

A stock that falls 50% needs a 100% gain to recover. Holding while it falls ties up capital that could earn elsewhere, and recovery can take years if at all. Hoping a Stage 4 stock will return to Stage 2 turns a controlled loss into an open-ended one.

blocks.title: Cheap is not a reason
blocks.x: A stock down 60% can easily fall another 50%. Weinstein’s rule is simple: do not buy Stage 4 stocks, regardless of price or the story.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: When a holding enters Stage 3, review the stop, reduce size or stop adding. Do not wait for Stage 4 confirmation to act on risk.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Stage 3 shows distribution: flat average, chopping price, churning volume. Stage 4 is a decline below a falling average. Avoid buying Stage 4 and treat Stage 3 as a signal to reduce risk.

quiz.q: Which sign is most associated with Stage 3 rather than Stage 2?
options: A rising 30-week MA with price well above it
A flattening 30-week MA, price chopping across it, and heavy volume with little price progress
A first breakout from a long base
quiz.why: The loss of progress with heavy volume and a flattening average indicates supply meeting demand at the top.

quiz.q: A stock fell 50%. How much must it gain to return to its previous high?
quiz.why: If a ₹200 stock falls to ₹100, it needs to double (+100%) to return to ₹200. Losses are asymmetric.

quiz.q: A Stage 4 stock is down 60% and looks cheap. What does stage analysis say?
options: Buy more as it is cheap
Avoid it: the trend is down and supply overhead is heavy; wait for a long base and a Stage 2 breakout
quiz.why: Price alone does not indicate value. The trend and structure still point down, and the odds are better elsewhere.

lessons.title: Classifying a stock’s stage in practice
lessons.summary: Turn the stage framework into a checklist you can apply to any weekly chart, and learn where it can mislead.

blocks.x: Stage classification is a judgement framework. A simple scorecard keeps it consistent and reduces bias.

blocks.label: Stage 2 scorecard
blocks.expr:
☐ Price > 30-week MA
☐ 30-week MA rising
☐ Relative strength positive (Mansfield above zero or rising RS line)
☐ Higher highs and higher lows
☐ Breakout or constructive consolidation near highs
☐ Volume confirms (expansion on advances, contraction on pullbacks)
blocks.note: Score one point for each. Six of six is a clear Stage 2. Four or five is probable but needs review. Below four, look at the other stages.

blocks.caption: Reading the score
head: Items met
Likely interpretation
Suggested action
rows: Eligible for setups; judge entry and risk
Early or late Stage 2, or messy
Check which items fail and why

blocks.x: Worked example

ABC Industries (fictional) trades at ₹540. Its 30-week MA is ₹480 and rising for the past 10 weeks. It broke out of a 6-month base at ₹520 two weeks ago on 2.2 times average volume. Mansfield RS crossed above zero three weeks earlier. The last pullback made a higher low at ₹505.

items: Price > 30-week MA (₹540 > ₹480): yes.
MA rising: yes.
RS positive: yes.
HH/HL: yes (₹505 is above the earlier low).
Breakout near highs: yes.
Volume confirms: yes (2.2x on the breakout).

blocks.x: Score 6 of 6: a clean early Stage 2. That does **not** say to buy at ₹540. It says the stock qualifies for setups. Whether ₹540 is a good entry depends on distance from the pivot (₹520, so 3.8% above), the stop, and the market.

blocks.title: Where the framework can mislead
blocks.x: Sharp V-shaped recoveries, low-liquidity small caps, stocks with recent corporate actions, and markets in transition can all distort the weekly picture. A stock can also meet the checklist and still fail at a breakout. The framework improves odds, it does not remove risk.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: Use the Watchlist stage label as a first pass, then check the checklist on the weekly chart yourself, in particular RS and volume.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A scorecard of price vs the 30-week MA, its slope, RS, structure, base and volume makes stage classification repeatable. Treat it as a framework, not a precise truth.

quiz.q: ABC trades at ₹540 above a rising ₹480 30-week MA, broke out on 2.2x volume, has positive Mansfield RS and a higher low. What does a 6/6 score tell you?
options: It qualifies as a clean early Stage 2; entry, stop and market still need judging
quiz.why: The score classifies the stock’s stage. It does not define entry timing, stop placement or position size.

quiz.q: Why use a scorecard rather than a gut feeling for stage classification?
options: It makes the process consistent and reduces bias from stories and emotion
quiz.why: A repeatable checklist forces the same questions on every stock, which helps avoid favouring familiar names.

quiz.q: A stock meets 3 of 6 Stage 2 items. What is the best handling?
options: Keep it on a watchlist and see which items fail and whether they are improving
quiz.why: A mixed score points to a transitional stock. Monitoring it costs nothing, and acting early costs risk.

lessons.title: Why bases form
lessons.summary: A base is a pause where the market digests a prior advance. The pattern names matter less than the supply and demand underneath.

blocks.x: After a stock advances, some holders take profits and new buyers hesitate. Price pauses and moves sideways or pulls back. This pause is a **base** or consolidation. A good base lets the market absorb supply, so that the next advance is not blocked by sellers.
What happens inside a base

items: **Profit-taking:** early buyers sell, creating the initial pullback.
**Supply absorption:** holders who want out are met by patient buyers at lower prices.
**Shakeouts:** sudden dips flush out weak holders and stop-loss orders.
**Institutional accumulation:** large buyers quietly build positions during quiet periods.
**Volatility contraction:** swings become smaller as sellers run out.
**Demand/supply balance:** eventually, supply dries up, and a small amount of demand moves the price.

blocks.caption: Healthy versus unhealthy bases
head: Feature
Healthy
Unhealthy
rows: Moderate for the stock and market
Excessive; far larger than the market’s decline
Near the middle to upper part of ranges

blocks.x: Pattern names are descriptions

Cup with handle, flat base and others are names for common shapes of this process. Real charts rarely look like textbook drawings. Learn the underlying logic, and you can judge imperfect examples sensibly: **is supply drying up, and is demand stepping in on strength?**

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Forcing a pattern name onto a chart. If you have to squint to see the pattern and explain away the flaws, there is no pattern.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Bases are periods where supply is absorbed and volatility contracts. The healthiest bases are orderly, tightening and supported by relative strength. Names describe shapes, the supply and demand logic decides quality.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a base in the context of supply and demand?
options: To let price drift without any activity
To absorb supply from profit-taking and weak holders so the next advance meets less resistance
quiz.why: A base is a digestion period. When supply dries up, demand can push price higher more easily.

quiz.q: Which feature is most consistent with an unhealthy base?
options: Wide, erratic swings with heavy volume on down days and weak closes
quiz.why: Heavy selling with erratic price action suggests distribution rather than orderly digestion.

lessons.title: Cup and handle
lessons.summary: A rounded recovery followed by a small pullback. One of the most studied bases in growth-stock trading.

blocks.x: The **cup and handle**, popularised by William O’Neil (and earlier described by William Jiler as a saucer with a platform), looks like a teacup from the side: a rounded decline and recovery (the cup) followed by a small pullback (the handle).
Structure

blocks.caption: Typical cup-and-handle characteristics
head: Part
Typical characteristics (guidelines, not rules)
rows: A meaningful uptrend before the base, often 30% or more
Rounded, U-shaped; a decline of roughly 12% to 35% in normal markets, deeper in bear markets; several weeks to many months
Recovers most of the way back toward the left-side high
A short, shallow pullback, often 1 to 4 weeks and usually in the upper half of the base, with volume dry-up
The high of the handle (a small buffer above it is common)
A move above the pivot on volume well above average

blocks.x: Why it works

The decline shakes out weak holders. The rounded recovery shows that buyers are returning gradually. The handle gives one last shakeout and lets remaining sellers exit. When supply is thin, a push through the handle’s high meets little resistance.
Volume

items: Volume tends to be heavier on the left side of the cup and quieter near the bottom.
Volume dries up in the handle, especially in the last few days.
Breakout volume is commonly at least 40% to 50% above average, and often much more.

blocks.x: Failure conditions

items: **V-shaped cup** with no time to base; a sharp drop and a sharp spike back.
**Too deep a cup** relative to the market.
**Handle too deep or too long,** or in the lower half of the base.
**A handle that drifts upward with volume rising** instead of a quiet dip.
**Breakout on weak volume** or a close back inside the handle.
**Poor relative strength.**

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Define the pivot on the chart before the breakout. Place an alert slightly above it. That removes the temptation to chase and lets you assess volume at the actual moment.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Calling any U shape a cup and handle. Check the prior uptrend, the depth, the symmetry and the handle’s location. A cup in a stock in Stage 4 is just a bounce.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A cup and handle is a rounded recovery with a shallow, quiet handle. Buy a decisive move above the handle high on strong volume, and treat failures like a close back inside the handle as a reason to exit.

quiz.q: What does the handle do in a cup and handle?
options: It provides a final, shallow pullback with low volume that shakes out remaining sellers before the breakout
It marks the bottom of the cup
quiz.why: The handle is a small, quiet pullback that clears the last supply. Thin supply then allows a breakout.

quiz.q: Which feature makes a cup and handle lower quality?
options: A handle that is deep, in the lower half of the base, and forms with rising volume
A handle high used as the pivot
quiz.why: A deep or lower-half handle on rising volume suggests supply remains, not that it has been absorbed.

quiz.q: Where is the pivot usually placed?
options: At the bottom of the cup
At the high of the handle, with a small buffer above
At the left-side peak of the previous year
quiz.why: The pivot is the level a stock must move above to resolve the base, typically the handle’s high.

lessons.title: Flat base
lessons.summary: A tight, shallow sideways pause after an advance. Often forms as a second-stage base in strong stocks.

blocks.x: A **flat base** is a shallow, sideways consolidation that forms after a stock has already advanced. It signals that holders are not selling much, even though price is not rising.

blocks.caption: Typical flat base characteristics
head: Feature
Guideline
rows: An uptrend and often a breakout from an earlier base
Shallow, usually 10% to 15% or less from high to low
At least about five weeks, often five to seven or longer
Tight range; closes near the middle to upper half
Declines, with dry-up on the right side
Above the pivot on above-average volume

blocks.x: Flat bases are strong because price refuses to fall. If a stock holds within 10% of its high for several weeks while the market wobbles, buyers are defending it. That resilience is itself a signal of demand.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Flat bases often appear after a first breakout, making them good tests of leadership. If a stock stays tight while the market corrects, mark it for the next breakout attempt.

blocks.title: Failure signs
blocks.x: Wide ranges, heavy volume on down days, closes near lows, or a base that is much deeper than 15%. A flat base that breaks below its low should be treated as a failed pattern.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A flat base is a tight, shallow, multi-week pause near highs. Orderly price action and dry-up in volume suggest holders are not selling, and a breakout above the high with volume is the trigger.

quiz.q: What is a typical depth for a flat base?
quiz.why: Flat bases are shallow by nature. If the pause becomes much deeper, it is a different pattern or an unhealthy one.

quiz.q: Why can a flat base signal strength?
options: Because the stock refuses to fall even without rising, suggesting holders are not selling and buyers are defending
Because volume is high on down days
Because it is far below the high
quiz.why: Holding tight near highs shows demand absorbing the little supply that appears.

lessons.title: High tight flag
lessons.summary: A rare, fast pattern: a huge advance followed by a very tight pause. High reward and high risk.

blocks.x: The **high tight flag** (also called the power play) is among the strongest continuation patterns, and one of the rarest. A stock advances sharply and then pauses in a very tight range.

blocks.caption: Typical characteristics
head: Part
Guideline
rows: A very fast advance, often 100% or more in about 4 to 8 weeks
A tight consolidation, usually 3 to 5 weeks, with a pullback of no more than about 10% to 25%
Huge volume on the advance; quiet on the flag
A move above the flag’s high on renewed volume

blocks.x: Why it is rare

Doubling in two months is unusual. It usually requires a catalyst such as a major earnings surprise, a new product, an approval or a sector rotation. Most stocks that surge that fast fall back, and the few that hold their gains in a tight range show exceptional demand.
Risks

items: **Extension:** after a 100% move, volatility is high and stops are wide in rupee terms.
**News dependence:** the catalyst may fade, and the stock may drop on any disappointment.
**Liquidity:** small caps can gap through stops.
**Position size must be smaller** because the stop distance is larger.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Chasing any stock that has doubled. The pattern requires a tight flag. A wide, sloppy pullback after a spike is a failed run, not a flag.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Because the risk per share is larger, reduce size so the rupee risk stays the same as for normal setups. Size is the control, not the stop width.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: The high tight flag is a rare, fast pattern with a large pole and a tight flag. It can be powerful, but extended prices and news risk require smaller size and strict stops.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a high tight flag from any stock that has doubled?
options: The advance must be followed by a very tight, shallow consolidation with quiet volume
quiz.why: The flag’s tightness shows that holders are not selling after a huge advance, which is the sign of strength.

quiz.q: Why should position size be reduced for a high tight flag?
options: The stop distance in rupees is larger because the stock is extended and volatile, so the same risk requires fewer shares
quiz.why: Risk per trade is shares times stop distance. A larger stop distance means fewer shares for the same risk.

lessons.title: VCP: the volatility contraction pattern
lessons.summary: Wide swings, then smaller, then tighter, as supply dries up. Mark Minervini’s signature setup and one of the best frameworks for timing breakouts.

blocks.x: The **Volatility Contraction Pattern (VCP)**, taught by Mark Minervini, is a base in which each pullback is smaller than the one before. It is a visual record of selling pressure drying up.

blocks.label: The VCP idea
blocks.expr: Wide swings → smaller swings → tighter swings → supply dries up → breakout
blocks.note: Each contraction is often about half the size of the previous one. Volume falls as the swings tighten.

blocks.x: Contractions

A VCP is described by its contractions (often written as T). For example: the stock pulls back 25% (T1), rallies, pulls back 12% (T2), rallies, pulls back 6% (T3), then tightens to a 3% pause (T4). Most VCPs have two to four contractions; sometimes five or six.

blocks.caption: Example VCP for a fictional stock
head: Contraction
High to low
Depth
Volume

blocks.x: Why it works

Each pullback occurs because some holders sell. The shrinking size shows fewer sellers each time. Eventually the last pullback is tiny and quiet: almost nobody wants to sell. At that moment even modest demand can lift the price, which is the **line of least resistance**.
Key ingredients

items: **A prior uptrend** in Stage 2, with the Trend Template conditions met.
**Contractions of decreasing depth,** roughly half each time.
**Volume dry-up** on the final contraction, ideally with a day or two of very low volume.
**Relative strength** strong; RS line near highs.
**A pivot** at the high of the last contraction.
**Breakout volume** clearly above average.

blocks.x: Failure signals

items: Contractions grow instead of shrink.
Heavy volume on down days in the final contraction.
Breakout on weak volume.
A close back below the pivot with heavy volume.
A market in a correction.

blocks.title: VCP is a concept, not one shape
blocks.x: VCPs appear inside cup-and-handles, flat bases and other bases. What matters is the progression from loose to tight with volume drying up.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: The Leadership Tight Base screen under Pullback finds Stage 2 leaders with RS above a high threshold, a tight 20-day range and volume contraction, which captures the quantitative side of a VCP. It does not draw contractions for you. Open the chart and count them yourself.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Counting any wobbly sequence as a VCP. The contractions must show a clear tightening, and the stock must already be in a strong trend.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A VCP is a base where pullbacks shrink and volume dries up, showing sellers are running out. The pivot at the last contraction’s high with a volume surge is the trigger, and failure signs are growing contractions or heavy selling.

quiz.q: In a VCP, what does a sequence of 25%, 12%, 6% pullbacks suggest?
options: Each wave of selling is smaller, suggesting supply is being absorbed and fewer sellers remain
quiz.why: Shrinking pullbacks mean fewer holders are willing to sell at each stage. That is the logic of the pattern.

quiz.q: Which condition would weaken a VCP setup?
options: Volume dry-up in the last contraction
Contractions that grow larger over time, with heavy volume on down days
A pivot at the last high
quiz.why: Growing contractions and heavy selling mean supply is not drying up.

quiz.q: Why is the TradeEdge Leadership Tight Base screen only a partial VCP detector?
options: It captures quantitative traits such as RS, tight range and volume contraction, but not the visual count and quality of contractions
It only looks at Stage 4 stocks
quiz.why: Screens apply numeric filters. Judging the shape and progression of contractions still needs your eyes.

lessons.title: Double bottom
lessons.summary: A W-shaped base where the second low tests the first. Often found after a correction in a recovering leader.

blocks.x: A **double bottom** looks like the letter W. Price falls to a first low, rallies, falls again to or slightly below the first low, and then recovers above the middle peak.

blocks.caption: Structure
head: Part
Description
rows: The rally between the two lows; this is the pivot
A retest of the first low, often undercutting it slightly, which shakes out weak holders
A move above the middle peak on strong volume

blocks.x: Volume and confirmation

items: Volume is often lower on the second low than on the first, showing weaker selling.
A breakout above the middle peak on volume well above average confirms.
A modest undercut of the first low followed by a quick recovery (a shakeout) is often a positive sign.
The pivot should sit below the overall high of the base. A W that makes new highs in the middle is a different formation.

blocks.x: When it is more reliable

Double bottoms are more common than cups and appear in many conditions, so quality varies. They work better when the stock was a leader before the correction, the base is not too wide and loose, and the market is rising again.

blocks.title: Failure signs
blocks.x: A W with wide, loose swings; three lows instead of two; heavy volume on down days; or a recovery stalling below the middle peak. A close below the second low invalidates the pattern.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: A pivot at the middle peak gives a clear, objective trigger. The second low provides the natural stop reference.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A double bottom is a W where the second low tests the first, often with a shakeout. The middle peak is the pivot, and volume on the breakout confirms. Avoid loose, sloppy Ws.

quiz.q: Where is the pivot of a double bottom?
options: At the middle peak between the two lows
quiz.why: The market must clear the supply at the middle peak to complete the W.

quiz.q: Why might a slight undercut of the first low be a positive sign?
options: It triggers stop orders and shakes out weak holders, so a quick recovery shows strong demand
quiz.why: A brief flush below support followed by a rapid recovery means sellers were exhausted.

lessons.title: Flags, pennants and tight consolidations
lessons.summary: Continuation patterns that pause a strong move. Tightness and low volume are the evidence.

blocks.x: Flags and pennants are short pauses within a strong trend. They form after a sharp move (the pole), and the trend usually resumes if the pause is orderly.

blocks.caption: Continuation patterns
head: Pattern
Shape
Volume
Resolution
rows: Small, parallel channel sloping slightly down after a sharp rise
Break above the flag’s upper line on volume
Small channel sloping slightly up after a sharp fall
Break below the lower line, continuing the decline
Small symmetrical triangle after a sharp move
Break in the direction of the prior move
A few days or weeks of narrow, sideways price
Break of the range on higher volume

blocks.x: What makes a good continuation

items: A **strong prior move** with volume.
A **shallow, orderly pause,** much smaller than the pole.
**Volume dry-up** during the pause.
**Duration** short relative to the pole; long flags lose the momentum logic.
**Breakout with volume** in the direction of the trend.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating a deep, loose pullback as a flag. If the pause retraces more than a third to a half of the pole, or volume stays high, it is probably a reversal in progress.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: A tight range under a recent high and above a rising 10-day or 20-day average is a common entry zone for momentum stocks. The stop goes below the range.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Flags, pennants and tight ranges are brief pauses in a strong trend. Shallow depth, short duration and dry-up in volume support continuation, and the breakout of the pause is the trigger.

quiz.q: Which feature is most consistent with a good bull flag?
options: A deep retracement of most of the pole on heavy volume
A shallow, orderly pullback after a sharp rise, with volume drying up
A long pause lasting several months
Rising volume on the down move
quiz.why: A flag is a brief, shallow pause. Heavy volume or deep retracement suggest the move is failing.

quiz.q: A pause retraces 60% of the pole on heavy volume. How should this be viewed?
options: As likely a reversal or failed move rather than a continuation pattern
quiz.why: Flags are shallow. Deep retracements on heavy volume point to real selling.

lessons.title: Failed patterns
lessons.summary: Patterns fail. Learn the common failure types, and how a failure can become information or even a new setup.

blocks.x: Every pattern in this track fails some of the time. Experienced traders treat failure as part of the process: they define it in advance, exit quickly, and learn from it.

blocks.caption: Types of failure
head: Type
What happens
What it tells you
rows: Price breaks above the pivot, then closes back below it
Demand was not enough to absorb supply
The base breaks down below its low instead of breaking out
A breakout that attracts buyers, then reverses sharply
Late buyers are trapped; supply overhead increases
A brief break below support or the handle low that quickly recovers
Weak holders flushed out; may strengthen the setup
Price dips below a prior low and then rallies back above it
A failed breakdown; sellers could not hold the level

blocks.x: Telling a shakeout from a real breakdown

items: **Speed of recovery:** shakeouts recover within days. Real breakdowns keep falling.
**Volume:** a shakeout often has a volume spike followed by dry-up. Real breakdowns show sustained heavy selling.
**Close:** a close back above the level within a day or two supports a shakeout.
**Market context:** a weak market makes real breakdowns likelier.

blocks.x: Failure as information

A stock that fails a breakout is telling you something about demand. If you exit at the stop, you lose a small amount and keep your capital. If the stock later forms a tighter base and breaks out again, you can re-enter. Many strong stocks need two attempts. The failure that shakes you out may build the base for the successful move.

blocks.title: Define failure before you enter
blocks.x: For each setup, write what failure looks like: for example “close back below the pivot on above-average volume” or “break of the handle low”. Then act on it. Hope is not a rule.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Moving the stop lower because the pattern “should work”. The pattern is not entitled to work. A failed pattern is a signal to exit.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Keep a record of failed setups with screenshots. After a few dozen, you will see which failure types are most common for your style and markets.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Patterns fail, and failure is defined in advance and respected. A failure can become information, or even a new setup if the stock rebuilds a tighter base.

quiz.q: A stock breaks above a pivot, then closes back below it on heavy volume two days later. What is this called, and what is the correct response?
options: A bull trap or failed breakout; exit according to the stop plan
quiz.why: The move failed to hold above the pivot and heavy volume shows real selling. The planned exit limits the loss.

quiz.q: What most reliably separates a shakeout from a breakdown?
options: How quickly price recovers and whether selling continues, together with volume and market context
quiz.why: Shakeouts reverse quickly with volume exhaustion, while breakdowns continue lower with sustained selling.

quiz.q: Why is a small loss on a failed breakout often better than holding?
options: It preserves capital for the next setup, and the stock may offer a better entry after rebuilding
Because it removes the need for rules
quiz.why: Capital preservation is the point of the stop. Holding hope turns small losses into large ones.

lessons.title: What is a breakout?
lessons.summary: A breakout is the resolution of a period of supply and demand balance. The best ones follow a clear sequence.

blocks.x: A **breakout** occurs when price moves decisively above a resistance level (or below support), ending a period of consolidation. It is a statement that demand has overwhelmed the supply that previously capped the price.

blocks.label: The sequence
blocks.expr:
Resistance
→ accumulation (supply absorbed)
→ tightening (volatility contracts)
→ demand expansion (volume rises)
→ breakout
blocks.note: Breakouts that follow this sequence tend to be higher quality than random pokes through a level.

blocks.x: Why breakouts can work

items: **No overhead supply:** at a new high, no holder is waiting to sell at breakeven.
**Momentum attraction:** screens, alerts and traders all notice a new high, bringing new buyers.
**Short covering and stop buying:** traders positioned the other way buy to exit.
**Institutional accumulation:** funds may keep buying over days as the stock proves itself.

blocks.x: Why many breakouts fail

items: The market is weak, so the breakout lacks follow-through.
The base was loose or too short, so supply remains.
Volume was thin, so little supply was absorbed.
The stock was already extended, with late buyers entering.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating every move above a line as a breakout. A genuine breakout is a resolution after supply has been absorbed. A poke through a level in a messy chart is noise.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: The Breakouts category under TechLens includes Volume Breakout, 52-Week High, Pivot Breakout, Fresh Breakout and Weekly Breakout Soon, which each filter for different stages of this process.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A breakout is the resolution of accumulation and tightening by demand expansion. Quality depends on trend, base, relative strength, volume and market. Weak breakouts fail often.

quiz.q: Which sequence best describes a high-quality breakout?
options: Heavy selling, then a random spike
Resistance, accumulation, tightening, demand expansion, breakout
A gap down, then a bounce
A sideways drift with no volume
quiz.why: Quality breakouts follow supply absorption and contraction before demand expands.

quiz.q: Why can a breakout in a market under heavy distribution be riskier?
options: Because individual stocks cannot move independently
Because follow-through buying is less likely, and breakouts fail more often in weak markets
quiz.why: Market conditions affect the odds. In a weak market, most breakouts struggle to hold.

lessons.title: Identifying the pivot
lessons.summary: The pivot is the line you act on. Define it, plan the buy zone, and understand chase risk.

blocks.x: The **pivot point** is the price level that, once exceeded, completes the base and triggers a buy. For a flat base it is the base high. For a cup and handle it is the handle high. For a VCP it is the high of the last contraction. For a double bottom it is the middle peak.
Pivot, buy zone and extension

blocks.caption: Zones around the pivot
head: Zone
Typical definition
Implication
rows: The resistance high (plus a small buffer)
From the pivot to roughly 3% to 5% above it
Entry still close enough that the stop stays reasonable
More than about 5% above the pivot
Risk per share rises; better to wait for a pullback or new base

blocks.label: Distance from pivot
blocks.expr: Extension % = (Current price − Pivot) ÷ Pivot × 100
blocks.note: Example: pivot ₹200, price ₹208. Extension = 8 ÷ 200 = 4%, inside a typical buy zone. At ₹220 the extension is 10%.

blocks.x: Chase risk

The further above the pivot you buy, the further your stop is from your entry (if the stop stays below the base), and so the larger the loss if it fails. At ₹208, a stop below the base at ₹190 risks ₹18 per share. At ₹220 it risks ₹30, which is 67% more risk for the same idea. Chasing destroys risk/reward before the trade begins.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Before the open, write the pivot, the upper limit of the buy zone, and the stop. Set an alert at the pivot. If the stock opens beyond the buy zone, skip it.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Buying a stock that gapped 8% above the pivot because “it is a breakout”. The gap changed the risk. Wait for a pullback or a new base.

blocks.title: NSE specifics
blocks.x: Check circuit limits. A stock that locks in an upper circuit on breakout day can be impossible to buy, and a stock that gaps up on the next session may open well beyond the buy zone.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: The pivot is the trigger level. Plan a buy zone of a few percent above it, avoid chasing extended prices, and write the numbers down in advance.

quiz.q: Pivot is ₹200 and the price is ₹208. What is the extension?
quiz.why: (208 − 200) ÷ 200 = 4%, inside a typical 3% to 5% buy zone.

quiz.q: Why does buying far above the pivot hurt the trade?
options: The stop is further from entry if kept below the base, so risk per share rises
quiz.why: A wider stop distance means either a bigger loss or fewer shares, and the reward potential is not larger.

quiz.q: A stock opens 8% above its pivot after a gap. What is a disciplined response?
options: Skip or wait for a pullback or a new base, because the entry is extended
quiz.why: Extended entries have worse risk/reward. A disciplined trader sticks to the pre-defined buy zone.

lessons.title: Breakout volume in practice
lessons.summary: How much volume is enough, how to check it intraday, and how institutional participation shows up.

blocks.x: Breakout volume is evidence that the move has real participation. This lesson applies the earlier volume concepts to the actual decision.
What to measure

items: **Relative volume** on the breakout day versus the 50-day average.
**Volume versus recent high-volume days:** is it the highest in months?
**Close location:** did buyers hold the move into the close?
**Follow-through volume** in the following days.

blocks.caption: Example breakout day for XYZ Technologies (fictional)
head: Item
Value
Reading
rows: 3% above the pivot, inside the buy zone

blocks.x: Institutional participation

Funds buy over many days. Footprints include a high-volume breakout day, then multiple up days with above-average volume, strong closes, and pullbacks that find buyers quickly. A single spike followed by fading volume and weak closes suggests retail excitement without sustained institutional buying.
Intraday check

If you act intraday, compare the volume so far with the stock’s typical volume at that time. Many platforms provide this. If you cannot, consider acting near the close, when the day’s volume and close location are clearer, at the cost of a slightly higher entry.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Record the relative volume of each breakout you take and its outcome. Your own results will show how much volume matters in your universe.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Relying on volume alone. A 4x volume day that closes at its low after a long advance can be a blow-off, not a breakout. Combine volume with location, base and market.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Check relative volume, comparison with recent history, close location and follow-through. Volume supports the thesis, but is never the whole thesis.

quiz.q: XYZ breaks out at ₹309 on 10,00,000 shares versus a 4,00,000 average, closing near the high, then holds above ₹300 for three days. How would you describe it?
options: Weak, because volume is only 2.5 times average
A supportive breakout with strong volume, a strong close and follow-through
quiz.why: 2.5x volume with a high close and follow-through are all supportive evidence.

quiz.q: Which pattern suggests retail excitement rather than sustained institutional buying?
options: A single volume spike followed by fading volume and weak closes
Several up days with above-average volume and strong closes
A volume dry-up in the base
quiz.why: Institutions build positions over days. A one-day spike that fades often lacks that persistence.

lessons.title: Proper breakout entry and stop placement
lessons.summary: Entry near the pivot, a stop that invalidates the idea, and a risk/reward worth taking.

blocks.x: A good entry is not just a price. It is a combination of entry, stop and size that gives acceptable risk compared with reward.
Entry

items: Buy as price moves above the pivot, within the buy zone (for example up to 3% to 5% above).
Prefer entries where volume is on pace to be above average.
Avoid buying on a gap far above the zone.
Some traders scale in: for example half at the pivot and the rest on follow-through.

blocks.x: Stop placement

The stop should be where the **breakout thesis is invalid**. For a breakout, that is typically below the pivot, below the handle low, or below the last contraction’s low, not simply a fixed percentage. A fixed maximum (for example 7% to 8%) acts as a cap, but if the logical stop is further away, the setup needs a smaller size or should be skipped.
Same stock, same stop level, but entering at ₹212 instead of ₹203 cuts reward/risk from 3.2R to 1.5R. Entry discipline is risk management.

blocks.title: Risk/reward is decided at entry
blocks.x: A trade with poor reward/risk at entry is hard to rescue later. Skipping marginal setups is a legitimate decision.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Reward is a scenario, not a prediction. Use the prior base depth, a measured move or the next resistance zone to define a reasonable target, and judge whether risk is worth it.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Placing the stop at a round percentage without checking structure. A stop inside the base’s normal volatility will be hit by noise, and one too far makes the trade too expensive.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Enter in the buy zone, place the stop where the thesis fails, and check reward/risk before acting. Extended entries shrink reward/risk fast.

quiz.q: Pivot ₹200, stop ₹190, target scenario ₹245. What is reward/risk if you enter at ₹203?
What should determine the stop for a breakout trade?
options: The level where the breakout thesis is invalid, such as below the last contraction low or the pivot, checked against maximum acceptable risk
quiz.why: A structural stop reflects when the idea is wrong. Percentages alone ignore structure.

quiz.q: The logical stop is 14% below the extended entry. What is the disciplined choice?
options: Skip the trade or cut the size so rupee risk stays within plan
quiz.why: If structure demands a distant stop, either size down or wait for a better entry.

lessons.title: When breakouts fail
lessons.summary: Small losses are the price of admission. Learn the signs, act quickly and decide whether re-entry makes sense.

blocks.x: Even high-quality breakouts fail. What separates good traders from others is not avoiding failures but handling them.
Signs of failure

items: **Close back below the pivot,** especially on above-average volume.
**Reversal on the breakout day,** closing near the low after a high-volume surge.
**Heavy-volume down days** soon after the breakout.
**Loss of the short-term averages** (for example the 10-day or 20-day) soon after breakout.
**Market turns down,** pulling most breakouts with it.

blocks.x: Squat versus failure

A stock may break out and then hover or dip slightly. That could be a normal retest. The difference: a retest holds above the pivot on light volume and recovers; a failure closes meaningfully below the pivot, usually with volume. Give the stock room that matches your stop, but do not widen the stop to avoid a loss.
The stop is the plan
If price hits your stop, you exit. Do not wait for a bounce. Do not average down. The loss is already defined, which is the whole point of defining risk before entry.
Re-entry

If a stock stops you out but its trend, relative strength and structure remain strong, it can set up again. A second attempt is reasonable if the stock forms a new pivot or reclaims the failed level with volume. The key is that re-entry is a **new trade with a new plan**, not an attempt to recover the loss.

blocks.caption: After a failed breakout
head: Condition
Likely next step
rows: Trend and RS intact, stock rebuilds a tight area above the pivot
Watch for a new pivot and a re-entry
Closes below the base low on heavy volume
Stand aside; most breakouts will struggle

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Revenge trading: re-entering immediately to win back the loss. Wait for a valid new setup.

blocks.title: A small loss is a business expense
blocks.x: A loss limited to 1R is part of the process. A loss that grows to 3R because you hoped is a rule violation.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Failed breakouts show as closes back below the pivot, heavy selling, or a turning market. Exit at the stop, and re-enter only if a new valid setup forms.

quiz.q: Which is the clearest sign of a failed breakout?
options: A close back below the pivot on above-average volume
A one-day pullback on light volume that holds the pivot
quiz.why: Closing below the pivot with volume shows supply overwhelmed the breakout.

quiz.q: After being stopped out of a strong stock, which approach to re-entry is sound?
options: Buy immediately at a higher price to win the loss back
Wait for a new valid setup with its own pivot, stop and size
quiz.why: Re-entry should be a new, rule-based trade. Revenge trades abandon the plan.

lessons.title: What makes a healthy pullback?
lessons.summary: Strong stocks rest. A healthy pullback is orderly, quiet and supported.

blocks.x: Trends do not move in straight lines. In a strong uptrend, prices advance, pause, and advance again. The pauses are **pullbacks**, and they are where many traders find lower-risk entries.
Features of a healthy pullback

items: **Price contraction:** the pullback is shallow compared with the preceding advance (for example less than a third to a half of the last leg).
**Lower volume:** selling is light compared with the advance.
**Support:** the decline stalls near a rising moving average (10-week, 50-day), a prior breakout level or a trendline.
**Relative strength holds:** the RS line stays near highs rather than diving.
**No heavy distribution:** no large down days on huge volume.
**Higher low** forms, preserving the uptrend structure.

blocks.caption: Healthy versus warning pullback
head: Feature
Healthy
Warning
rows: Gives back most of the advance
Holds rising average or breakout level

blocks.x: Example: PQR Engineering rises from ₹300 to ₹400 in six weeks. It then pulls back to ₹372 (−7%) over seven sessions on volume 40% below average, stopping at the rising 50-day average. That is shallow, quiet and supported. If instead it fell to ₹330 in three sessions on 2x volume, it would be a warning.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Measure the pullback as a percentage of the prior advance, not only of price. A 10% pullback after a 15% advance is much deeper than a 10% pullback after a 60% advance.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Buying a pullback in a stock that never had a strong advance to begin with. A pullback needs an uptrend to continue.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A healthy pullback is shallow, quiet, supported at a rising average or prior breakout level, with relative strength holding and a higher low forming.

quiz.q: Which pullback is healthier?
options: A 7% decline on 40% below-average volume that stops at the rising 50-day average
A 20% decline on 2x volume that slices through the 50-day average
A decline with the RS line collapsing
A decline that forms a lower low
quiz.why: Shallow depth, light volume and support at a rising average are the healthy markers.

quiz.q: Why measure pullback depth relative to the prior advance?
options: A 10% dip after a 15% run is a big giveback, but after a 60% run it is modest, so proportion matters
quiz.why: Context sets what is normal. The same percentage means different things after different advances.

lessons.title: Pullbacks to the 10-week and 50-day averages
lessons.summary: The two most-watched support zones for leaders. Learn the signal, the risk and the entry mechanics.

blocks.x: In strong trends, leaders often pull back to a rising average and then resume. The 10-week average (about the 50-day) is the common intermediate level, with the 21-day EMA and 20-day SMA for faster stocks.
Trend context first

A pullback entry only makes sense when the trend is clearly up: price above rising 50, 150 and 200-day averages, strong RS and sound structure. A pullback to the 50-day in a downtrend is a bounce attempt in a falling stock, not a continuation.
The setup

items: Identify a leader in Stage 2 or meeting the Trend Template.
Wait for the pullback to approach the 10-week or 50-day average on contracting volume.
Look for a **reversal signal** near the average: a strong close, a hammer, an inside bar break, or a day on increased volume closing in the upper half of the range.
Enter as price moves above the signal candle’s high, with a stop below the signal candle’s low or the average.

blocks.caption: Example pullback entry for ABC Industries (fictional)
head: Item
Value
rows: Closes ₹488 near its high on rising volume
Retest of ₹520 high, then higher: +₹30 ≈ 1.8R, more if it breaks out

blocks.x: Notice how a pullback entry gives a tighter stop than chasing a breakout, but the reward is smaller if it only returns to the prior high. Many traders use pullbacks as add-on entries to an existing winner.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Combine a pullback to the average with a nearby prior breakout level or trendline. Several supports in the same area make a stronger zone.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating the average as a guarantee. Averages are zones. If price closes decisively below it on heavy volume and the average flattens, the thesis is wrong.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Pullbacks to a rising 10-week or 50-day average in a confirmed uptrend can offer tight-risk entries. Wait for a reversal signal, place the stop below the low and the average, and respect failure.

quiz.q: Why is trend context essential before a pullback entry?
options: A pullback to an average in a downtrend is just a bounce in a weak stock, not a continuation
quiz.why: A pullback entry assumes the larger trend is up. Without it, you are catching a falling stock.

quiz.q: Entry ₹490, stop ₹473, prior high ₹520. What is reward/risk to the prior high?

lessons.title: Buying constructive weakness
lessons.summary: A healthy pullback and the start of a downtrend can look alike at first. Learn the differences before you buy.

blocks.x: The hardest question in pullback trading is: **is this a pause or the beginning of something worse?** No rule is perfect, but several clues separate them.

blocks.caption: Healthy pullback versus beginning of a downtrend
head: Clue
Healthy pullback
Early downtrend
rows: Breaks the average and fails to reclaim it

blocks.x: Using multiple clues

No single clue decides it. A stock can undercut its 50-day for a day (a shakeout) and still be healthy. Look for the weight of evidence: if most items lean healthy, a pullback entry is reasonable. If most lean weak, wait.
The role of the market

Leading stocks pulling back while the market is healthy is common. When the market itself is breaking down, pullbacks in leaders can become deeper corrections. Check the market regime before buying weakness.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Averaging into a falling stock because “it is a pullback in a leader”. If the stock closes below its stop, the pullback thesis has failed.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Pre-define the level at which a pullback becomes a failure: for example a weekly close below the 10-week average on heavy volume, or a break of the last higher low.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Constructive weakness is quiet, shallow and supported, with RS and structure intact in a healthy market. When volume, structure, RS and the market all lean negative, the pullback is more likely a trend change.

quiz.q: Which clue most strongly favours a healthy pullback over an early downtrend?
options: A higher low forming with light volume on declines and RS holding near highs
quiz.why: Quiet selling, preserved structure and holding RS are the signs of a pause.

quiz.q: Why check the market regime before buying a pullback in a leader?
options: In a market correction, even leaders can have deeper declines, so pullbacks are riskier
quiz.why: Stocks are influenced by the broader market. Pullbacks tend to be deeper and longer in weak markets.

lessons.title: Reclaim setups
lessons.summary: When a stock breaks a level and quickly takes it back, the failed breakdown can be a useful signal.

blocks.x: A **reclaim** happens when price closes below a significant level and then recovers above it. The break flushed out sellers, and the recovery shows buyers took control.

blocks.caption: Common reclaim types
head: Setup
What happens
What it suggests
rows: Closes below the 50-day (or 10-week), then closes back above on strong volume
The break was a shakeout; the trend continues
Falls back below the pivot, then closes above it again
A failed failure; the original breakout may resume
Breaks below a clear support or base low, then closes back inside
Briefly dips below a prior low and rallies strongly
Stops triggered and absorbed by buyers

blocks.x: How to trade a reclaim

items: **Confirm the context:** the stock should be in an uptrend or a strong base. A reclaim in a Stage 4 stock is usually a bounce.
**Wait for the close** back above the level, with volume ideally above average.
**Enter above the reclaim candle’s high.**
**Stop below the undercut low,** the logical point where the thesis fails.

blocks.x: Example: PQR trades in a base with a low of ₹250. It dips to ₹244 intraday, then closes at ₹256 on 1.8x volume. The undercut cleared stop orders under ₹250, and the close back above shows demand. Entry is above the day’s high; the stop sits below ₹244. The risk is small relative to the base.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Buying the undercut before it recovers. You cannot tell a shakeout from a breakdown until the close. Waiting costs a small price for much more information.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Reclaims work best when the market is also recovering. A reclaim during a market correction is weaker.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A reclaim is a quick recovery of a lost level, showing sellers failed. Confirm with a close and volume, enter above the reclaim candle, and stop below the undercut low.

quiz.q: Why wait for the close before treating an undercut as a reclaim?
options: Until the close you cannot tell whether it is a shakeout or a real breakdown
Because closes are always above the open
quiz.why: Intraday dips can recover or continue. The close shows where the balance settled.

quiz.q: Where does the stop usually go in an undercut-and-reclaim trade?
quiz.why: If price returns below the undercut low, the reclaim thesis has failed.

lessons.title: Why the market regime matters
lessons.summary: Most stocks move with the market. The same setup has different odds in different regimes.

blocks.x: Individual stocks are influenced by the broader market. In strong markets, breakouts tend to follow through and pullbacks are brief. In weak markets, most breakouts fail and rallies fade. The **market regime** is the backdrop that shapes the odds for every setup.

blocks.caption: Regimes
head: Regime
Typical features
Approach
rows: Index above rising averages; many leaders; breakouts follow through
Be more active; normal to larger size
Index falls below key averages; distribution; leaders fall
Extended downtrend; most stocks in Stage 4
Index range-bound; breakouts fail often; leaders mixed
Be selective; smaller size; shorter holding

blocks.title: The principle
blocks.x: A good stock setup has a lower probability of working when the overall market regime is hostile. Strong stocks can survive weak markets, but most do not.
Practical use

items: Check the index before the stock: trend, averages, breadth.
Adjust size and the number of positions to the regime.
Pay attention to **leaders**: if new leaders are breaking out and holding, the market is healthy. If breakouts keep failing, the regime is poor even if the index looks fine.
Use the trading results themselves as feedback. A string of stop-outs may mean the regime has changed.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Fighting the regime: forcing breakout trades in a correction because the chart looks perfect. The odds have changed even if the pattern has not.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: The market regime sets the odds for every setup. Match exposure and selectivity to the regime, and use the behaviour of leaders as a real-time gauge.

quiz.q: Why does the market regime matter for an individual stock setup?
options: Most stocks are influenced by the market, so setups have lower odds in hostile regimes
It does not; stocks are independent
It only matters for index funds
quiz.why: Correlation means follow-through is less likely when the market is falling.

quiz.q: Breakouts keep failing even though the index looks fine. What might it mean?
options: The regime may be deteriorating beneath the surface, so reduce risk
quiz.why: Leaders’ behaviour can warn before the index does.

lessons.title: Index trend analysis
lessons.summary: Apply what you have learned about trend to NIFTY 50, Bank NIFTY and sector indices.

blocks.x: The same tools that analyse a stock work on an index: structure, averages, volume and relative strength. Use them to classify the regime.
Indices to follow

items: **NIFTY 50:** large-cap benchmark and the main reference.
**Bank NIFTY:** the banking sector, a heavy driver of the NIFTY and index-derivative activity.
**Broader indices:** NIFTY Midcap and Smallcap indices show how the wider market behaves, which is often where growth-stock setups live.
**Sector indices:** IT, Pharma, Auto, Metals, Realty, FMCG and others for sector context.

blocks.x: A simple classification
