If the NIFTY is above rising 50 and 200-day averages with higher highs and lows, the regime is constructive. If it is below a falling 50-day and has made a lower low, defensive. Mixed readings are a transition: be selective.
Large-cap versus broad market

The NIFTY 50 can be held up by a handful of heavyweights while the average stock falls. Compare it with midcap and smallcap indices. If the NIFTY makes a new high but midcaps and smallcaps lag, the market is narrow, and breakout setups in smaller stocks are riskier.

blocks.title: Index volume
blocks.x: Cash indices have no traded volume of their own. Volume analysis for the market is often done using aggregate NSE cash-market volume, index futures, or ETFs tracking the index. Be clear which series you use and stay consistent.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Looking only at the NIFTY 50. It can hide weakness in the broader market where many setups occur.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Classify the regime with the same structure and average rules used for stocks, and compare large-cap, midcap and smallcap indices to see how broad the market really is.

quiz.q: The NIFTY 50 makes a new high, but the Midcap and Smallcap indices are lagging and falling. What does this suggest?
options: A narrow market, so breakout setups in smaller stocks carry more risk
quiz.why: A few heavyweights can lift the NIFTY while most stocks weaken. Narrow markets are less reliable.

quiz.q: Why can’t you read volume directly from the NIFTY 50 index?
options: A cash index is a calculation and has no traded volume of its own, so analysts use aggregate market volume, futures or ETFs
Because it trades only on weekends
quiz.why: The index is a basket calculation. Volume must come from the constituents or related instruments.

lessons.title: Market breadth
lessons.summary: Breadth asks how many stocks participate. It often turns before the index.

blocks.x: **Market breadth** measures how many stocks are participating in a move. A healthy advance has many stocks rising. A weak one is carried by a few.

blocks.caption: Common breadth measures
head: Measure
What it shows
Healthy
Warning
rows: Cumulative net number of advancing minus declining stocks
Falling while the index makes new highs
A sharp rise in advancers after a decline

blocks.x: Breadth thrust

A **breadth thrust** occurs when an unusually large share of stocks advances in a short period, often after a market low. It shows broad and urgent buying and has historically been associated with the start of strong rallies. Different studies use different thresholds, and thrusts are not guaranteed signals.
Breadth deterioration

When the index rises but fewer stocks are above their 50-day averages, new highs shrink and the A/D line lags, the market is **narrowing**. That does not mean an immediate fall, but it increases risk: when the few leading names stumble, nothing supports the index.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: TradeEdge has a Market Breadth tab. Use it to check advance/decline readings and participation before selecting setups, particularly when the index is near highs.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating breadth divergences as timing signals. They can persist for weeks or months. Use them to adjust risk, not to predict the exact top.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Breadth shows whether many stocks support a move. Expanding highs and a rising share above averages is healthy. A narrowing market increases risk, but is not a precise timing tool.

quiz.q: The NIFTY makes a new high while the percentage of stocks above their 50-day average falls. What does it suggest?
options: Breadth deterioration: the rally is narrowing and risk is rising
That all stocks are in Stage 2
quiz.why: Fewer stocks participating means less support for the index. It is a warning, not a timer.

quiz.q: What is a breadth thrust?
options: A sudden, broad surge in advancing stocks, often after a decline, showing urgent widespread buying
quiz.why: It reflects participation across many stocks, which is why it has been associated with strong market beginnings.

lessons.title: Distribution and follow-through
lessons.summary: Two heuristics from William O’Neil’s market-timing work. Useful frameworks, never guarantees.

blocks.x: William O’Neil studied past market tops and bottoms and noticed recurring patterns in how an index behaves on volume. Two are widely used.
Distribution days

A **distribution day** is commonly defined as a day when an index falls meaningfully (for example about 0.2% or more) on higher volume than the previous session. It suggests institutions are selling. A cluster of distribution days (commonly four to six within about four to five weeks) is regarded as a sign of pressure that can precede a correction. Thresholds vary by source and era.
Follow-through days

After a correction, a rally attempt begins when the index has an up day following a low. A **follow-through day** typically occurs on the fourth day or later of the rally attempt, when the index rises strongly (commonly around 1.25% to 2%) on higher volume than the previous day. It suggests that large buyers are returning. Many rallies that start this way continue, but a number fail.

blocks.caption: Distribution versus follow-through
head: Concept
When it matters
What it suggests
Limitation
rows: Thresholds are heuristic; can cluster without a correction
Buyers returning; a new rally may be starting
Can fail; needs leaders to confirm
A few days after a follow-through day
Index falls below the low of the rally attempt
Signals the attempt failed and caution is needed

blocks.x: Defensive positioning

When distribution accumulates and leaders start failing, defensive steps include raising cash, tightening stops, reducing size, and avoiding extended entries. When a follow-through day appears and leaders break out successfully, exposure can be increased gradually. Many practitioners add exposure in steps and require individual stocks to confirm.

blocks.title: Volume source
blocks.x: In India, consider using aggregate NSE cash volume or a liquid index ETF or futures series for these calculations. Be consistent.

blocks.title: These are heuristics
blocks.x: They come from historical US markets. They have worked often but not always, and parameters differ among authors. Treat them as a framework to organise your thinking. Never present them as guaranteed signals.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Distribution days flag institutional selling and follow-through days flag buyers returning. Both are rule-of-thumb market-timing tools, best used with leaders’ behaviour and your own results.

quiz.q: What is a distribution day, commonly?
options: A day when the index falls noticeably on higher volume than the prior day, suggesting institutional selling
A day when the index rises on low volume
quiz.why: It highlights selling pressure by combining decline and volume expansion.

quiz.q: Why should follow-through days be treated with caution?
options: They can fail, and the rally needs confirmation from leading stocks
They only appear in bear markets
quiz.why: Heuristics improve odds but do not guarantee outcomes.

quiz.q: Which is a sensible use of these concepts?
options: Selling everything the moment a fourth distribution day appears, with no other check
Using them to adjust exposure gradually alongside breadth, leader behaviour and your own trade results
quiz.why: Rules of thumb are best used as part of a broader judgement.

lessons.title: Sector rotation
lessons.summary: Money moves between sectors. Aligning stock leadership with sector leadership improves odds.

blocks.x: Capital does not flow evenly through the market. At any time some sectors lead and others lag. **Sector rotation** is the shift of leadership from one group to another as conditions change.
Leading and lagging

items: **Leading sectors:** have strong relative strength versus the NIFTY, many stocks in Stage 2 and many breakouts.
**Lagging sectors:** weak RS, many stocks in Stage 3 or 4.
**Rotation:** leadership changes. Sectors that led one cycle often lag the next.

blocks.x: Why it helps stock selection

A strong stock in a strong sector has tailwinds: sector inflows, peers confirming the trend, and attention. A strong stock in a weak sector faces headwinds. Historically a large share of big winners were part of leading industry groups. When stock and sector leadership align, odds tend to improve.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: The Sector Rotation module uses an RRG-style chart to show whether each sector is leading, weakening, lagging or improving relative to the market. Use it to shortlist sectors before picking stocks.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Keep a short list of the top three to five sectors. Look for the strongest two or three stocks inside each. Avoid the laggards of leading groups, which rarely lead.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Buying the cheapest stock in a hot sector because it has not moved yet. Laggards usually lag for a reason. Leaders in a leading group offer better odds.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Sectors rotate. Combine sector strength with stock-level leadership, and use relative strength to see where capital is flowing.

quiz.q: Why does aligning stock and sector leadership help?
options: A strong stock in a strong sector has tailwinds from group inflows and peer confirmation
It removes the need for stops
quiz.why: Group strength supports individual stocks and signals broad demand.

quiz.q: A hot sector contains one stock that has not moved and trades at a low multiple. What is the usual risk in buying it as the “cheap one”?
options: It is probably lagging for a reason, and laggards rarely lead
It is guaranteed to catch up
quiz.why: Relative weakness in a strong group is typically informative, not an opportunity by itself.

lessons.title: CAN SLIM: the technical components
lessons.summary: William O’Neil’s method has fundamental and technical parts. Here we focus on the technical ones.

blocks.x: **CAN SLIM** is William O’Neil’s growth-stock framework. The fundamental letters (C and A for earnings, N partly for new products) are covered in the fundamental analysis course. The technical and market letters are the focus here.

blocks.caption: The technical and market components
head: Letter
Meaning
Technical interpretation
rows: Buy stocks breaking out to new highs from sound bases, not those far below highs
Volume behaviour: dry-up in bases, surges on breakouts; smaller share floats can move faster
Relative strength: buy the leaders of leading groups
Evidence of accumulation by quality funds, visible in volume and strong closes
Follow the index and breadth; most stocks follow the market

blocks.x: The technical workflow

items: Check the **market** direction first (M).
Find the **leading groups** and the **leaders** in them with high relative strength (L).
Look for stocks near highs forming **sound bases** (N).
Confirm **volume** behaviour and signs of institutional demand (S, I).
Buy a **breakout** from the pivot, within the buy zone, with a stop.
Follow selling rules: cut losses quickly and manage winners.

blocks.title: Leaders, not cheap stocks
blocks.x: O’Neil’s studies of big winners found they were usually strong stocks making new highs, not bargains. The question is not “is it cheap?” but “is it leading, and is the base sound?”.

blocks.title: Limitations
blocks.x: The framework was built mostly on US growth stocks. The market, the liquidity and the index structure differ in India. Use it as a way of thinking, test it on Indian data, and avoid treating thresholds as fixed.

blocks.title: Combining with fundamentals
blocks.x: Many practitioners require strong earnings growth in addition to technical strength. Technical leadership without fundamental support can be speculative.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: The technical side of CAN SLIM is: healthy market, leading group, leading stock, sound base, volume confirmation, and a disciplined breakout entry with defined risk.

quiz.q: According to CAN SLIM’s technical logic, what is a better candidate?
options: A stock 50% below its high that looks cheap
A leading stock in a leading group breaking out from a sound base near a new high
The lowest-priced stock in the market
quiz.why: The approach prefers strength: leaders breaking out with demand evidence.

quiz.q: Why is “M” (market direction) the first check?
options: Most stocks follow the market, so setups have better odds in healthy markets
quiz.why: Market regime sets the background odds for every setup.

lessons.title: The Minervini Trend Template
lessons.summary: Eight conditions that define a Stage 2 uptrend. Understand why each is there, rather than memorising the numbers.

blocks.x: Mark Minervini’s **Trend Template** is a set of eight technical conditions he uses as a first filter to find stocks in a confirmed Stage 2 uptrend. A stock must meet them to be considered for his setups.

blocks.caption: The eight criteria
head: Condition
Purpose
rows: The stock is above its long-term trend lines
Medium-term trend is above long-term trend
200-day average rising for at least one month (preferably 4 to 5)
The long-term trend is up, not flat or turning down
Short-term trend leads: full bullish alignment
The stock is currently strong, not in a deep pullback
Price at least about 30% above its 52-week low
Has already shown strong demand; not a stock bouncing near lows
Price within about 25% of its 52-week high (closer is better)
Relative strength rating 70 or higher (80 to 90 preferred)

blocks.x: Why each condition exists

items: **1 to 5:** together define the alignment of averages seen in the Moving Averages track. They say price, short, medium and long trends all agree.
**6:** a stock only 5% above its low has not proven itself. Real uptrends have typically already advanced.
**7:** stocks far below their highs carry a lot of overhead supply.
**8:** adds the leadership filter from the Relative Strength track.

blocks.title: Not universal truths
blocks.x: The numbers (30%, 25%, 70) are guidelines from his experience. They are not natural laws. Different markets and periods may justify different values, so test before assuming they are optimal. Do not hard-code them as truth in your thinking.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: TradeEdge includes the Minervini screen (all eight criteria) and the Trend Template 7 of 8 screen, which allows one criterion to be missed. The relaxed version lists more names, including stocks that are just emerging, and you must judge which criterion fails and why.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: The template is a filter, not a trigger. Passing it means the stock is in a strong trend. You still need a base, a pivot, volume and a stop.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: The Trend Template combines price, three averages, slope, distance from highs and lows, and relative strength to identify Stage 2 stocks. It filters candidates, it does not time entries.

quiz.q: Which criterion ensures the long-term trend is genuinely up and not flat?
options: The 200-day average rising for at least a month
quiz.why: A rising 200-day average shows the long-term trend direction. Price above a flat average does not.

quiz.q: Why does the template require price to be within about 25% of its 52-week high?
options: Stocks near highs have less overhead supply from trapped holders
Because 25% is a law of nature
quiz.why: Overhead supply is the main reason stocks far below highs struggle to rise.

quiz.q: What is the right way to use the Trend Template numbers?
options: As useful guidelines to be tested, not immutable truths
quiz.why: They reflect one practitioner’s experience. Responsible use includes testing in your own market.

lessons.title: Stage 2 plus Trend Template plus RS
lessons.summary: Weinstein, O’Neil and Minervini describe overlapping ideas. Learn where they agree and where they differ.

blocks.x: The three frameworks reach similar conclusions from different directions. Understanding the overlap helps you build one coherent process instead of a patchwork.

blocks.caption: Comparison of frameworks
head: Aspect
Weinstein
O’Neil
Minervini
rows: Buy leaders breaking out from sound bases
Buy Stage 2 leaders at low-risk pivots with tight risk
Breakout from Stage 1 base on volume
Pivot of cup, flat base and others

blocks.x: Where they overlap

items: Price above a rising long-term average (30-week is about the 150-day).
Strong relative strength.
Breakouts from bases with volume.
Avoiding declining stocks.
Cutting losses quickly.

blocks.x: Where they differ

items: **Entry precision:** Minervini puts more weight on VCP tightness and low-risk pivots, Weinstein on the weekly breakout and stage, O’Neil on base patterns and the market.
**Stops:** O’Neil’s 7% to 8% rule of thumb is simple, Minervini’s stops are tied to the setup and capped, Weinstein’s are tied to support.
**Holding:** Weinstein’s approach is more positional, using the 30-week as a trailing guide, whereas the others often take partial profits sooner.

blocks.x: A combined filter

blocks.label: Combined view
blocks.expr:
Weinstein: Stage 2 on the weekly chart
+ Minervini: Trend Template met on the daily chart
+ O’Neil: leading group and sound base
+ RS: strong rating and RS line near highs
blocks.note: Each lens removes a different kind of weak candidate.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Mixing contradictory rules from different authors, such as a 7% stop with a 15% wide base. Choose one consistent set and test it.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Use weekly Stage analysis for context, the Trend Template to filter, and the base and volume to time. Write the combined process in a checklist.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: The three frameworks share a core: strong, leading, trending stocks near highs, bought at low-risk pivots with defined stops. Choose one consistent set of rules instead of mixing contradictory ones.

quiz.q: Which idea is shared by Weinstein, O’Neil and Minervini?
options: Buy the cheapest stocks near lows
Prefer strong, leading stocks in uptrends and cut losses quickly
quiz.why: All three emphasise strength, trend, relative strength and loss control.

quiz.q: The 30-week moving average is approximately equal to which daily average?
quiz.why: 30 weeks × 5 sessions = 150 sessions.

quiz.q: Why is mixing contradictory rules a problem?
options: It makes the process inconsistent and hard to test, so you cannot learn whether it works
quiz.why: A clear rule set lets you measure results and improve. Mixed rules hide what is working.

lessons.title: Stop loss: where the idea is wrong
lessons.summary: A stop is not a percentage you pick. It is the price at which your reason for the trade no longer holds.

blocks.x: A **stop loss** is a predefined exit if the trade moves against you. It caps the loss and keeps one failure from damaging the account.

blocks.title: The stop principle
blocks.x: The stop should invalidate the trade thesis, not simply satisfy an arbitrary percentage.
Types of stops

blocks.caption: Stop methods
head: Method
How it works
Strength
Weakness
rows: Below a swing low, pivot, base low or signal candle
Tied to the reason for the trade
A fixed percent below entry (for example 7%)
Ignores structure and the stock’s volatility
Entry minus a multiple of Average True Range (for example 2 × ATR)
May sit in meaningless places relative to structure
Wider for volatile stocks, tighter for calm ones
Exit if the trade does not move within N days
May exit before a delayed move

blocks.label: Average True Range (ATR)
blocks.expr:
True Range = max( High − Low, |High − Previous close|, |Low − Previous close| )
ATR(14) = Wilder-smoothed average of True Range over 14 periods
blocks.note: ATR measures a stock’s typical daily movement in rupees. Example: ATR ₹8 on a ₹400 stock is 2% of price per day.

blocks.x: Choosing a stop

items: Find the **structural level** where the thesis fails (for example below the last contraction low).
Check that the stop is **outside normal noise**: compare the distance with ATR. A stop closer than about one ATR is often hit by ordinary movement.
Check the **maximum risk** you accept per share. If the structural stop is too far, reduce size or skip.

blocks.x: Example: ABC enters at ₹500. The last contraction low is ₹472 and ATR(14) is ₹9. A stop at ₹470 is ₹30 away (6%), well beyond one ATR, so noise will not trigger it. A stop at ₹495 would be inside one ATR and likely to be hit by noise.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Moving a stop lower after entry because the stock is “just a pullback”. That changes risk after the fact. Stops can be moved up to protect profit, but not widened.

blocks.title: Gap risk
blocks.x: Stops are triggered by prices, and a stock that gaps below your stop on bad news opens at the gap price, not at your stop. Results, regulatory news and overnight global moves can cause this, which is why position size matters as much as the stop.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Place the stop where the idea fails, check it against volatility and your maximum risk, and never widen it. If the logical stop is too far, reduce size or skip the trade.

quiz.q: What should determine where a stop is placed?
options: The level at which the trade thesis is invalidated
The price you want the stock to reach
quiz.why: A stop tied to structure reflects why you entered. Arbitrary numbers can sit in noise or exceed acceptable risk.

quiz.q: ATR(14) is ₹9. Entry ₹500. Which stop is most likely to be hit by normal noise?
quiz.why: ₹495 is only ₹5 below entry, which is less than one ATR (₹9). Normal daily movement could reach it.

quiz.q: A stock gaps below your stop at the open on bad news. At which price are you likely to exit?
options: At or near the gap price, which can be worse than the stop
quiz.why: A stop becomes a market order when triggered. Gaps skip prices, so slippage can exceed the planned loss.

lessons.title: Position sizing
lessons.summary: Size the trade so that being wrong costs a fixed, small part of the account. This is the single most important calculation.

blocks.x: **Position sizing** decides how many shares to buy. The right method starts not with how much you want to invest but with how much you are willing to lose.

blocks.label: Position size
blocks.expr:
Position Size = Capital at Risk ÷ Risk Per Share
Risk Per Share = Entry Price − Stop Price
blocks.note: Capital at risk is a fixed percentage of your account, commonly 0.5% to 1% per trade for many traders. It is a personal decision.

blocks.x: Worked example
If the stop hits, the loss is about ₹10,000 (1% of the account), ignoring costs and slippage. If the stop were wider, at ₹450 (₹50 risk), size would be 200 shares. **Same risk, different size.**
What position sizing teaches

items: A wide stop does not mean more risk, it means **fewer shares**.
A tight stop allows more shares, but check that it is outside normal noise.
Position value can be large even when risk is small. Check concentration separately.
Liquidity matters: do not buy more shares than the stock can trade without moving price.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Calculate size before you enter, with a calculator or spreadsheet. If the position value exceeds your concentration limit (for example 20% to 25%), cap the size.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Choosing shares by feel, such as always buying 500 shares. The same 500 shares can risk ₹5,000 on one trade and ₹30,000 on another.

blocks.title: Costs
blocks.x: Brokerage, STT, exchange charges and slippage reduce results. For small accounts and tight stops, include a cost estimate in the risk per share.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Position size equals capital at risk divided by risk per share. Risk a fixed small percentage, size from the stop distance, and cap size for concentration and liquidity.

quiz.q: Capital ₹10,00,000, risk 1%, entry ₹500, stop ₹475. How many shares?
quiz.why: Risk = ₹10,000. Risk per share = ₹25. 10,000 ÷ 25 = 400 shares.

quiz.q: If the stop were ₹450 instead of ₹475 with the same 1% risk, what changes?
quiz.why: Risk per share doubles to ₹50, so size is 10,000 ÷ 50 = 200. A wider stop reduces shares, not risk.

quiz.q: Why is “I always buy 500 shares” a poor sizing method?
options: Rupee risk varies with each stop distance, so the same shares can risk very different amounts
quiz.why: Shares are not risk. Risk depends on shares times stop distance.

lessons.title: Risk/reward, R multiples and expectancy
lessons.summary: Think in R, the amount you risk. A strategy can be profitable even when it loses more often than it wins.

blocks.x: **1R** is the amount you risk on a trade. If you risk ₹10,000, a ₹30,000 profit is **+3R** and a stopped-out loss is **−1R**. Measuring in R makes trades comparable regardless of size.

blocks.label: R multiple
blocks.expr: R multiple = (Exit price − Entry price) ÷ (Entry price − Stop price)
blocks.note: Example: entry ₹500, stop ₹475, exit ₹575. R = 75 ÷ 25 = +3R.

blocks.x: Reward-to-risk
If you risk ₹25 per share to potentially make ₹75, the reward/risk is 3:1. Before entering, estimate a realistic reward scenario and compare it with risk.
Expected value

blocks.label: Expectancy in R
blocks.expr: Expectancy = (Win rate × Average win in R) − (Loss rate × Average loss in R)
blocks.note: It is the average result per trade in R over many trades.

blocks.x: A 45% win rate with an average winner of 3R and an average loser of 1R produces +0.80R per trade. Over 100 trades that is +80R. At ₹10,000 per R, that is ₹8,00,000 before costs, drawdowns and sample uncertainty.

blocks.title: Win rate is not the goal
blocks.x: Many beginners focus on win rate. A system that wins 70% but averages 0.5R winners and 2R losers loses money: (0.7×0.5) − (0.3×2.0) = −0.25R. What matters is the combination of win rate and payoff.

blocks.title: Caveats
blocks.x: Expectancy estimated from a small number of trades is uncertain. Costs, slippage and changing markets can reduce it. Treat these numbers as an illustration of the logic, not a promise.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Record every trade’s result in R. After 30 to 50 trades, calculate your own win rate and average winner and loser. These are the real inputs for improving the process.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Measure trades in R. Expectancy combines win rate with average win and loss in R. Strategies with lower win rates can be profitable when winners are much larger than losers.

quiz.q: Entry ₹500, stop ₹475, exit ₹575. What is the R multiple?
A system wins 45% of trades with an average winner of 3R and an average loser of 1R. What is its expectancy?
A system wins 70% of trades, with average winners of 0.5R and average losers of 2R. What is the result?
options: Profitable because win rate is high
quiz.why: A high win rate does not offset poor payoff. The average loser is four times the average winner.

lessons.title: Portfolio-level risk
lessons.summary: Individual trade risk is only part of the picture. Correlation, concentration and gap risk matter at the portfolio level.

blocks.x: Risking 1% per trade seems safe. But if you hold ten positions that all fall together, the portfolio risk is not 1%. Portfolio risk depends on how positions relate to each other.
Key risks

blocks.caption: Portfolio risk factors
head: Risk
What it is
How to manage
rows: Positions that move together, such as stocks in the same trend or theme
Treat highly correlated positions as one larger position
Cap position value as a percent of account
Sum of risk across all open trades if all stops hit
Set a maximum (for example 5% to 6% of capital)
A stock opens beyond its stop on news
Smaller size around events; avoid oversized positions in volatile names
A broad sell-off hits most stocks at once
Reduce exposure when the regime deteriorates

blocks.label: Total open risk
blocks.expr: Open risk = Sum of (Position size × Risk per share) for all open positions
blocks.note: Example: six trades each risking 1% means 6% of the account is at risk if all stops hit.

blocks.x: Six positions at 1% each is 6% of the account at risk. If four are in the same sector and the sector falls sharply, gaps can make the realised loss larger than planned. Some practitioners cap sector exposure and reduce total open risk when markets weaken.

blocks.title: Small and mid cap risk
blocks.x: Illiquid names can gap through stops, and lower and upper circuits can prevent exit for a day or more. Use smaller sizes and count liquidity as a risk.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Diversifying by number of stocks rather than by risk. Ten similar stocks behave like one or two.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Keep a simple table: ticker, sector, position value, risk at stop. Total each column. If sector or total risk exceed limits, do not add.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Manage risk at the portfolio level: cap total open risk, sector exposure and position size, treat correlated positions as one, and respect gap and market-wide risk.

quiz.q: Six open trades each risk 1% of capital. What is the total open risk if all stops hit?
quiz.why: Open risk sums across positions: 6 × 1% = 6%.

quiz.q: Four of six positions are in the same sector and are highly correlated. How should they be viewed?
options: As closer to one larger position, since they tend to move together
quiz.why: Correlated positions share the same drivers, so their risks add rather than offset.

lessons.title: Managing a winning trade
lessons.summary: The initial stop protects capital. Later stops protect profit. Choose a method in advance.

blocks.x: Entry is the beginning. How a trade is managed after it works often decides whether it becomes a small gain or a large one.
A typical sequence

items: **Initial stop:** below the thesis-invalidation level.

**Break-even:** once the stock reaches a multiple of risk (for example +1.5R to +2R) and holds, many traders move the stop to entry. This protects capital but can cause a stop-out in a normal pullback, so do it thoughtfully.
**Trailing stop:** raise the stop as the stock advances, below higher lows or a moving average.
**Partial profits:** sell part at a target or after a large move, and trail the rest.

blocks.caption: Trailing methods
head: Method
How
Fits
rows: Stop below the most recent higher low
Exit on a close below the 10-day EMA, 50-day or 10-week average
Strong leaders; choose by how tightly you want to follow
Stop at highest close minus a multiple of ATR (for example 3 × ATR)
Stop a fixed percent below the highest price

blocks.x: Example: ABC is bought at ₹500 with a ₹475 stop (1R = ₹25). At ₹550 (+2R) the stop moves to ₹500 (break-even). At ₹600 the stop trails to ₹560, just below the last higher low. If it later falls to ₹560, the trade exits at +2.4R.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Match the trailing method to the stock’s behaviour. A tight trail on a volatile mid cap will exit on noise. A wide trail on a calm large cap gives back too much.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Moving to break-even too early. A stock that has just broken out will often retest the pivot. Stops that sit exactly at entry are frequently hit by that normal retest.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Protect capital first, then profit. Use a pre-chosen trailing method that matches the stock’s volatility, and consider partial profits to bank some gain.

quiz.q: Entry ₹500, stop ₹475. The stock reaches ₹600 and the stop trails to ₹560. If the stock falls and exits at ₹560, what is the R multiple?
Why can moving the stop to break-even too early backfire?
options: Breakouts often retest the pivot, and a stop at entry is likely to be triggered by that normal retest
quiz.why: A retest near entry is common. A stop exactly there turns normal noise into a loss of opportunity.

lessons.title: When to sell
lessons.summary: A list of objective reasons to exit, so the decision is not made in the middle of fear or greed.

blocks.x: Selling is the hardest decision because it is judged against what happens next. Pre-defined reasons make it easier.

blocks.caption: Reasons to sell
head: Reason
What you see
Typical response
rows: Close back below the pivot on volume
Largest down day or week in a long time on big volume
Loses the last higher low or a key average on volume
Weekly close below the 10-week average with volume
RS line breaks down while price stalls
Review; a warning that leadership is fading
Very steep, extended advance on huge volume

blocks.x: Selling into strength versus weakness

Selling **into strength** (during a sharp advance) usually gives better prices but risks leaving a larger move. Selling **into weakness** (after the trend breaks) is more certain but gives back profit. Many traders combine: take partial profits into strength and exit the remainder on a technical violation.
The plan versus the emotion

items: Write sell rules before entry.
Differentiate a **plan-based sale** (a rule triggered) from an **emotional sale** (fear or boredom).
Review exits regularly: did you sell by rule, too early, or too late?

blocks.title: Events
blocks.x: Results announcements and regulatory events can gap the stock. Decide in advance whether to hold through an event, and size accordingly.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Selling a strong stock because it is “up a lot”. Price gain alone is not a sell reason. Evidence of weakness, a rule or a better use of capital is.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Sell for objective reasons: stops, failed breakouts, distribution, trend and average violations, stage transitions, fading RS, or a deteriorating market. Write the rules before you enter.

quiz.q: Which is a rule-based reason to exit?
options: The stock is up 40% and feels expensive
A weekly close below the 10-week average on heavy volume, as defined in the plan
quiz.why: Rules triggered by price and volume evidence are objective, unlike feelings.

quiz.q: What is the trade-off of selling into strength versus weakness?
options: Strength often gives better prices but may leave a bigger move, while weakness gives more certainty but returns some profit
quiz.why: Each approach has a cost. Combining partial selling and a technical exit balances them.

lessons.title: Scaling in
lessons.summary: Add to winners, not losers. Each addition must be confirmed and risk-controlled.

blocks.x: **Scaling in** means building a position in stages rather than all at once. Done well, it increases exposure only when the trade is working.
Common approaches

items: **Initial position, then add on confirmation:** start with a partial size (for example half) at the pivot, add the rest as the stock follows through.
**Pyramid:** add smaller amounts as the stock rises, so the average cost rises more slowly than the price.
**Add on a constructive pullback:** a new entry at a rising average or a retest of the breakout level.

blocks.caption: Example pyramid
head: Step
Price
Shares
Comment
rows: Follow-through confirmed, stop moved to ₹500 for the whole position
Smaller add; whole position stop raised to ₹520

blocks.x: Total shares: 350. Average cost: (200×500 + 100×520 + 50×540) ÷ 350 = (1,00,000 + 52,000 + 27,000) ÷ 350 = ₹511.4. A stop at ₹520 locks in a small profit on the combined position, so the added shares did not increase risk beyond the original plan.

blocks.title: Risk control for adds
blocks.x: Before each add, recalculate total risk to the stop. The combined position should not risk more than your plan allows.

blocks.title: Do not average down
blocks.x: Adding to a loser lowers your average price but increases risk in a trade that has already told you it is not working. Scaling in is for confirmed strength.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Scale in on confirmation with smaller adds, keep total risk within plan by raising the stop, and never add to losing positions.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between pyramiding and averaging down?
options: Pyramiding adds to winners on confirmation, averaging down adds to losers
quiz.why: Adding to strength is consistent with the thesis. Adding to weakness fights the market.

quiz.q: Why should each add be smaller than the previous one?
options: So average cost rises slowly and the position is not heavily exposed to a pullback at the highest price
quiz.why: Smaller adds at higher prices limit exposure at the least favourable entry points.

lessons.title: Scaling out
lessons.summary: Taking partial profits can reduce regret and lock in gains, if it follows a plan rather than emotion.

blocks.x: **Scaling out** means selling a position in parts. It balances two risks: giving back profit if the trade reverses, and missing a large move if you sell too early.
Common approaches

items: **Sell a portion at a target** (for example half at +2R or +3R) and trail the remainder.
**Sell into a climactic run,** keep a smaller core with a trailing stop.
**Sell a fraction on each violation of a short-term average,** and the rest on a major violation.

blocks.x: Average outcome: (3R + 4.8R) ÷ 2 = 3.9R. If the stock had reversed after Target 1, the remaining half would still have exited at +2R, so the trade would have returned about 2.5R on average.
Premature profit-taking

Selling too early is a common error. If you cut every winner at +1.5R while letting losers reach −1R, expectancy shrinks. A plan with a core position for the trend helps avoid this, because you know part of the position is designed to capture a larger move.

blocks.title: Plan versus emotion
blocks.x: A trading plan sells a portion because a rule says so. Emotional selling happens because the gain feels fragile. The result can look similar, but only one is repeatable.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Decide your partial profit rule before entry, for example half at +2R. Note the reason for each sale in your journal.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Scaling out balances regret and risk. Use pre-defined targets and trailing stops for the remainder, and avoid cutting every winner short.

quiz.q: Entry ₹500, stop ₹475. Half is sold at ₹575 and half exits at ₹620. What is the average R multiple?
quiz.why: Half at +3R and half at +4.8R: (3 + 4.8) ÷ 2 = 3.9R.

quiz.q: Why can cutting every winner at +1.5R damage a system?
options: Average winners become small compared with losers, lowering expectancy
It increases the win rate permanently
quiz.why: If losers are −1R and winners are capped near +1.5R, you need a very high win rate to be profitable.

lessons.title: From chart analysis to screening
lessons.summary: A screen is a set of rules that selects stocks. It extends your attention, but it does not replace judgement.

blocks.x: India has thousands of listed stocks. You cannot read every chart. **Screening** converts a visual idea into numeric conditions and lists every stock that satisfies them.

blocks.label: What screening does
blocks.expr:
Subjective chart observation
→ Objective conditions
→ Repeatable candidate generation
blocks.note: The screen is a funnel. It narrows thousands of stocks to a short list worth a human review.

blocks.x: A good screening workflow

items: **Define the idea** in words: “strong stocks near highs that are tightening”.
**Translate** each part into a measurable condition: price vs averages, RS rating, distance from high, volume ratio.
**Run the screen** and get a candidate list.
**Review the charts** of each candidate manually.
**Record** which screen results turned into trades and how they performed. Adjust the thresholds.

blocks.x: Strengths and limits

blocks.caption: Screens versus judgement
head: Screens do well
Screens do poorly
rows: Judging the quality of a pattern’s shape
Applying the same rules every day
Reading the context of news and events
Surfacing leaders you did not know
Distinguishing a clean base from a messy one

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: TechLens → Screens provides ready-made screens grouped by theme: Market Leaders, Breakouts, Pullback and Legend Screens. The next lessons explain what typical conditions mean so you can interpret the results.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating the screen output as a buy list. It is a research list. Every name still needs a chart review, a stop and a size.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Screening turns chart ideas into objective rules and lists candidates consistently. It cannot judge shape quality, context or market regime. Always review the chart.

quiz.q: What is the right role of a screen output?
options: A research shortlist to be reviewed on charts
quiz.why: Screens find candidates consistently. Judgement, risk definition and sizing still follow.

quiz.q: Which is something screens do poorly?
options: Applying the same rules to every stock
Judging the shape quality of a base and the context of news
quiz.why: Shape quality and context need human judgement.

lessons.title: A Trend Template screen
lessons.summary: Worked example: translating the Trend Template into conditions and understanding every line.

blocks.x: Here is an example screen built from the Trend Template ideas. Each condition has a purpose.

blocks.label: Example Trend Template screen
blocks.expr:
SMA50 > SMA150 > SMA200
Close > SMA50
Close > SMA200
SMA200 today > SMA200 about 22 trading days ago (rising)
Close ≥ 1.30 × 52-week low
Close ≥ 0.75 × 52-week high  (within 25% of the high)
RS Rating ≥ 75
blocks.note: These are illustrative thresholds. Parameters differ among practitioners, and you should test them.

blocks.caption: Reading each condition
head: Condition
What it checks
What happens if you remove it
rows: Includes stocks in transition or recovering from downtrends
Includes stocks still in long-term downtrends
Includes stocks above a flat or falling long-term line

blocks.x: What you will see in the results

items: A relatively small list in a healthy market and a very short list in a weak one. The count itself tells you about the regime.
Extended stocks and stocks near pivots mixed together. Next steps (pivot proximity, base quality) narrow them.
Illiquid stocks, which you must filter separately with minimum turnover.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: The Minervini screen uses all eight criteria. The Trend Template 7 of 8 screen allows one failure and is sorted by criteria met and RS rating, so you can see which stocks narrowly miss. Use it to find stocks about to qualify, and check which criterion is failing.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Add a liquidity filter (for example average daily turnover above a minimum rupee value) to avoid names that you cannot trade with your size.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Tuning thresholds until the screen shows past winners. That is hindsight selection. Choose thresholds from logic and test them on data you did not use to design them.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A Trend Template screen stacks alignment, slope, distance from high and low, and RS. Every condition filters out a type of weak candidate. Add a liquidity filter and avoid tuning to past winners.

quiz.q: What does requiring SMA200 to be higher than it was about a month ago check?
options: That the long-term trend is rising rather than flat or falling
quiz.why: Comparing the average with its own value earlier measures slope.

quiz.q: A Trend Template screen returns only a handful of stocks. What might that indicate?
options: Few stocks are in confirmed uptrends, which may reflect a weak market regime
quiz.why: The number of stocks meeting strict trend criteria is itself a read on market health.

quiz.q: Why is tuning thresholds until past winners appear a mistake?
options: It uses hindsight, so the screen may not work on new data
quiz.why: Fitting to known winners can create a screen that explains the past but fails on new data.

lessons.title: A fresh breakout screen
lessons.summary: Detect stocks that have just moved above a resistance level with participation and strength.

blocks.x: A fresh breakout screen looks for stocks that have just crossed a recent high, with confirming conditions.

blocks.label: Example fresh breakout screen
blocks.expr:
Close > highest high of the prior 20 trading days (the pivot)
Close ≤ 1.03 × pivot  (not too extended)
Volume ≥ 1.5 × 50-day average volume
SMA50 > SMA150 > SMA200
RS Rating ≥ 70
Close within about 10% of 52-week high
blocks.note: A bar with Close in the upper half of its range can be added to filter weak closes.

blocks.caption: Condition meanings
head: Condition
Purpose
rows: A recent resistance has been cleared
Buy zone: avoids chasing extended moves

blocks.x: What the screen cannot tell you

items: Whether the 20-day high is the true pivot of a good base, or just a short-term high inside a messy range.
Whether the base was tight and quiet before the move.
Whether the market backdrop supports follow-through.
Whether liquidity allows your position size.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: The Fresh Breakout screen follows this pattern: it checks the close against the 20-day pivot, a ceiling of 103% of the pivot, relative volume of at least 1.5, trend alignment and an RS rating threshold. The Weekly Breakout Soon and 52-week-high screens use the same logic on different horizons.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Buying every name on the list. Many are low-quality breakouts. Sort by base quality and market context after the screen.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A fresh breakout screen checks pivot clearance, extension, volume, trend and RS. It does not judge base quality or market backdrop, so review each chart.

quiz.q: Why include “Close ≤ 103% of the pivot”?
options: To exclude breakouts already extended beyond a reasonable buy zone
quiz.why: A stock far above its pivot has worse reward/risk.

quiz.q: What does a breakout screen not tell you?
options: Whether price is above the prior 20-day high
Whether the base before the breakout was tight and healthy
quiz.why: Shape and quality of the base need visual review.

lessons.title: What can and cannot be screened: VCP and tight bases
lessons.summary: Hard filters can approximate tightness and volume dry-up. They cannot replace your eyes.

blocks.x: Not every chart pattern can be captured by simple numeric filters. VCP is a good example.
What can be measured

items: **Tightness:** the high-low range over the last 10 or 20 days as a percent of price.
**Contraction:** whether the recent 10-day range is smaller than the prior 10-day range.
**Volume dry-up:** recent average volume versus earlier average, or volume near its lowest in the base.
**Trend and leadership:** Stage 2, RS rating, proximity to highs.
**Proximity to a pivot:** distance of price from the recent high.

blocks.x: What is hard to measure

items: **The count and shape of contractions** (are they successive and about half the size?).
**Whether the base is orderly or erratic** beyond a simple range number.
**Context:** news, results dates, sector situation.
**Whether a shakeout is constructive.**

blocks.caption: Hard filters versus human interpretation
head: Hard quantitative filters
Human chart interpretation
rows: Is the shape a clean VCP or a messy range?
Is the last contraction dry enough, with a shakeout?
Is this stock a real leader with a catalyst?

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: The Leadership Tight Base screen requires RS Rating above 80, Stage 2, a 20-day range of 10% or less, a recent 10-day range tighter than the prior 10 days, and contracting volume. It finds candidates that look like late-stage VCPs. The VCP screen as such was removed because numeric filters cannot judge pattern quality on their own.

blocks.title: Not every pattern can be an SQL filter
blocks.x: A tight 20-day range also describes dull, illiquid stocks that never go anywhere. That is why RS, Stage and liquidity filters are paired with it.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Use screens to find tight leaders, then use your eyes to count contractions, check the volume dry-up, and decide the pivot.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Hard filters approximate tightness, contraction and volume dry-up. Pattern quality, contraction sequence and context still need human interpretation.

quiz.q: Which is easiest to capture in a numeric screen?
options: A 20-day range of 10% or less with RS above 80
Whether contractions step down cleanly in a convincing shape
quiz.why: Range, RS and Stage are numeric. Shape quality and context are not easily reduced to numbers.

quiz.q: Why pair a tight-range filter with RS and Stage filters?
options: A tight range alone also describes dull stocks that go nowhere, so leadership and trend add meaning
Because tight ranges are always bullish
quiz.why: Tightness is only meaningful in a leading stock in an uptrend.

lessons.title: A pullback screen
lessons.summary: Find strong stocks that have pulled back quietly toward support.

blocks.x: A pullback screen looks for stocks whose trend is strong, but which have recently dipped toward a rising average with calm volume.

blocks.label: Example pullback screen
blocks.expr:
SMA50 > SMA150 > SMA200  (strong trend)
RS Rating ≥ 75
Close within 3% of SMA50 or within 3% of the 10-week average
Close ≥ 0.85 × 52-week high  (not too deep)
5-day average volume < 0.8 × 50-day average volume  (volume contraction)
Close > SMA200
blocks.note: A recovery filter such as Close > previous day’s high can capture a reversal day.

blocks.caption: Reading each condition
head: Condition
Purpose
rows: A real trend exists to continue
The pullback has reached a common support

blocks.x: The results are **candidates for a timing review**. You still check structure (is there a higher low?), the market regime, and look for a reversal signal near the average before acting.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: TechLens → Screens → Pullback contains pullback screens, including Leadership Tight Base, which finds leaders whose range has contracted. Use them for candidates and check that RS and volume support the setup.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Buying the first stock on the list because it is near its average. A pullback is only constructive if structure, volume and RS support it. If any of these is poor, skip.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A pullback screen selects strong, aligned stocks near support with quiet volume. It is a candidate generator. Structure, signal candles and market conditions decide the entry.

quiz.q: Why include a volume contraction condition in a pullback screen?
options: Quiet volume suggests the pullback is light profit-taking rather than heavy distribution
quiz.why: Healthy pullbacks tend to have contracting volume.

quiz.q: A stock passes the pullback screen, but the market is in a correction and the stock has formed a lower low. What should you do?
options: Buy because it passed the screen
Skip or wait, since structure and market conditions argue against a healthy pullback
quiz.why: Screens identify candidates. Structure and regime can invalidate them.

lessons.title: The complete setup framework
lessons.summary: A setup is a chain. Every link must hold before capital is committed.

blocks.x: A setup is not a single signal. It is a chain of conditions from the broad market to the exit plan.

blocks.label: The chain
blocks.expr:
Market regime
↓
Sector strength
↓
Stock trend
↓
Relative strength
↓
Base
↓
Volume
↓
Entry
↓
Stop
↓
Position size
↓
Exit
blocks.note: If an early link is weak, the later ones cannot fully compensate. If all are strong, the odds improve, but are not guaranteed.

blocks.caption: What each link asks
head: Link
Question
Where covered
rows: Is the stock in Stage 2 with aligned averages?
Is the entry near the pivot and not extended?

blocks.x: Using this chain avoids a common error: starting with a pretty chart and justifying it afterwards. Starting with the market and working down protects you from attractive setups in hostile conditions.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Print or keep the chain as a checklist. A trade that cannot answer every link should either be skipped or taken at reduced size.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Strong in one link but weak elsewhere, for example a perfect chart during a market correction. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A complete setup runs from market to exit plan, in order. Each link adds evidence, and a weak link calls for reduced size or no trade.

quiz.q: Why start with the market regime rather than the stock chart?
options: Because setups have different odds in different regimes, and starting from the market prevents justifying an attractive chart in a hostile environment
Because the market determines exact prices
quiz.why: The market sets the background odds. Evaluating it first avoids bias toward a favourite chart.

quiz.q: A stock shows a perfect base but the market is in a correction. What does the chain suggest?
options: Ignore the market and buy full size
A weak link calls for waiting or reduced size
quiz.why: A weak early link lowers the odds, even if later links are strong.

lessons.title: Worked example: a breakout setup
lessons.summary: A fictional case from market check to position size and management. Not a recommendation.

blocks.title: Hypothetical example
blocks.x: ABC Industries is a fictional company with invented numbers, used only to illustrate the process. It is not a real security or a recommendation.
1. Market and sector

NIFTY 50 is above rising 50-day and 200-day averages. Midcap index is also in an uptrend, and about 62% of stocks are above their 50-day average. The sector index (Engineering) has a rising RS line versus the NIFTY, and several constituents are in Stage 2. Verdict: supportive.
2. Stock trend and relative strength

ABC trades at ₹198 with SMA50 ₹185, SMA150 ₹168 and SMA200 ₹160 (rising). It is 7% below its 52-week high of ₹213 and 62% above its low. RS rating 88, Mansfield RS above zero and rising. All Trend Template criteria are met.
3. The base
Over 12 weeks ABC formed a VCP: pullbacks of 18%, 9%, 5% and a final 3% tight pause. Volume in the last pause fell to 55% of the 50-day average. The pivot is ₹200 (the high of the last contraction).

blocks.caption: The plan before the open
head: Item
Value
rows: Prior high ₹213, then a measured move toward ₹240

blocks.x: 4. The breakout day

ABC opens at ₹199, trades above ₹200 mid-morning on rising volume and closes at ₹207, near the day’s high of ₹208. Volume is 2.4 times average. The entry at ₹201 was triggered by a buy-stop at the pivot. Close of ₹207 is 3.5% above the pivot, so the stock is now outside the buy zone for new buyers, but the existing position is fine.
5. Management

items: Stop stays at ₹187 until the stock holds and makes a new high.
After a retest holding ₹202 and a new high at ₹215, the stop moves to ₹201 (break-even) and then trails below higher lows.
Half of the position is sold at ₹236 (about +2.5R). The rest trails the 10-day EMA.
The remainder exits at ₹248 when the stock closes below the 10-day EMA on heavy volume.

blocks.title: What the example teaches
blocks.x: Every number was set before entry: pivot, stop, size, targets and exit rules. The process works even though the outcome is not guaranteed. The same setup in another case could stop out at −1R.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A complete breakout trade has a market check, a stock qualification, a pivot, a stop, a size and an exit plan, all written before entry.

quiz.q: Entry ₹201, stop ₹187, risk ₹10,000. How many shares (approximately)?
quiz.why: Risk per share = ₹14. 10,000 ÷ 14 ≈ 714 shares.

quiz.q: Why were the pivot, stop, size and exit rules written before the open?
options: So decisions are made calmly, not during price movement, which reduces emotional errors
quiz.why: Pre-defined plans remove improvisation during stress.

quiz.q: The stock closes 3.5% above the pivot on breakout day. What does that mean for a new buyer?
options: It is still inside the 3% buy zone
It is slightly beyond the buy zone, so a new entry carries more extension risk
quiz.why: Beyond the zone, reward/risk worsens for new buyers, though an existing position is managed normally.

lessons.title: Worked example: a pullback setup
lessons.summary: A fictional continuation entry at a rising average. Compare its risk profile with the breakout.

blocks.title: Hypothetical example
blocks.x: XYZ Technologies is fictional and its numbers are invented for illustration. This is not a recommendation.
1. Market and sector
The NIFTY is in an uptrend. IT sector RS line is rising. Verdict: supportive.
2. Stock context

XYZ broke out of a base at ₹300 five weeks ago and ran to ₹372 (+24%) with strong volume. It then pulled back for seven sessions to ₹348 on volume 40% below average, touching its rising 50-day average (₹346). RS line stays near highs, and the structure shows a higher low versus the earlier ₹310 swing low. Weekly: price above a rising 10-week average.
3. Signal

On day eight XYZ forms a small hammer-like candle with a low of ₹344, closes at ₹354 in the upper half of its range on volume 20% above the previous day. The next morning it trades above the signal candle’s high of ₹355.

blocks.caption: The plan
head: Item
Value
rows: Retest of ₹372 high, then a breakout toward ₹400

blocks.x: Notice the concentration cap: the risk-based size (666 shares) would exceed 20% of the account, so the position is capped at 560 shares, risking about ₹8,400 (0.84% of the account). The cap overrides the risk formula.
Comparison with a breakout

blocks.caption: Breakout versus pullback
head: Feature
Breakout (ABC)
Pullback (XYZ)
rows: At support, with a signal candle
Close below the average and signal low

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Pullback entries often have tighter stops but less obvious reward to the first target. Their value is greatest when a breakout above the prior high is likely.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A pullback setup has a tight, structural stop, but the reward to the first target can be modest. Check concentration and reward/risk before acting.

quiz.q: Risk-based size is 666 shares (₹2,37,000), but the concentration cap is 20% of ₹10,00,000. What is the position?
options: About 560 shares, because the cap overrides the formula

quiz.q: Why can a pullback entry have a tighter stop than a breakout?
options: The entry is at a support level with a nearby invalidation point, so the stop sits close below it
quiz.why: At support, the thesis is wrong if price drops a short distance below, so the structural stop is nearer.

lessons.title: Worked example: a failed breakout
lessons.summary: What it looks like when the thesis fails, and why a small loss is the plan working.

blocks.title: Hypothetical example
blocks.x: PQR Engineering is fictional. The numbers are invented to illustrate the process.
The setup

PQR formed a 10-week flat base with a ₹250 pivot. It met Stage 2 and Trend Template conditions, RS rating 82. The market was neutral, with breadth slightly weakening. Plan: entry ₹251, stop ₹236 (below the base low), risk ₹15 per share. Risk 1% of ₹10,00,000 = ₹10,000, so size ≈ 666 shares.
What happened

items: **Day 1:** PQR breaks out to ₹258 intraday but closes at ₹253 with a long upper wick on volume of 1.3x average. The signal is mediocre.
**Day 2:** the stock gaps up slightly to ₹255 and fades to close at ₹248, back below the pivot, on 1.6x volume.
**Day 3:** the market falls 1.4%. PQR closes at ₹241 on 2.0x volume.
**Day 4:** the stock opens at ₹238 and trades to ₹235, hitting the ₹236 stop. The exit fills at ₹235.

blocks.caption: Result
head: Item
Value
rows: ₹16 (slightly more than the planned ₹15 due to slippage)

blocks.x: What went right

items: The loss was close to the planned 1% despite slippage.

The warning signs were visible earlier: mediocre breakout volume and a close below the pivot on Day 2. A trader whose plan said “exit on a close back below the pivot on above-average volume” would have exited at about ₹248 for a −0.2R loss.
The account was preserved for the next setup.

blocks.x: What to review

In the journal: was the market warning visible (weakening breadth)? Was the breakout volume below the ideal level? Would a rule such as “do not add size when the market is neutral” or “exit on a close below the pivot” have improved the result? A failed trade is data, not a verdict.

blocks.title: The lesson
blocks.x: A good process still produces losses. A loss of about 1R from a valid setup is a cost of doing business. A large loss from ignoring the plan is the actual damage.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A failed breakout handled by the plan costs about 1R or less. Review the signs, refine the rules and move on.

quiz.q: Which exit rule would have reduced the loss in this example?
options: Exit on a close back below the pivot on above-average volume
quiz.why: Day 2 closed back below ₹250 on 1.6x volume. Exiting there would have lost roughly ₹3 per share rather than ₹16.

quiz.q: The loss was slightly above 1R because of slippage. What does this show?
options: Stops can fill slightly worse than planned, so sizing should account for some slippage
quiz.why: Fast moves and gaps can produce worse fills. Planning for modest slippage is part of risk management.

quiz.q: How should a failed trade be treated after the exit?
options: Reviewed in the journal for signs missed and for rule improvements, without assuming the process is wrong
Used as a reason to double the next size
quiz.why: Losses carry information. Review separates a bad outcome from a bad decision.

lessons.title: What is a backtest?
lessons.summary: A backtest applies exact rules to past data to see how they would have performed. It is evidence, not proof.

blocks.x: A **backtest** simulates a trading strategy on historical data. Instead of asking “does this look like it works?”, you ask “what would have happened if I had followed these exact rules?”.
What a backtest needs

blocks.caption: Components of a rule-based strategy
head: Component
Question it answers
Example
rows: NSE stocks with average turnover above ₹5 Cr
Close above the 20-day high with relative volume ≥ 1.5, Trend Template met
Below the 10-day low, maximum 8% below entry
Close below the 10-week average, or stop hit
1% of equity risk per trade, max 20% in one stock
Max 8 open positions, max 25% per sector

blocks.x: Costs and slippage

Backtests that ignore costs overstate results. Each trade has brokerage, STT, exchange fees and **slippage**: the difference between the price you expected and the price you got. High-turnover strategies and illiquid stocks are especially sensitive. Test with conservative cost assumptions.
What a backtest can and cannot tell you

items: **Can:** show whether the rules had a positive expectancy in the past sample, how big losing streaks and drawdowns were, and how sensitive results are to parameters.
**Cannot:** guarantee that future results will resemble the past. Markets change, and your data may be flawed.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Backtesting a vague idea like “buy strong breakouts” by looking at charts. If you cannot write the rules so that another person gets the same trades, it is not a backtest. It is a story.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A backtest applies precise, complete rules including costs to historical data. It is evidence about an idea, with limits, not proof about the future.

quiz.q: Which description is a rule-based strategy suitable for backtesting?
options: Buy strong stocks that look good
Buy when the close exceeds the 20-day high, relative volume ≥ 1.5 and Trend Template is met; stop below the 10-day low; exit on close below the 10-week average
quiz.why: Only explicit rules can be replicated and tested objectively.

quiz.q: Why include slippage and costs in a backtest?
options: Ignoring them overstates results, especially for active strategies and illiquid stocks
They are optional for all strategies
quiz.why: Real trading has frictions. Results without them can be misleadingly good.

lessons.title: Look-ahead bias
lessons.summary: Using information that was not available at the time of the decision. A subtle error that can make bad strategies look brilliant.

blocks.x: **Look-ahead bias** occurs when a backtest uses information that would not have been known at the moment of the trade.
Examples

blocks.caption: Common look-ahead errors
head: Error
Why it is wrong
rows: Entering at the day’s low or the exact breakout price using the full day’s data
You do not know the day’s low until the day ends
Using today’s close to decide to buy at today’s open
The close happens after the open
Using the 52-week high computed including today when deciding at the open
Today’s high was unknown at the open
Using financial results before they were announced
The data was not public yet
Using an RS rating calculated with data up to a later date
The rating would have been different at the time
Adjusting for later splits incorrectly or using today’s index membership

blocks.x: How to avoid it

items: Decide signals using only data available **before** the trade. For example, a signal at today’s close executes at tomorrow’s open or tomorrow’s trigger.
Lag any derived indicators properly.
Use point-in-time data for fundamentals and index constituents where possible.
Check suspiciously good results: ask “what did I know at that time?”

blocks.x: Example: a rule “buy when the stock breaks above its 20-day high” tested using daily bars. If the backtest buys at the 20-day high exactly on any day when the high exceeded it, it assumes perfect execution at the trigger price, even though gaps can open far above it. A realistic test would use the gap-up open as the entry when price opens above the trigger.

blocks.title: The test
blocks.x: For every input, ask: at the moment of this decision, would I have had this number? If not, the test is contaminated.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Believing results that look too good. A strategy with a 90% win rate and tiny drawdowns usually has a data or timing error.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Look-ahead bias uses future information. Make signals depend only on data available at decision time, and execute with realistic fills.

quiz.q: A backtest buys at today’s low whenever the day’s range touched a signal. What is the problem?
options: You cannot know the day’s low until the day ends, so the fill is unrealistic
quiz.why: Using the full day’s data to pick a fill is look-ahead. A real order cannot target the unknown low.

quiz.q: A breakout rule buys at the 20-day high price. On a day the stock gaps up 5% above that price at the open, what should a realistic test assume?
options: Execution near the gap-up open price, not at the trigger
Execution at the next day’s low
quiz.why: Gaps skip prices. Real fills occur at the first available price beyond the trigger.

lessons.title: Survivorship bias
lessons.summary: Testing only on companies that still exist today produces flattering results.

blocks.x: **Survivorship bias** occurs when a test includes only stocks that survived to the present and excludes those that were delisted, merged, suspended or went bankrupt.
Why it matters

Suppose you test a strategy on today’s NIFTY 500 constituents going back ten years. Stocks that collapsed, were demoted from the index or delisted are missing, while today’s winners are overrepresented. The result looks better than what a trader could have actually achieved, because at the time, you could not know which stocks would succeed.

blocks.caption: Survivorship bias in practice
head: Biased test
Better test
rows: Index constituents as they were at each past date
Stocks with full price history to today
Ignoring stocks that dropped off lists
Treat delisting as a loss, with realistic exit

blocks.x: Survivorship bias especially affects strategies that buy weak or beaten-down stocks, because many never recover. It also flatters strategies that hold through long drawdowns.

blocks.title: Indian market note
blocks.x: Small and mid caps have high churn: suspensions, delistings, and companies that stop trading. Point-in-time data matters even more here.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: When you use a screen result history, ask whether the historical universe included stocks that no longer exist. If not, treat the numbers as optimistic.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Survivorship bias hides failures, making tests look better than reality. Use point-in-time universes and include delisted stocks where possible.

quiz.q: Why is testing only on today’s index constituents misleading?
options: It excludes stocks that failed or were removed, so results are too optimistic
quiz.why: At the time of trading you could not know which stocks would survive, but the biased test acts as though you did.

quiz.q: Which strategy is most distorted by survivorship bias?
options: Buying beaten-down stocks hoping for recovery
Buying only after confirmed new highs
quiz.why: Many beaten-down stocks never recover or are delisted, and a survivor-only test hides them.

lessons.title: Overfitting
lessons.summary: A strategy fitted to past noise will look perfect and fail in live trading.

blocks.x: **Overfitting** (curve fitting) happens when rules are tuned so tightly to past data that they capture random noise rather than a real pattern. The result looks excellent in the test and disappoints live.
Common causes

items: **Too many conditions:** each additional filter fits the past better, but leaves fewer trades and less reliability.
**Parameter optimisation:** searching for the best moving-average length, stop percentage and volume threshold until the equity curve looks perfect.
**Many tests, one winner:** try 200 variations and the best one will look good by chance.
**Small samples:** 25 trades are too few to tell skill from luck.

blocks.caption: Signs of overfitting
head: Sign
Why it is a warning
rows: Results collapse when a parameter changes slightly
The edge depends on a precise value, which is rarely real
Very many conditions with few trades
Fitting noise with too little data

blocks.x: Protecting against it

items: **Start from logic:** have a reason, such as supply and demand, why the rule should work.
**Keep rules simple,** with few parameters.
**Test parameter robustness:** results should stay decent across a range of values (for example 40, 50 and 60-day averages), not only one.
**Use out-of-sample data:** design on one period, test on another you did not touch.
**Use walk-forward testing:** repeatedly optimise on a window and test on the next.
**Require enough trades** for the conclusion (many dozens or hundreds).
**Paper or small-size forward test** before full commitment.

blocks.title: The principle
blocks.x: A robust strategy performs reasonably across many nearby parameter values, many time periods and many stocks. A fragile one performs well only at one setting in one period.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Treating the best backtest result as the true strategy performance. The best of many tries is biased upward. Expect worse live results.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Overfitting fits noise. Keep rules simple, logical and robust across parameters, and validate on out-of-sample data and enough trades.

quiz.q: A strategy’s results collapse when the moving-average length changes from 47 to 50 days. What does this suggest?
options: Fragility and probable overfitting: the result depends on a precise parameter
quiz.why: Real edges tend to survive small parameter changes. A sharp dependence suggests fitted noise.

quiz.q: What is out-of-sample testing?
options: Testing on data not used to design or tune the rules
Testing only on the best period
quiz.why: Evaluating on unseen data checks whether the rules generalise.

quiz.q: Why is the best of 200 tested variations likely to disappoint live?
options: With many tries, one will look good by chance, so its performance is biased upward
Because it has too few conditions
quiz.why: Selection from many noisy results inflates the winner’s apparent quality.

lessons.title: Performance metrics
lessons.summary: The numbers that describe a strategy: expectancy, profit factor, drawdown, CAGR and ratios. Each answers a different question.

blocks.x: A single number never tells the full story. Use several metrics to understand returns, risk and reliability.

blocks.caption: Key metrics
head: Metric
Meaning
Question it answers
rows: How many rupees earned per rupee lost?
What is a typical trade worth?
Return per unit of worst drawdown
How much can we trust the statistics?

blocks.label: Expectancy
blocks.expr: Expectancy = (Win Rate × Average Win) − (Loss Rate × Average Loss)
blocks.note: Express in rupees per trade, percent or R.

blocks.x: Numerical example
A backtest has 100 trades. 40 are winners with an average win of ₹12,000, and 60 are losers with an average loss of ₹4,000.

blocks.label: Other formulas
blocks.expr:
CAGR = (Ending value ÷ Starting value)^(1 ÷ years) − 1
Maximum drawdown = (Trough − Peak) ÷ Peak
Calmar = CAGR ÷ |Max drawdown|
Sharpe = (Strategy return − Risk-free return) ÷ Standard deviation of returns
blocks.note: Example: ₹10,00,000 grows to ₹18,00,000 in 4 years. CAGR = 1.8^(0.25) − 1 ≈ 15.8%. If the worst drawdown was 24%, Calmar ≈ 15.8 ÷ 24 ≈ 0.66.

blocks.x: Reading them together

items: A high win rate with a poor payoff ratio is fragile. A low win rate with a high payoff ratio requires patience.
A profit factor above about 1.5 after costs is usually considered decent, but depends on the sample.
A great CAGR with a 60% drawdown may be unlivable. Ask if you would keep trading through it.
A strategy with 20 trades has unreliable statistics, however good they look.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Choosing a strategy by CAGR alone. Compare it with drawdown, number of trades, costs and robustness.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Use expectancy, profit factor, drawdown, CAGR, risk-adjusted ratios and sample size together. A good-looking single metric can hide fragility.

quiz.q: 100 trades: 40 winners averaging ₹12,000 and 60 losers averaging ₹4,000. What is the expectancy per trade?
What is the profit factor of the same results?
quiz.why: Gross profit ₹4,80,000 ÷ gross loss ₹2,40,000 = 2.0.

quiz.q: Why can CAGR alone be a poor way to choose a strategy?
options: It ignores drawdown, sample size and robustness, so a high CAGR can hide an unlivable risk profile
quiz.why: Return must be judged against risk and reliability. Calmar and Sharpe help, but sample size and robustness still matter.

lessons.title: From trading idea to rule-based strategy
lessons.summary: Convert a vague preference into precise, testable rules.

blocks.x: Most trading ideas begin as feelings: “I like strong breakouts.” A rule-based strategy replaces each vague word with a number or a yes/no test.
A translation exercise

blocks.caption: From idea to rule
head: Vague idea
Precise rule
rows: Trend Template criteria met and RS rating ≥ 80
Close above the highest high of the previous 20 sessions
Close no more than 3% above the 20-day high
NIFTY 50 close above its 50-day average and 50-day above 200-day
Initial stop at the lower of the 10-day low and 8% below entry
Exit when the close is below the 10-week average, or stop is hit
Risk 1% of equity per trade; max position 20%; max 8 positions

blocks.x: Each row removes judgement. Two people running these rules on the same data should produce the same trades.
A development process

items: **Idea and rationale:** why should this work (supply and demand, momentum, behaviour)?
**Write rules** completely, including universe, entry, exit, size and costs.
**Backtest** on one period.
**Check robustness** across parameters and sub-periods.
**Validate** on out-of-sample data.
**Forward test** with small size and compare live results with expectations.
**Monitor** performance and drawdown versus the backtest, and define when to pause.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: TradeEdge screens already implement many of these rules (for example the Fresh Breakout screen and Trend Template). Understanding the rules behind a screen lets you judge whether its results fit your plan.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Adding discretionary exceptions in live trading (“this one looks different”). If exceptions are common, the rules are incomplete. Record them in the journal and revise the rules, rather than breaking them case by case.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Keep strategy rules in one page. If it takes ten pages to describe, it is probably overfit or unclear.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A rule-based strategy replaces vague words with numbers and yes/no tests, then is tested, validated out of sample, forward tested and monitored.

quiz.q: Which pair converts a vague phrase into a precise rule?
quiz.why: Precise rules use measurable conditions so results can be replicated.

quiz.q: Why record discretionary exceptions in a journal instead of just making them?
options: Frequent exceptions show the rules are incomplete, and recording them lets you refine the rules rather than drift
quiz.why: Tracking exceptions turns improvisation into data to improve the system.

lessons.title: Why traders break their own rules
lessons.summary: The hardest part of trading is not analysis. It is doing what the plan says when your emotions say otherwise.

blocks.x: Most traders know the rules: cut losses, size properly, follow the plan. Most still break them. The gap between knowing and doing is psychological.

blocks.caption: Common psychological traps
head: Trap
What it feels like
What it causes
rows: Anxiety after losses; hesitation at valid entries
Missed trades, exiting winners too early
Wanting more than the plan allows
Oversizing, holding past targets, not taking profit
Fear of missing out as a stock runs
Anger after a loss; need to “win it back”
Losses feel about twice as painful as equal gains feel good
Looking only for evidence that supports your view
A winning streak feels like skill

blocks.x: The disposition effect

Research finds that investors tend to sell winners too soon and hold losers too long. It is the behavioural mirror of the rule “cut losses and let winners run”. Rules and written plans exist to counter it.
Making discipline easier

items: **Decide in advance:** write entry, stop, size and exit before the trade. Execution becomes following instructions.
**Use orders:** stop orders and alerts reduce the need for in-the-moment decisions.
**Limit risk per trade** so no single loss triggers panic.
**Reduce size after losses** instead of increasing it.
**Take breaks** after a series of losses or after an emotional trade.

blocks.title: The principle
blocks.x: You cannot remove emotion. You can design a process where emotion has less influence.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Believing a better indicator will fix emotional errors. Rule-breaking happens with any system.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Fear, greed, FOMO, revenge trading, loss aversion and bias push traders away from their plans. Pre-defined rules, orders and small risk reduce their influence.

quiz.q: What is the disposition effect?
options: Selling winners too early and holding losers too long
quiz.why: It is a behavioural tendency documented among investors, and it works against good risk management.

quiz.q: Why use stop orders and written plans?
options: They turn decisions into pre-agreed actions, reducing in-the-moment emotional influence
