quiz.why: Discipline is easier when the decision has already been made.

lessons.title: FOMO and chasing
lessons.summary: Buying a stock far above its proper entry can destroy risk/reward before the trade begins.

blocks.x: **FOMO** (fear of missing out) is the urge to buy because a stock is rising and you are not in it. It shows up as buying at the high of the day, buying after a gap, or buying a breakout that was missed yesterday.
The mathematics of chasing

blocks.caption: Same stock, different entries (stop fixed at ₹187, target ₹240)
head: Entry
Risk per share
Reward
Reward/Risk

blocks.x: The stock, stop and target are the same. Only the entry changed. Reward/risk fell from 2.8R to 0.6R. If you must keep the same rupee risk, you buy fewer shares, and potential profit shrinks. If you keep the same size, your risk rises.
How to handle it

items: **Define the buy zone in advance** and skip anything beyond it.
**Remember the next setup:** there are always new bases and pullbacks. Missing one trade costs nothing; chasing it can.
**Wait for a pullback or a new base** if the stock gets extended.
**Track missed trades** to see that most extended entries offered worse outcomes than waiting.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Set an alert at the pivot and an upper alert at the end of the buy zone. If the upper alert triggers first, close the chart and move on.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Justifying a chase because the stock is strong. Strength is not the issue. Price relative to your stop is.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Chasing worsens reward/risk: the stock and stop stay the same while your entry moves away. Use a pre-defined buy zone and wait for the next setup instead.

quiz.q: Stop ₹187, target ₹240. What is reward/risk if you enter at ₹220 instead of ₹201?
options: It falls from about 2.8R to about 0.6R
quiz.why: At ₹220, risk is ₹33 and reward ₹20, which gives 0.6R. The chased entry destroys the trade’s asymmetry.

quiz.q: What practical tool prevents impulsive chasing?
options: A pre-defined buy zone with an upper alert, beyond which the trade is skipped
quiz.why: A pre-decided limit removes the choice in the moment.

lessons.title: Accepting small losses
lessons.summary: A controlled loss is a business expense, not a failure.

blocks.x: A **small, controlled loss** is the cost of searching for winners. No strategy wins every time. What destroys accounts is not small losses but large ones that grew because the trader refused to accept them.

blocks.title: Reframe
blocks.x: A controlled loss is a business expense, not a failure.
Why it is hard

items: Losses hurt more than equal gains please (loss aversion).
Selling makes the loss real, so holding keeps hope alive.
Ego attaches to being right about the stock.

blocks.x: The arithmetic of loss

blocks.label: Gain needed to recover a loss
blocks.expr: Required gain = Loss ÷ (1 − Loss)
blocks.note: A 10% loss needs +11.1%. A 25% loss needs +33%. A 50% loss needs +100%.

blocks.x: A trader taking 1R losses of 1% of equity can lose ten in a row and be down about 9.6%, then recover with a 10.6% gain. A trader who lets one loss reach 50% needs a 100% gain. Small losses protect the ability to keep trading.
Practices that help

items: Use stop orders where possible so exit is automatic.
Record the loss in R, without commentary on yourself.
Review whether the rules were followed, not just the outcome.
Celebrate rule-following, including when the result is a small loss.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Evaluating decisions only by outcomes. A trade that followed the rules and lost was a good decision. A trade that broke the rules and won was a bad one that got lucky.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Small losses are costs of doing business. Losses compound against you, so keep them small, automate exits when possible, and judge your process by rule-following rather than outcome.

quiz.q: What gain is needed to recover from a 50% loss?
quiz.why: A 50% loss requires doubling the remaining capital, a 100% gain.

quiz.q: A trader follows every rule and takes a −1R loss. How should it be classified?
options: A good decision with a normal bad outcome
quiz.why: Process quality is separate from result in any single trade.

lessons.title: The trading journal
lessons.summary: A journal turns experience into data. It is the feedback loop that improves the process.

blocks.x: Memory is unreliable. After a few weeks, you remember best the dramatic trades and forget the ordinary ones. A **trading journal** records each trade objectively so you can learn from patterns instead of anecdotes.
What to record

blocks.caption: Journal fields
head: Field
Why it matters
rows: Breakout, pullback, reclaim: shows which setups work for you
Reveals how results vary with conditions
Preserves the chart context as you saw it

blocks.x: What to review

items: **Weekly:** were rules followed? Which mistakes repeated?
**Monthly:** results by setup type and market regime; average winner and loser in R; win rate.
**Quarterly:** is the strategy behaving as tested? Should size or selectivity change?

blocks.x: After 50 to 100 trades, patterns often show clearly, such as breakouts in weak markets losing consistently, or early exits cutting the average winner.

blocks.title: TradeEdge application
blocks.x: TradeEdge’s Trading Journal lets you log trades, track partial sells and see analytics such as win rate and P&L over time. Use it consistently, and add notes about setup and mistakes where possible.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Logging only results and not reasons. Without setup, regime and mistake fields, a journal tells you what happened but not why.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: Take a screenshot at entry and at exit. Reviewing the chart you actually saw avoids hindsight bias.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A journal records each trade’s setup, regime, risk, exit, result in R, mistakes and lessons. Regular reviews turn experience into measurable improvement.

quiz.q: Why record the result in R rather than only in rupees?
options: R standardises results across different position sizes, making trades comparable
quiz.why: A ₹10,000 gain may be 1R or 5R depending on risk. R shows quality independent of size.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of recording the market regime for each trade?
options: You can see how setups perform in different conditions and adjust selectivity
quiz.why: Performance often varies strongly with market conditions, which only shows if regime is recorded.

lessons.title: The TradeEdge technical framework
lessons.summary: Ten layers of evidence, from the market to risk management, combined into one repeatable decision process.

blocks.x: This framework brings together everything in the course. It does not predict. It organises evidence so each decision is explicit.

blocks.label: The layers
blocks.expr:
Market Regime
+ Sector Strength
+ Weinstein Stage
+ Trend Template
+ Relative Strength
+ Price Structure
+ Base Pattern
+ Volume
+ Breakout / Pullback
+ Risk Management
blocks.note: Each layer removes a different kind of weak trade.

blocks.caption: Layer by layer
head: Layer
Question
Evidence
TradeEdge tool
rows: Is entry valid and not extended?
Fresh Breakout, Weekly Breakout Soon, pullback screens

blocks.title: Using the framework
blocks.x: Work top-down. If the market is hostile, reduce exposure and selectivity. If the stock fails Stage or Trend, stop. Only stocks that pass all layers reach the entry and sizing decision.

blocks.title: Not a prediction
blocks.x: A stock that satisfies every layer still has a meaningful chance of failing. The framework raises the quality of candidates and defines risk. It does not eliminate uncertainty.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: The framework stacks ten layers of evidence from the market to risk management. It improves selection and discipline, but cannot guarantee any single outcome.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the TradeEdge technical framework?
options: To organise evidence so each decision is explicit, improving selection and discipline
quiz.why: It is a decision-support structure, not a prediction engine.

quiz.q: Why work top-down from the market to the stock?
options: So a hostile market or a failed trend check stops weak trades before they reach the entry decision
Because stocks are independent of markets
quiz.why: Early layers filter out trades with poor odds, avoiding attractive-looking but ill-timed setups.

lessons.title: The scorecard
lessons.summary: A simple scoring grid to compare candidates and identify weak links. A decision aid, not a model.

blocks.x: A scorecard puts the layers on a common scale so you can compare setups and spot weak links quickly.

blocks.caption: TradeEdge scorecard
head: Component
What a high score means
Score
rows: Index above rising averages; healthy breadth; leaders working
Sector RS rising; several stocks in Stage 2
Stage 2; Trend Template met; averages aligned and rising
High RS rating; RS line near highs; Mansfield RS positive
Tight, orderly, adequate duration, supply absorbed
Dry-up in base; surge on breakout; supportive closes
Clean pivot, strong close, inside buy zone, follow-through
Logical stop, reward/risk of 3R or better, size within limits

blocks.x: How to use it

items: Score each component honestly from 0 to 10, based on written criteria.
Add them up (maximum 80).
**Look at the minimum, not only the total.** A 9 in everything except a 3 in market regime should give pause.
Define thresholds in advance, for example “trade only if total ≥ 60 and no component below 5”.
Record the score in the journal and later compare it with outcomes.

blocks.x: Example: DEF Ltd (fictional): market 7, sector 8, trend 9, RS 8, base 7, volume 6, breakout 7, risk/reward 6 = 58. Under a threshold of 60, the setup is skipped or taken smaller. Volume and risk/reward are the weak links. A better entry or a tighter base could change the score.

blocks.title: A decision aid, not a model
blocks.x: The score is not a probability and has no proven predictive power by itself. Its value is consistency: it forces the same questions every time and reveals the weakest link.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Fudging scores to justify a stock you like. Write the scoring rules down and score before you look at the chart’s appeal.

blocks.title: Practical use
blocks.x: After 50 or more trades, compare scores with results in R. If high scores do not do better, revise the criteria.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A scorecard standardises evaluation and highlights weak links. Use total and minimum thresholds set in advance, and test them against your own results.

quiz.q: DEF scores market 7, sector 8, trend 9, RS 8, base 7, volume 6, breakout 7, risk/reward 6. What is the total?
Why examine the lowest component, not only the total?
options: A strong total can hide a critical weak link, such as a hostile market
The lowest score is always the best
quiz.why: A single poor layer can dominate the risk even when others are strong.

quiz.q: What best describes the scorecard’s status?
options: A decision-support framework whose value is consistency, to be validated against your own results
quiz.why: It does not predict, but it standardises analysis.

lessons.title: From screen to trade
lessons.summary: The complete workflow, from screening to journal review.

blocks.x: Here is the end-to-end workflow, which you can adapt to your own style.

Screen
↓
Shortlist

Open chart

Analyse structure

blocks.note: Most of the work happens before the order is placed.

blocks.caption: What happens at each step
head: Step
Action
rows: Run TechLens screens (for example Trend Template, Fresh Breakout, Leadership Tight Base)
Remove illiquid names; keep a manageable list (5 to 15)
Weekly first for stage and trend, then daily

blocks.x: Time allocation

Do the analysis outside market hours, when you are calm. During the session, your task is mostly to follow the plan: alerts trigger, orders execute, stops protect. Analysis done in the heat of price movement tends to be worse.

blocks.title: Daily routine
blocks.x: Evenings: review open positions, update stops, run screens, build tomorrow’s alert list. Mornings: confirm alerts and plans. During the day: act only on pre-defined triggers.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.x: Skipping the shortlist step and acting on the first interesting screen result. Most of the edge is in what you reject.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Screen, shortlist, chart, structure, market, validation, entry, stop, size, execution, journal, review. Do the thinking in advance and let execution be mechanical.

quiz.q: When is the best time to do chart analysis and plan trades?
options: During volatile market hours, in real time
Outside market hours when calm, with alerts and orders prepared in advance
quiz.why: Calm preparation produces better decisions than reacting to every tick.

quiz.q: Which step comes immediately after defining the stop?
quiz.why: Size depends on the stop distance, so it must follow the stop definition.

lessons.title: The final technical analysis checklist
lessons.summary: One page to review before every trade.

blocks.x: Use this checklist as a gate. Every box should be answered with evidence, not hope.

items: ☐ Market trend favourable
☐ Sector strong
☐ Stock in Stage 2
☐ Price above key moving averages
☐ Moving averages aligned
☐ Relative strength strong
☐ Base is constructive
☐ Volume pattern healthy
☐ Breakout or pullback is valid
☐ Entry is not extended
☐ Stop is technically logical
☐ Risk/reward acceptable
☐ Position size calculated
☐ Portfolio concentration acceptable
☐ Exit plan defined
☐ Trade journal prepared

blocks.x: How to use it

items: If two or more boxes fail, skip the trade.
If one box fails, ask whether the failure is a hard stop (such as market or stage) or something that can be solved with smaller size.
If you cannot answer a box, treat it as unchecked.

blocks.title: Process over outcome
blocks.x: The checklist exists to ensure that you did the work before risking capital. A trade taken with a full checklist that loses is still a good decision.

blocks.title: Reminder
blocks.x: Nothing in this course guarantees profits. Educational content only. Markets involve risk of loss.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: Check every box with evidence before entering. When boxes fail, skip, reduce size or wait.

quiz.q: If two or more checklist boxes fail, what is the sensible action?
options: Skip the trade or wait for a better setup
quiz.why: Multiple failures mean the setup does not meet your own standards.

quiz.q: A checklist box cannot be answered with evidence. How should it be treated?
options: As unchecked, which is a reason for caution
quiz.why: Unknowns are risks. Do not assume them away.

lessons.title: Capstone: build your own technical trading plan
lessons.summary: Write the plan that turns this course into a process you can follow, test and improve.

blocks.x: The final exercise is to write a one-page trading plan, answering the questions below in specific, measurable terms. Use this lesson as a template and write your answers in your journal or notes.
1. Market

**What market conditions will I trade?** Example: NIFTY above rising 50-day and 200-day averages, breadth healthy, leaders holding breakouts. State what makes you reduce or stop: for example four or more distribution days, NIFTY below the 50-day and breadth deteriorating.
2. Universe
**What stocks will I consider?** Example: NSE stocks with average daily turnover above ₹5 Cr, price above ₹50, Trend Template met, RS rating ≥ 80, in leading sectors.
3. Setup
**What exact setup am I looking for?** Example: tight base or VCP near highs with volume dry-up in the last pause; or a pullback to a rising 50-day with a reversal signal.
4. Entry
**What confirms entry?** Example: price above the pivot within a 3% buy zone with volume ≥ 1.5 × average; or a break above the signal candle’s high at a rising average.
5. Stop
**Where is the thesis invalidated?** Example: below the last contraction low or the signal candle’s low, never more than 8% from entry. If the logical stop is wider, reduce size or skip.
6. Position size
**How much capital will I risk?** Example: 1% of equity per trade; size equals risk divided by risk per share; max 20% of the account in one stock; max 6% total open risk; max 25% in one sector.
7. Exit

**What causes me to exit?** Example: stop hit, close back below the pivot on above-average volume, weekly close below the 10-week average on heavy volume, or a sustained market breakdown. Partial profit at +2R, remainder trailing.
8. Review

**How will I measure whether the system works?** Example: journal every trade in R, review weekly for rule compliance, monthly for win rate, average win/loss, expectancy, and maximum drawdown. Pause and review if drawdown exceeds a pre-set limit (for example 8% of equity).

blocks.title: Important
blocks.x: The examples above are illustrations, not recommendations. Your plan must fit your capital, time, risk tolerance and regulations. This course is for education, not investment advice, and no strategy guarantees profits.

blocks.title: Next step
blocks.x: Start small. Trade the plan with minimal size for a few months, journal everything, and refine the rules only on the basis of enough data.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.x: A written plan covering market, universe, setup, entry, stop, size, exit and review converts knowledge into a process. Test it small, record everything, and improve it with evidence.

quiz.q: Your stock passes the screen and has a logical stop 14% below entry. Your plan caps stops at 8%. What follows from your plan?
options: Use an 8% stop regardless of structure
Reduce size so the rupee risk is acceptable or skip the trade
quiz.why: If the logical stop exceeds your limit, you cannot force a tighter stop without hiding the real risk. You reduce size or skip.

quiz.q: A trader risks 1% per trade, buys at ₹250 with a stop at ₹235 on a ₹20,00,000 account. About how many shares?
quiz.why: Risk = ₹20,000. Risk per share = ₹15. 20,000 ÷ 15 ≈ 1,333 shares (₹3,33,250, about 16.7% of the account).

quiz.q: Which sequence best reflects the course’s decision hierarchy?
options: Market regime, trend, structure, relative strength, volume, pattern, entry, risk, management
quiz.why: The course moves from broad context to specific entry and then to risk and management.

quiz.q: A strategy wins 40% of trades with a 3R average win and a 1R average loss. What is its expectancy per trade?

lessons.title: Profit & Loss analysis
lessons.summary: Sales rose 22% but profit rose 71%. Find out exactly why, and whether it can last.

blocks.x: 1. Where did the extra profit come from? Common-size view

Raw materials, power and other costs all fell as a share of revenue while employee cost rose a little. The result is a 3.6-point jump in EBITDA margin. Part of this is operating leverage: fixed costs spread over 22% more sales. Part is better product mix and input costs. The report does not allow us to split these exactly, so treat the split as something to probe in the concall.

Revenue +22.0%

blocks.x: 3. Quality of profit

items: **Other income** is small: ₹19.2 crore, about 4% of PBT. Profit is not propped up by treasury income.
**Tax rate** is steady: 28.0% against 27.4%. No tax windfall flatters profit.
**Interest** fell even as the business grew, a sign of deleveraging.
**Minority interest:** a partly-owned subsidiary lost about ₹10.8 crore attributable to outside holders. Profit attributable to owners is ₹327.5 crore, higher than total profit of ₹316.7 crore.

**Per-share check:** reported EPS ₹81.08 equals total profit divided by 3.906 crore shares. Profit to owners works out to about ₹83.9 a share. Verify the method in the EPS note before relying on either number.

**Receivables** rose 33.5% against revenue growth of 22%. This needs a closer look (see red flags).

blocks.x: 2. Is it safer than last year?
3. Funding mix and maturity

Of ₹1,010 crore borrowings, ₹578 crore is long-term and ₹432 crore short-term. Long-term loans fund the expansion, which suits the long life of the assets. Short-term borrowings fell from ₹612 crore to ₹432 crore, easing refinancing pressure. Equity also gained ₹24.5 crore from outside holders in a subsidiary, a sign of partner confidence.

lessons.summary: All the key ratios side by side, and a breakdown of why return on equity rose from 16.9% to 23.2%.

blocks.x: DuPont: why did ROE rise?

blocks.label: ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier
blocks.note: Net margin uses profit attributable to owners. Turnover = revenue ÷ closing total assets. Multiplier = total assets ÷ owners' equity.

items: **Margin rose** from 8.9% to 12.8%: the main engine.
**Asset turnover rose** from 0.75 to 0.81: assets worked a little harder despite CWIP building up.
**Leverage fell** from 2.53 to 2.24: the return improved while the company used less borrowed money. This is the best kind of ROE improvement.

blocks.title: Is it creating value?
blocks.x: ROCE of 21.3% is well above a plausible cost of capital of roughly 10 to 12% (borrowings carry interest of about 8%, and equity is costlier). Growth at these returns creates value, as long as the new capacity earns similar returns.

blocks.title: Caution on ROE
blocks.x: ROE here uses closing equity because the opening-year figure for FY25 is not in this report. Using average equity would show a slightly higher ROE for FY26. FY26 is also a strong year: judge returns over 5 to 10 years, not one.

quiz.q: ROE rose while the equity multiplier fell. What does that mean?
options: The gain came from better margins and efficiency, not more debt
quiz.why: A falling equity multiplier means leverage declined, so the higher ROE came from operating performance.

lessons.summary: Revenue rose 7%, yet profit rose 47%. Margins, lower interest and a lower tax rate each played a part.

blocks.x: 1. Cost structure as a share of revenue

Essentially the whole gain came from **materials cost**: 3 points less of every rupee of sales went on raw material. That points to better product mix and pricing, most likely in chemicals, rather than cost-cutting elsewhere. It also means margin depends on prices and mix that can change.
2. Why profit grew faster than EBITDA

blocks.label: The profit bridge, in plain steps
blocks.expr:

Interest fell 26% (₹98 crore):  helps PBT

blocks.note: If the FY25 tax rate of 26.6% had applied in FY26, profit after tax would be about ₹1,690 crore, up about 35% rather than 46.7%. The tax rate is one of the largest reasons profit grew so fast.

items: **Exceptional item:** ₹85 crore one-off charge for the impact of the new labour codes. It lowers this year's profit but should not repeat.
**Other income** is small, about 4% of PBT. Profit is not propped up by treasury returns.
**Tax rate:** a key audit matter concerned an uncertain tax position on past income from sale of carbon-credit certificates. Always read why the rate changed.

blocks.title: P&L verdict
blocks.x: Real operating strength: core profit before other income grew about 45%. But 11 percentage points of PAT growth leaned on a lower tax rate, and the margin gain depends on materials prices and mix. Judge FY27 on whether margin and tax rate hold.

lessons.summary: Leverage is modest and improving, but ₹1,889 crore is tied up in unfinished projects and working capital is stretching.

blocks.x: 1. Safety

blocks.x: The thesis in plain words

SRF is a large, conservatively financed chemicals-led manufacturer having a margin recovery year. FY26 saw revenue +7%, EBITDA margin up 3.1 points to 21.6%, profit up 47%, CFO of ₹2,554 crore, free cash flow of ₹738 crore and net debt/EBITDA of 1.1x. It is spending heavily on new capacity while leverage falls.

head: Strengths
Concerns
rows: Margin up 3.1 points with real cash backing
11 points of PAT growth came from a lower tax rate
Cash cycle lengthened 15 days; CFO/EBITDA down to 75%
Diversified across chemicals, films and textiles
Cyclical businesses and a recovery-year margin
₹1,889 crore of CWIP not yet earning

blocks.x: Raw size and debt amounts are not comparable on their own: SRF's ₹3,830 crore net debt is about 1.1 times its EBITDA, which is lower than Privi's and Azad's in relative terms. Always compare debt to earning power, not to rupees. SRF has the largest free cash flow and a moderate ROE, while Privi has the highest ROE and Azad the highest margin but negative cash. **No single metric picks the best company.**
What to monitor each quarter

items: EBITDA margin in chemicals, and the effective tax rate.
Working-capital days and CFO ÷ EBITDA.
Capex progress and when CWIP is commissioned.
Net debt/EBITDA and short-term maturities.
Hedging and currency effects.

blocks.title: The real skill
blocks.x: The same eight-step method exposed four very different businesses. Margin, cash, safety, returns and growth each tell part of the story. Read all three statements together.

blocks.x: This case study illustrates a method on a real filing. It does not recommend any investment. Check the latest filings and consider your own goals, or speak to a qualified adviser, before investing.

options: It measures debt relative to earning power
Rupee amounts are illegal to compare
quiz.why: A large debt can be safe for a large earner and risky for a small one. Net debt/EBITDA scales it.

quiz.q: Which company in the table has the highest free cash flow?
quiz.why: SRF's ₹738 crore is the largest, ahead of ACE at ₹324 crore and Privi at ₹230 crore.

lessons.title: Meet the company: niche chemicals with global reach
lessons.summary: Structure directing agents, phase transfer catalysts, battery salts and pharma and agro intermediates, sold mostly to customers abroad.

blocks.x: Tatva Chintan makes **specialty chemicals** used inside other products: catalysts that make reactions cleaner and faster, high-purity salts used to build zeolites for emission control and refining, salts for energy storage, and intermediates for pharmaceutical and agrochemical makers. Its products are small in volume but critical to customers' processes, which makes them hard to replace.

What it tells an analyst
rows: Strong growth off a weak base
Profit after tax ₹42.1 crore against ₹5.7 crore the year before
A recovery year, not a new level of growth
Exports about 75% of revenue (61.5% a year ago)
Earns in foreign currency and relies on global demand
Structure directing agents (SDAs) 40% of sales: second-largest global producer, largest in India
Two large agro products moved into sustained commercial supply during the year
Years of development turning into revenue

blocks.title: How we will analyse it
blocks.x: Same routine as the Privi and SRF case studies, plus two extra lessons: one on the product lines and customers, and one on the three-year cycle, because FY25 was an unusually weak year and FY26 must be judged against both. All figures are consolidated, year ended 31 March 2026, converted from ₹ million to **₹ crore** (1 crore = 10 million).
Why it sits with Privi and SRF

All three make specialty or fine chemicals for global customers, and all three invest heavily in plants. Tatva Chintan is the smallest, with the thinnest balance sheet cushion and the least cash conversion, which makes it a useful contrast.

items: How much of FY26's profit jump is recovery from a trough, and how much is a new level of earnings?
Which products drive growth, and which are shrinking?
How is growth being funded, and is that comfortable?
What price is reasonable if earnings swing this much from year to year?

blocks.title: Education, not advice
blocks.x: This is a worked example of analysing a filing. It is not a recommendation to buy, hold or sell any share.

quiz.q: Why does an export share rising from 61% to 75% matter?
options: Profit becomes more exposed to global demand and exchange rates
quiz.why: A larger export share means sales depend more on overseas customers and on currency movements.

lessons.title: Products and customers: where growth comes from
lessons.summary: Structure directing agents grew 71% and now lead the business, while phase transfer catalysts fell 6.5% and domestic sales dropped 18%.

blocks.x: 1. What the mix says

items: **SDAs** nearly doubled their weight in the business (31% to 40% of revenue). They are used to build zeolites for emission control and petrochemical refining, so growth links to cleaner-vehicle and refining demand.
**PASC** grew 26%, helped by two large agro products entering commercial supply. Agro and pharma intermediates can be lumpy, because a few products and customers dominate.
**PTC**, the original franchise, fell 6.5% and slipped from 33% to 23% of revenue. A mature product can shrink if customers destock or competitors cut prices.
**Electrolyte salts** are small (₹16.5 crore) but growing fast, an early-stage option linked to energy storage.
**Domestic sales fell 18%** while exports rose 62%. The company is now far more reliant on overseas customers.

blocks.title: Concentration
blocks.x: Two product lines (SDA and PASC) account for 72% of revenue, and a handful of products drive PASC growth. The risk of customer or product concentration is real even though the report does not list individual customers.

blocks.title: Product verdict
blocks.x: Growth came mainly from one niche leadership product (SDAs) and two new agro products, while the old PTC franchise declined. A broader base would make future earnings steadier.

quiz.q: SDA revenue rose from ₹119.7 crore to ₹204.5 crore. What was the growth?
Why is a falling domestic share and rising export share a risk factor?
options: Profit depends more on foreign demand and currency movements
It removes the need for inventory
quiz.why: Exports bring currency risk and tie the business to global conditions.

lessons.title: Profit & Loss analysis
lessons.summary: Revenue rose 32% but EBITDA nearly tripled and profit rose 7.4 times. About half of each extra rupee of revenue turned into EBITDA.

blocks.x: Our EBITDA of ₹93.2 crore equals the company's own reported figure, and the margin of 18.4% matches too, so the numbers tie.
1. Cost structure as a share of revenue

Almost 8 of the 9.5 points of margin came from **materials**, which suggests better product mix (more high-value SDAs and the new agro products), better prices and better utilisation. The rest came from fixed costs such as employees and overheads spreading over more sales.
2. Operating leverage in numbers

blocks.label: The incremental margin
blocks.expr:
Extra revenue:  505.9 − 382.7 = 123.1 crore
Extra EBITDA:    93.2 −  34.2 =  59.0 crore
Incremental EBITDA margin = 59.0 ÷ 123.1 = 48%
blocks.note: About 48 paise of every extra rupee of sales became EBITDA, against an average margin of 18%. That is the signature of operating leverage and a rich mix. It also works in reverse: if sales or mix fall back, profit falls much faster than sales.

blocks.x: 3. The profit bridge: ₹49.4 crore more PBT

The entire gain came from the operating business. Other income is small (6% of PBT), so profit is not propped up by treasury returns, unlike several other case studies. Depreciation grew 33% as new plants started to be depreciated, and will keep rising.

items: **Tax rate** rose to 26.2% from 24.6%, so no tax windfall.
**EPS** grew with profit (7.4x) because the share count did not change.
**Exceptional items:** none reported.

blocks.title: P&L verdict
blocks.x: A genuinely stronger operating year with clean, operations-led profit. But part of the jump is a rebound from an unusually weak FY25. The next lesson places FY26 against FY24 to see how much is truly new.

quiz.q: Revenue rose ₹123 crore and EBITDA rose ₹59 crore. What is the incremental EBITDA margin?
quiz.why: 59 ÷ 123 = 48% of the extra revenue became extra EBITDA.

quiz.q: Where did almost all of the 9.5-point margin gain come from?
options: Lower materials cost as a share of revenue
quiz.why: Materials fell from 52.0% to 44.4% of revenue, 7.6 of the 9.5 points.

lessons.title: From trough to recovery: the three-year view
lessons.summary: FY25 was a trough. Set FY26 against FY24 and the picture is a healthy recovery, not a breakout.

blocks.x: One year's growth number can mislead when the previous year was abnormal. FY25 profit was only ₹5.7 crore. A seven-fold rise sounds spectacular, but measured against FY24 the picture is calmer.

blocks.label: Two-year compound growth (FY24 to FY26)
blocks.note: Averaged across the dip, growth is mid-teens, strong but ordinary. The seven-fold PAT rise is mostly the reversal of a bad year.

blocks.x: 1. What the cycle teaches

items: **Margins recovered to their old level** (17 to 18%) but have not yet moved above it. The new agro products have restored profitability rather than lifted it to a new plateau.
**Revenue is 29% above FY24**, while the capital base grew. Investments in plants made earlier have turned into sales.
**Earnings are volatile.** EBITDA halved in FY25 and then nearly tripled. A business whose profit swings this much deserves a lower multiple on peak earnings.

blocks.title: Normalise before you value
blocks.x: Average EPS across the three years is ₹11.2, well below the FY26 figure of ₹17.98. A price that looks reasonable on FY26 earnings may look expensive on a through-the-cycle average. Always ask what a normal year looks like.

blocks.title: Cycle verdict
blocks.x: FY26 confirms the business can earn an 18% EBITDA margin. Whether that is a new floor or a good year is the central question for investors.

quiz.q: Profit rose 7.4 times, but FY24 to FY26 growth is about 17.7% a year. Why the gap?
options: FY25 was an unusually weak base
quiz.why: A very low FY25 base makes the one-year growth enormous. Over two years the growth rate is much more modest.

quiz.q: Why normalise earnings before valuing a volatile business?
options: Peak-year profit can overstate repeatable earning power
quiz.why: A single strong year may not repeat, so a through-the-cycle average gives a safer base.

lessons.title: Balance Sheet analysis
lessons.summary: Debt tripled to ₹120 crore, all of it short-term. Inventory is the largest current asset and still growing faster than sales.

blocks.x: 1. Safety

Leverage is modest, and interest cover improved sharply because profit grew. But **96% of borrowings are short-term working-capital loans**, which need renewing, and undrawn facilities fell from ₹184 crore to ₹106 crore. Cash and bank balances are only ₹8.8 crore, so the company relies on lenders for flexibility.
2. Working capital

Inventory jumped ₹62 crore, much of it finished goods and work-in-progress built for growing export orders. The days figure is overstated because stock includes conversion costs, but the trend is clear: stock is growing faster than sales, and suppliers funded part of the build, since payables rose 78%.

blocks.title: Equity is huge relative to profit
blocks.x: Equity of ₹782 crore comes largely from share issues and retained profit since the IPO. Assets are growing faster than equity, so the balance sheet is now more leveraged than a year ago, though still modestly.

blocks.title: Balance sheet verdict
blocks.x: Conservative by most measures, but the direction is toward more short-term debt, thinner cash, heavier stock and shrinking headroom. Growth needs funding, and today lenders provide it.

quiz.q: Borrowings ₹120 crore, cash and bank ₹9 crore, EBITDA ₹93 crore. Net debt ÷ EBITDA is about?
Why does having 96% of debt short-term matter?
options: It must be renewed regularly, so lender support is needed
quiz.why: Short-term loans mature soon. If lenders tighten credit, refinancing could become hard.

lessons.title: Cash Flow analysis
lessons.summary: Profit jumped sevenfold but cash from operations rose only 27%. Capex of ₹114 crore pushed free cash flow to −₹82 crore, financed by new borrowing.

blocks.x: 1. Why did profit not become cash?

Operating profit before working capital was ₹101 crore, a threefold rise. But working capital absorbed ₹62 crore: inventory ₹62 crore and receivables ₹22 crore, partly offset by ₹20 crore more from payables. Without that drain, CFO would have been about ₹93 crore.
2. Sources and uses in FY26

₹ crore

blocks.x: Operations paid for only about a quarter of the capex. The rest came from new borrowing of ₹84 crore and from drawing down cash. That is the standard pattern of a business building capacity ahead of demand, as long as the plants fill and CFO then grows.

blocks.title: Three-sign reading
blocks.x: CFO positive, investing negative, financing positive: the growth-phase pattern. It is healthy if cash flow catches up with profit in FY27, and risky if working capital keeps absorbing it.

blocks.title: Cash flow verdict
blocks.x: The weakest link. Profit looks excellent, but cash conversion of 34% and negative free cash flow mean growth is currently funded by lenders. The key test for FY27 is whether capex falls and CFO rises.

quiz.q: CFO is ₹31.5 crore and capex is ₹113.8 crore. What is free cash flow?
quiz.why: FCF = CFO − capex = 31.5 − 113.8 = −₹82.3 crore.

quiz.q: Why did CFO rise only 27% when operating profit tripled?
options: Working capital, mainly inventory, absorbed ₹62 crore
quiz.why: Inventory and receivables growth consumed much of the extra operating profit.

lessons.title: The ratio dashboard and DuPont
lessons.summary: Returns improved sharply but remain low: ROCE is 6.6% and ROE is 5.4%, because a large capital base is still working its way into profit.

head: Ratio
FY25
FY26
Direction
rows: ROCE (EBIT incl. other income ÷ equity + borrowings)

blocks.x: DuPont: why is ROE only 5.4%?

blocks.label: ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier
blocks.note: Turnover = revenue ÷ closing total assets. Multiplier = total assets ÷ equity.

items: **Net margin** rose a lot, and was the entire reason ROE improved.
**Asset turnover is only 0.50:** each rupee of assets produces 50 paise of revenue. Chemical plants, stock and an equity base from earlier fundraising all sit in the asset base.
**Leverage** of 1.28 is low. ROE is not flattered by debt.

blocks.title: Returns versus cost of money
blocks.x: ROCE of 6.6% is below what the company pays on short-term borrowings plus a fair return for owners. Even in a strong year, the capital base earns less than its cost. Value is created only when profit grows into the capital already invested, which depends on plants filling and margins holding.

blocks.title: Caution
blocks.x: ROE and ROCE use closing balances. Capital employed includes plants not yet earning. Even at the FY24 peak, returns were similarly modest (ROE about 4%), so low capital efficiency is a feature of this business model, not only of FY26.

quiz.q: ROCE of 6.6% is below the cost of borrowing plus a fair owner return. What does that imply?
options: Growth is not yet creating much value
quiz.why: Value is created only when returns exceed the cost of capital. At 6.6% the margin of safety is thin.

lessons.title: Red flags and quality checks
lessons.summary: Clean accounts with small contingent liabilities. The flags are cash conversion, short-term debt, stock build and volatility.

blocks.x: The three that matter most

items: **Cash conversion and funding:** growth is being funded by short-term borrowing, which depends on lender goodwill.
**Earnings volatility:** profit swung from ₹30 crore to ₹6 crore to ₹42 crore in three years. Valuing the peak is risky.
**Low returns on a large capital base,** even in a good year.

blocks.title: Questions for the concall
blocks.x: How sustainable are the volumes of the two large agro products? What caused the FY25 trough and what protects against a repeat? How will inventory normalise? What is the plan to term out short-term debt? When do the new plants contribute?

blocks.title: Red-flag verdict
blocks.x: The accounts look clean and contingent liabilities are negligible. The risks are operational and financial: volatile earnings, thin cash and short-term debt funding growth.

quiz.q: Which pair of findings best questions how reliable FY26 earnings are as a base for valuation?
options: FY25 was a trough and profit swings widely year to year
A large export base and strong brand
quiz.why: Volatile earnings make a single year an unreliable guide, so a multi-year average is safer.

lessons.title: Valuation: what price would make sense?
lessons.summary: The report has no price, so we map any price to multiples, then test them against a through-the-cycle profit.

blocks.label: How to use it
blocks.expr:
Today's P/E = Price ÷ 17.98

EV/EBITDA = EV ÷ 93.2

blocks.x: What you must believe

items: **FY26's 18% EBITDA margin is repeatable** (the FY24 peak was 17%). If margin slips toward FY25's 9%, profit falls sharply.
**Volumes of the new agro products persist** and SDAs continue to grow.
**Working capital normalises** so that free cash flow turns positive and short-term debt can be reduced.
**Returns climb** as plants fill, from today's ROCE of about 6.6% toward double digits.

blocks.title: Use scenarios
blocks.x: Build good, base and bad cases for profit growth and exit P/E, as in 'Putting it together'. Because FY25 shows how far earnings can fall, the bad case should assume margins give back a large part of the FY26 gain.

blocks.title: Not a price target
blocks.x: The table is a tool, not a target. Compare Tatva Chintan's multiples with Privi and SRF, and with its own history, in FinSight before drawing a conclusion.

quiz.q: EPS is ₹17.98. At a P/E of 45, what is the price?
Why look at P/E on a three-year average EPS?
options: It shows how expensive the price is against through-the-cycle earnings
quiz.why: A single recovery year can overstate earning power. Averaging across a cycle gives a more conservative base.

lessons.title: The verdict, and Tatva Chintan beside Privi and SRF
lessons.summary: Three specialty-chemicals companies, three different profiles.

blocks.x: The thesis in plain words

Tatva Chintan is a niche specialty-chemicals maker with leadership positions and an improving mix. FY26 revenue rose 32%, EBITDA tripled to an 18.4% margin, profit rose 7.4x and exports reached 75% of sales. But that profit is a rebound from a trough, cash conversion was only 34% of EBITDA, free cash flow was −₹82 crore, borrowings tripled and are almost all short-term, and returns on capital are still low.

head: Strengths
Concerns
rows: Operations-led profit growth, not treasury income
CFO only 34% of EBITDA; free cash flow negative
Niche leadership: largest SDA maker in India, second-largest globally
FY26 profit is a rebound from a weak FY25; earnings volatile
Interest cover about 20x; leverage still modest
ROCE 6.6% and ROE 5.4%, below cost of capital

blocks.x: Three specialty-chemicals companies

Tatva Chintan grew fastest but is the smallest, with the weakest cash conversion and the lowest returns. Privi shows what a mature specialty business can look like: high returns, strong cash and falling debt. **Growth alone does not make a business better. Returns on capital and cash conversion decide how much of the growth reaches shareholders.**
What to monitor each quarter

items: EBITDA margin: does 18% hold?
Inventory, receivable days and cash from operations.
Short-term borrowings and undrawn facilities.
SDA growth, the new agro products and the fate of PTC.
Capex progress and plant utilisation.

blocks.title: The real skill
blocks.x: A recovery year looks strongest when you compare it with the trough. Placing it against a three-year view, and checking cash flow and returns, tells you how much is truly new.

blocks.title: Education, not advice
blocks.x: This case study illustrates a method on a real filing. It does not recommend any investment. Check the latest filings and consider your own goals, or speak to a qualified adviser, before investing.

quiz.q: Why can't growth alone rank Tatva Chintan above Privi?
options: Privi converts more profit to cash and earns far higher returns on capital
quiz.why: Cash conversion and returns on capital show how much of growth reaches shareholders. Privi leads on both.

quiz.q: What is the first step when you see a profit rise of 7.4 times?
options: Check whether the previous year was an unusually weak base
quiz.why: A very low base exaggerates growth. A multi-year view shows the underlying trend.

lessons.title: Meet the company: what Azad makes and why it matters
lessons.summary: Mission-critical engineered parts for turbines, oil and gas, and aerospace, sold almost entirely abroad.

blocks.x: Azad Engineering makes **highly engineered, precision components** such as turbine and aerospace parts, where a tiny error can ground an aircraft or stop a power plant. Customers qualify a supplier slowly and rarely switch, which is the source of the company's pricing power and long contracts.

What it tells an analyst
rows: Earns in foreign currency, so exchange rates swing profit
Standalone revenue: Energy and Oil & Gas about 81%, Aerospace & Defence about 17%
Dependent on two end markets, one dominant
Order book about ₹6,500 crore, roughly 11 times FY26 revenue (management estimate, unaudited)
Strong visibility, but it must be converted to sales over time
Four dedicated customer factories: three running by March 2026, a fourth (for Baker Hughes) in April 2026
Deep customer ties, but also heavy capital tied up ahead of revenue
Strong promoter stake. Pledge not checked here

The questions that matter for Azad

items: How much of the profit jump is core business and how much is other income?
Does growth consume more cash than the business generates?
Are returns on the fresh capital likely to match the old business?
What has to go right for the order book to turn into profit?

blocks.title: Education, not advice
blocks.x: This is a worked example of analysing a filing. It is not a recommendation to buy, hold or sell any share.

quiz.q: An order book of 11 times annual revenue mainly gives the company…
options: Revenue visibility over several years, if delivered on time
quiz.why: A large order book shows demand, but delivery, cost control and customer timing still decide the profit.

lessons.title: Profit & Loss analysis
lessons.summary: Profit rose 54%, but strip out other income and the core picture is closer to 25%. See what really drove the year.

blocks.x: 1. Cost structure as a share of revenue

A margin above 35% is exceptional for a manufacturer. Notice what moved it: the **materials line** fell from 13.9% to 9.6% of revenue, while employee cost rose. That materials fall needs an explanation: the company built ₹72 crore of extra work-in-progress and finished stock in the year, which reduces the cost charged to this year's profit. Stock building is normal for long-cycle parts, but part of the margin gain is timing, not permanent.
2. Headline growth vs core growth

blocks.label: Strip out other income
blocks.expr:
PBT FY25: 124.0   core PBT = 124.0 − 10.6 = 113.4
PBT FY26: 187.3   core PBT = 187.3 − 45.7 = 141.7
Headline PBT growth: +51.0%   Core PBT growth: +24.9%
blocks.note: Other income was 24% of PBT in FY26 against 8.5% the year before. It came mainly from interest on the cash raised in the QIP and unrealised foreign-exchange gains. Both can shrink: the cash is being spent on capex, and exchange rates move.

blocks.x: 3. Why PAT grew faster than EPS

PAT rose 54.3% but EPS only 40.3%. The company issued new shares during FY25, so FY25's EPS was computed on fewer weighted shares. The slower EPS growth is a share-count effect, a good reminder to compare **per-share** growth, not just total profit.

items: **Depreciation** jumped 79% as new plant came into use, and will keep rising as CWIP of ₹257 crore is commissioned.
**Finance cost** rose 68% as borrowings nearly doubled to fund the build-out.
**Tax rate** eased to 28.7% from 30.2%, a small help.

blocks.title: P&L verdict
blocks.x: A genuinely strong business: 32% revenue growth and about 37% EBITDA margin. But the headline 54% profit growth overstates the core, thanks to other income and stock building. Judge the next year on core profit: will margins hold as depreciation and interest climb?

quiz.q: PBT is ₹187 crore and other income is ₹46 crore. What is core PBT?
quiz.why: Core PBT excludes other income: 187 − 46 = ₹141 crore (rounded).

quiz.q: Why does building up unsold stock raise this year's profit?
options: Costs of unsold stock are held on the balance sheet, not charged to profit yet
quiz.why: Cost of goods sold uses materials consumed minus the increase in stock. More closing stock means a smaller charge now.

lessons.title: Balance Sheet analysis
lessons.summary: The cash pile from the share issue has been spent on plant, stock and debt-funded growth. Net cash has turned into net debt.

blocks.x: 1. The story in one line

In FY25 the company raised about ₹700 crore of equity and parked most of it in bank deposits. In FY26 it spent that cash. Cash and bank balances fell by ₹512 crore, borrowings rose ₹213 crore, and the money went into plant (+₹347 crore), work in progress (+₹177 crore), inventory (+₹140 crore) and receivables (+₹88 crore).
2. Working capital: the heavy part

A cycle of about 11 months means cash is locked up for a long time between buying material and collecting payment. That is common in forged and precision parts, which have long production and shipping cycles, but it lengthened by 71 days in one year. Payables barely grew, so suppliers are not funding the build-up; the company is.

blocks.title: Returns on capital: the key insight
blocks.x: Operating capital employed (equity + borrowings − cash and bank balances) rose from ₹940 crore to ₹1,801 crore. Core EBIT on it fell from **14.0% to 9.6%**. Much of the new capital sits in CWIP and stock that are not yet earning. The test is whether returns recover once the new factories fill with orders.

blocks.title: Balance sheet verdict
blocks.x: Still conservatively geared (debt/equity 0.30), but the balance sheet has changed character from cash-rich to capital-hungry. The watch items: interest cover, working-capital days, and how fast CWIP converts to earning assets.

quiz.q: Borrowings ₹457 crore, cash and bank ₹185 crore. What is net debt?
quiz.why: Net debt = borrowings − cash and bank balances = 457 − 185 = ₹272 crore.

quiz.q: Capital employed more than doubled but core EBIT grew less. What happens to ROCE?
options: It falls until the new assets start earning
quiz.why: Returns are profit divided by capital. If capital grows faster than profit, the ratio drops until the investment pays back.

lessons.title: Cash Flow analysis
lessons.summary: Profit of ₹134 crore, yet operating cash flow was negative ₹119 crore. Follow the money into stock, receivables and advances.

blocks.caption: Consolidated cash flow, ₹ crore
head: Item
FY25
FY26
rows: Operating profit before working capital changes

blocks.x: 1. Why did cash turn negative?

Working capital absorbed ₹303 crore. The biggest items were inventory (₹140 crore), other assets such as advances and balances with authorities (₹74 crore) and receivables (₹74 crore). Tax paid also rose to ₹49 crore. Operating profit before these changes was a healthy ₹233 crore, so the business earns well but is spending it as fast as it comes in.
2. Sources and uses of cash in FY26

The expansion was paid for by two things: the old QIP cash (deposits maturing) and new debt. Operations contributed nothing. That is acceptable for a one-off build-out, provided cash from operations turns positive once the factories are full.

blocks.title: Three-sign reading

blocks.x: 1. Where the profit comes from

items: **Aerospace** earns about 82% of segment EBITDA from 48% of revenue. Revenue grew 27.6% but EBITDA only 12.5%, so its margin slipped from 26.0% to 22.9%. The company describes this as margin normalisation amid growth investments and project mix.

**Hydraulics** improved: EBITDA rose 48.5% and margin from 5.3% to 7.4%. India Hydraulics grew 22.5% while the UK business fell 25.5% as the company moved production to Bangalore and rationalised products.
**Metallurgy** is the weak link: EBITDA fell 72% to ₹2.8 crore on ₹358 crore of revenue, a margin under 1%. The business faces weak German auto demand, high energy costs and fierce competition.

blocks.label: Segment EBITDA vs group EBITDA
blocks.expr:
Segment EBITDA total: 21,625 lakh (₹216.3 crore)
Group EBITDA:          18,268 lakh (₹182.7 crore)
Gap (corporate and unallocated costs): about ₹33.6 crore
blocks.note: About ₹34 crore of costs sit outside the three segments, roughly one-sixth of segment profit. This is why the consolidated margin (11.3%) is so much lower than the aerospace margin.

blocks.x: 2. The goodwill question

The auditors flagged **impairment of goodwill** as a key audit matter. Goodwill linked to Metallurgy was ₹38.2 crore, while the segment earned only ₹2.8 crore of EBITDA. If the foundry's outlook weakens further, some of that goodwill could be written off. A write-off would not use cash but would reduce profit and equity.

blocks.title: Segment verdict
blocks.x: A strong aerospace franchise is carrying the group, with a recovering Indian hydraulics business, while the German foundry drags. The group's future depends on aerospace growing without further margin erosion and on the Metallurgy problem being contained.

quiz.q: Aerospace revenue grew 27.6% but EBITDA only 12.5%. What happened to its margin?
quiz.why: Profit grew more slowly than sales, so each rupee of revenue earned less profit than before.

quiz.q: Why is goodwill a risk when a segment earns almost nothing?
options: It may have to be written off if the segment's outlook worsens
quiz.why: Goodwill is justified by expected future profit. If a segment's profit collapses, impairment may be required.

lessons.title: Balance Sheet analysis
lessons.summary: Net debt is about 2.5 times EBITDA, interest cover is under 2 times, and stock keeps growing. This is a stretched balance sheet in a growth phase.

blocks.x: 1. Leverage and safety

Interest cover of 1.8 times means operating profit before other income only just covers the interest bill with some margin. A modest fall in profit would squeeze it. Debt rose ₹78 crore in the year, most of it long-term (non-current borrowings up from ₹175 crore to ₹249 crore), which is better for stability than short-term debt. Short-term debt is still 53% of the total.
2. Working capital

A cycle of about 140 days is long, as expected in aerospace where parts are built to programme schedules, but it did not worsen. Inventory rose ₹65 crore in absolute terms, partly work-in-progress for new programmes.

blocks.title: Items to check
blocks.x: Other non-current assets jumped from ₹4.0 crore to ₹30.8 crore, which may be capital or programme advances. Intangibles under development rose to ₹35.4 crore (product and programme development). Both tie up money before revenue arrives.

blocks.title: Balance sheet verdict
blocks.x: Manageable but not comfortable. Net debt of 2.5 times EBITDA and 1.8 times interest cover leave little room for an earnings shock. The aerospace growth story needs funding, and that depends on lenders' continued support.

quiz.q: Interest cover of 1.8x means…
options: Operating profit covers interest only 1.8 times, leaving a thin cushion
quiz.why: A low cover means a modest drop in profit could make the interest bill hard to service.

quiz.q: Borrowings ₹529 crore, cash and bank ₹68 crore, EBITDA ₹183 crore. Net debt ÷ EBITDA is about?

lessons.title: Cash Flow analysis
lessons.summary: Operating cash flow fell 34% to ₹95 crore. After leases and interest almost nothing was left, so the year was funded by ₹69 crore of new borrowing.

blocks.x: 1. Why did CFO fall so much?

Operating cash flow before working capital grew 15%, in line with EBITDA. But working capital absorbed ₹95 crore, against ₹12 crore the year before: inventory ₹58 crore, other assets ₹25 crore, receivables ₹30 crore, offset partly by ₹28 crore of extra payables and by provisions. Other liabilities also fell ₹14 crore. Tax paid was lower, which helped.
2. Sources and uses in FY26

Interest and leases together cost ₹79 crore, nearly the whole of cash from operations after capex. The group had to borrow ₹69 crore, a net increase in debt, to fund its needs and build cash. That is the pattern of a business that is investing and servicing a heavy fixed-cost base.

blocks.title: Three-sign reading
blocks.x: CFO positive, investing negative, financing roughly neutral to positive. The key is that financing was positive only because of new borrowing.

blocks.title: Cash flow verdict
blocks.x: Adequate but weak. CFO covers capex, but not capex plus interest plus leases. A recovery in working capital, as aerospace programmes deliver and stock converts into sales, is needed to relieve borrowing.

quiz.q: CFO is ₹95 crore and capex is ₹66 crore. What is free cash flow before leases?
quiz.why: FCF = CFO − capex = 95 − 66 = ₹29 crore (rounded).

quiz.q: Why does free cash flow after leases matter for this company?
options: Lease payments are a real recurring cash cost
quiz.why: Leased plants and buildings must be paid for every year, so cash left after leases is a truer measure of spare cash.

lessons.title: The verdict, and the three precision-engineering companies side by side
lessons.summary: Azad, Sansera and Dynamatic: three companies in one sector with very different financial shapes.

blocks.x: The thesis in plain words

Dynamatic is an aerospace-led engineering group growing well, with an excellent aerospace franchise and an improving Indian hydraulics business. But the consolidated margin is flat at 11%, interest cover is under 2 times, net debt is 2.5 times EBITDA, a German foundry is near break-even with goodwill at risk, and FY26 profit fell 25% after exceptional charges and a 35% tax rate.

Concerns

Marquee customers: Airbus, Boeing, Dassault, Bell

blocks.x: Azad, Sansera and Dynamatic compared

Sansera has the strongest balance sheet and returns, Azad the highest margin and fastest growth, and Dynamatic the weakest margin and the highest leverage but the only positive free cash flow. **In one sector, three different risk profiles exist.** Peers can be compared on every ratio, but each business also has its own story, such as aerospace dependence or a foundry in Europe.
What to monitor each quarter

items: Interest cover and net debt to EBITDA.
Aerospace revenue growth and segment margin.
Metallurgy results, and any goodwill impairment.
Working capital days and cash from operations.
Further exceptional items, including final labour-code rules.

blocks.x: Breaking a group into segments and then comparing it to similar companies shows where the real engine and the real risk lie. The same sector can host the strongest and the most stretched balance sheet.

lessons.title: Profit & Loss analysis
lessons.summary: Revenue +30%, EBITDA +34%, profit +35%. Margins held at about 26.7%, and the company's own EBITDA figure ties to our calculation.

blocks.x: A useful check: adding other income to our EBITDA gives ₹2,750 crore, exactly the figure management reports (up 35%). Our figure of ₹2,622 crore excludes other income, so we see the core business more cleanly.
1. Cost structure as a share of revenue

Materials fell 3 points of revenue, probably reflecting the shift toward higher-value defence products and better input prices. But **employee cost and other expenses rose** 2.3 points together as the business scaled up, so only 0.7 points reached the margin. Costs of growth are real.
2. Quality of profit

items: **Other income** is 5.4% of PBT, up from 4.1%. Small enough not to distort the picture.
**Core profit** (PBT before other income and the share of associates) rose 34.6%, close to the headline. The growth is real.
**Tax rate** edged up from 25.9% to 26.6%. No tax windfall flatters profit.
**Hyperinflation:** subsidiaries in hyperinflationary economies caused a non-cash loss of ₹95 crore (₹65 crore last year), added back in the cash flow. It reduces reported profit but not cash.
**Owners vs total profit:** ₹59 crore of profit belongs to minority holders in subsidiaries.

blocks.title: P&L verdict
blocks.x: Clean, high-quality profit growth backed by volume. The margin is stable and strong. The concern is not profit but whether that profit is turning into cash, which the next lessons examine.

quiz.why: 2,622 + 128 = ₹2,750 crore, the figure management reports.

quiz.q: Materials fell 3 points of revenue but the margin rose only 0.7 points. Why?
options: Employee cost and other expenses rose as a share of revenue
quiz.why: The savings on materials were largely used up by higher employee and other operating costs.

lessons.title: Balance Sheet analysis
lessons.summary: Assets grew 32%. Net cash of ₹315 crore turned into net debt of ₹884 crore, while inventory and receivables grew far faster than sales.

blocks.x: 1. From net cash to net debt

The company spent its investment portfolio (₹529 crore of current investments is now zero) and borrowed another ₹528 crore. Even so, debt is only 0.3 times EBITDA and interest is covered 17 times, so the balance sheet remains strong. What changed is the **direction**: it used to hold surplus cash and now funds growth with borrowing.
2. Working capital: where the cash went

Inventory grew 67% and receivables 50%, against revenue growth of 30%, while payables barely moved. The cycle lengthened by 57 days. Defence products have long production and delivery cycles, and stock of components and work-in-progress builds before delivery, which explains part of this. It still ties up a great deal of money.

blocks.title: Other liabilities matter here
blocks.x: Other liabilities (non-current ₹788 crore and current ₹674 crore) are large. They typically include advances received from customers, which fund the business interest-free but must be earned by delivering. Confirm the composition in note 17.

blocks.title: Balance sheet verdict
blocks.x: Strong, with low leverage. The watch items are the speed at which net cash disappeared, the fast build in stock and receivables, and heavy reliance on customer advances.

quiz.why: Net debt = borrowings − liquid funds = 1,468 − 584 = ₹884 crore.

quiz.why: Stock growing faster than sales means each rupee of sales needs more days of stock.

lessons.summary: Profit rose 35% but cash from operations fell 75% to ₹621 crore. Last year's ₹2,468 crore was inflated by customer advances, so look at two years together.

blocks.x: 1. The swing in working capital

In FY25, working capital **released** ₹814 crore, mainly because other liabilities rose ₹1,167 crore (which includes customer advances). In FY26 it **absorbed** ₹1,577 crore: receivables ₹634 crore, inventory ₹701 crore and other assets ₹359 crore. The ₹2,391 crore swing in working capital between the two years outweighs the ₹804 crore rise in operating profit, which is why CFO fell.

blocks.title: Why look at two years
blocks.x: FY25's 126% conversion was abnormal because advances flowed in, and FY26's 24% is abnormally low because stock and receivables were built. Averaged over two years, CFO is about 67% of EBITDA, still decent, and free cash flow is slightly positive at ₹343 crore.
2. Sources and uses in FY26

Capex of ₹1,739 crore was 73% higher than last year. It was paid for with operating cash, the sale of the investment portfolio and new borrowing. This is a classic growth-investment pattern, but with much less help from operations than before.

blocks.title: Cash flow verdict
blocks.x: The weakest part of the year, and the key test for FY27. If working capital releases as deliveries are completed and advances are earned, CFO should recover. If stock and receivables keep rising, borrowing will keep increasing.

quiz.why: Swings in working capital distort single years. Averaging reveals the underlying conversion.

Defence revenue growth and order inflow.

What makes ACE different
The first two case studies were growth stories. ACE is a **steady, cash-rich business in a flat year**. The interesting questions are not about growth but about quality and capital allocation:

items: How strong are margins and cash flow when sales stop growing?
What does a near-zero-debt balance sheet with a huge treasury mean for returns?
How much of profit comes from investing the cash rather than from selling equipment?

lessons.title: Profit & Loss analysis
lessons.summary: Revenue fell 1.4% yet profit rose 1.4%. Margins held, but one-fifth of profit came from the treasury.

blocks.x: 1. Cost structure as a share of revenue

Materials cost two-thirds of every rupee of sales, so **steel and component prices** drive margin. In a year when revenue slipped, the company still held its EBITDA margin around 15.4% by trimming material and other costs. Employee cost grew 15.6% on a shrinking top line, which is the one cost line that ran against the trend.
2. The share of profit from the treasury

blocks.label: Core vs reported profit
blocks.note: Other income was about 20% of PBT (18% the year before). It comes mostly from interest on bonds and deposits (₹55 crore) and gains on investments carried at fair value (₹44 crore). So the 'growth' in profit this year came entirely from the treasury, not from selling equipment.

items: **Credit losses:** about ₹11 crore of impairment on receivables in each of the last two years, about 3.8% of year-end receivables. Not alarming, but persistent.
**Interest cost** fell 23% as short-term borrowings were cleared.
**Tax rate** is steady at about 25.4%.
**EPS** matches the profit growth (+1.4%) because the share count did not change.

blocks.title: P&L verdict
blocks.x: A resilient operating business: margin steady, earnings flat in a soft year. But with revenue falling and core profit slightly down, it is the treasury income and lower interest that kept headline profit growing. The question for next year is whether demand revives.

quiz.q: Revenue fell 1.4% but PBT rose 1.4%. What should you check?
options: How much came from other income and lower interest
quiz.why: Profit can rise on treasury gains or lower finance costs even while the core business shrinks.

quiz.q: PBT is ₹556.7 crore and other income is ₹110.1 crore. About what share of PBT is other income?

lessons.title: Balance Sheet analysis
lessons.summary: Almost no debt, ₹1,361 crore of net cash, and negative working capital. The treasury is 42% of total assets.

blocks.x: 1. The treasury

Investments plus cash and bank balances total **₹1,361 crore, 42% of all assets** (36% a year earlier). Net cash, after the tiny borrowings, rose from ₹959 crore to ₹1,361 crore. This is a company that earns more than it can use in the business, and parks the surplus in financial investments.
2. Working capital: other people's money

A **negative** cycle means suppliers and customers fund the business: payables of about 151 days exceed inventory plus receivables. That is a sign of strong bargaining power and an efficient dealer model, and explains the very high returns on operating capital. The flip side is that it relies on suppliers continuing to extend credit, and inventory days rose 17 days in a flat year.

blocks.title: How to read this
blocks.x: Treat the large payables as a feature to monitor rather than a flaw. The risk shows up if sales fall sharply: inventory would pile up while suppliers still need paying.

blocks.title: Balance sheet verdict
blocks.x: Fortress-like on safety. The questions are about **use of capital**: ₹1,361 crore of treasury earns financial-market returns rather than the high returns the equipment business earns, which dilutes overall returns on equity.

quiz.q: A company has liquid investments and cash of ₹1,361 crore and borrowings of almost nil. What is net cash?
quiz.why: Net cash = liquid funds − borrowings = 1,361 − 0.1 ≈ ₹1,361 crore.

quiz.q: A negative cash conversion cycle means…
options: Suppliers and customers fund the operating cycle
quiz.why: Payables outlast the time money is tied up in stock and receivables, so the business needs little of its own capital for operations.

lessons.summary: Food delivery, quick commerce, going-out and B2B supplies: a consumer platform with no debt and a very large cash pile.

All figures are consolidated, year ended 31 March 2026, in **₹ crore** as reported.
What makes platform businesses different

items: **Revenue is not the same as scale.** What a platform counts as revenue depends on whether it takes a commission or sells goods itself.
**Segments matter more than the total.** One mature business can fund several young ones.
**Profit can come from the treasury,** not the platform, when the company holds a huge cash pile.
**Stock-based pay is a real cost** even though it uses no cash.

blocks.title: Education, not advice
blocks.x: This is a worked example of analysing a filing. It is not a recommendation to buy, hold or sell any share.

quiz.q: Why is segment revenue growth for food delivery (+26%) more meaningful than the group's +169%?
options: It is not distorted by the accounting change in quick commerce
quiz.why: The group figure is inflated by the change in how quick commerce revenue is recorded. Food delivery's model did not change.

lessons.title: The big accounting shift: why revenue grew 169%
lessons.summary: Blinkit moved from earning a commission to selling goods itself. Revenue jumped, but economics did not change as much as the headline suggests.

blocks.x: Until mid-2025 Blinkit worked as a **marketplace**: third-party sellers sold goods, and Blinkit recorded only its **commission** as revenue. From the June 2025 quarter it began moving to a combination of marketplace and **inventory-led** model, buying goods and selling them directly. In that case it records the **full selling price** as revenue and the purchase cost as an expense.

blocks.label: Same sale, two ways to record it
blocks.expr:
Marketplace:    customer pays 100. Seller gets 82. Blinkit records revenue of 18 (commission).
Inventory-led:  customer pays 100. Blinkit buys at 82. Revenue = 100, cost of goods = 82.
blocks.note: Gross profit is the same 18 in both cases, but revenue is 5.5 times larger and margins as a percentage of revenue look 5.5 times smaller. Nothing changed economically except how it is shown.

blocks.x: What changed in the numbers

head: % of revenue
FY25
FY26
Why
rows: Cost of goods (net of inventory change)
Goods are now bought and sold, so their cost appears
Spread over a much bigger revenue number
Delivery and marketing relative to a larger base
Looks lower because revenue includes goods value

blocks.x: Hyperpure's non-restaurant sales also fell as Blinkit began buying goods itself, so part of the old B2B revenue moved into quick commerce. That is one reason B2B shrank 13%.

blocks.title: What to do when revenue is not comparable
blocks.x: Compare **segments whose model did not change** (food delivery, going-out), compare **profit and cash flow** (which are real in either model), and compare **gross profit** if it is disclosed. Never compare margins on revenue across the model change.

blocks.title: Questions for the concall
blocks.x: What is the gross order value and take rate for quick commerce? What share of orders is inventory-led? How will margins look once the transition is complete?

quiz.q: A customer pays ₹100 and the supplier gets ₹82. What does a marketplace record as revenue?
quiz.why: A marketplace records only its commission. An inventory-led seller would record the whole ₹100.

quiz.q: Why do margins on revenue look lower after the model shift?
options: Revenue now includes the full goods value, a much bigger base
quiz.why: The same gross profit is divided by a much larger revenue figure, so the percentage falls.

lessons.title: Balance Sheet analysis
lessons.summary: No debt and ₹16,356 crore in cash and investments, yet inventory jumped twelvefold and lease liabilities more than doubled.

blocks.x: 1. The treasury

Cash, bank balances and investments (current and non-current) total **₹16,356 crore, 40% of assets**, down from ₹16,806 crore (47%). The company has no borrowings. Some of the non-current investments are strategic stakes measured at fair value (for example CureFit and Shiprocket, carrying ₹1,781 crore), and the fair-value fall was recorded in other comprehensive income (−₹515 crore), not in profit.
2. What the money is funding

items: **Inventory** rose from ₹176 crore to ₹2,181 crore because of the move to inventory-led quick commerce, a direct consequence of the model shift.
**Leased assets and lease liabilities** more than doubled to ₹4,294 crore and ₹4,592 crore: dark stores and warehouses are rented, not owned. Lease liabilities are debt-like obligations.

**Goodwill** of ₹5,737 crore (₹4,528 crore from the Blinkit, Orbgen and entertainment ticketing acquisitions) is a key audit matter. A weak outlook for any of those businesses could force a write-off.
**Payables** doubled, so suppliers funded most of the extra inventory.

blocks.x: DuPont: ROE of 1.2%

blocks.label: ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier
blocks.note: Revenue basis changed in FY26, so the margin fell and asset turnover rose mechanically. Their product, ROE, is the number to trust.

items: **ROE is only 1.2%** on equity of ₹30,973 crore. Equity includes ₹16,356 crore of cash and investments that earn treasury returns, and ₹5,737 crore of goodwill from acquisitions.
**Leverage is low** (equity multiplier 1.31, driven by leases), so ROE is not helped by debt.
**Returns on the platform itself** are negative, since core operating profit after depreciation is a loss.

blocks.title: How to read a company still scaling
blocks.x: A low ROE is normal while a business is investing for scale. The question is whether profit grows fast enough, relative to the equity and cash already committed, to eventually earn attractive returns. Today the equity base is large compared with profit.

blocks.title: Caution
blocks.x: The model change breaks margin and turnover comparisons. Use segment results and cash flow when judging progress.

quiz.q: ROE is 1.2% on a large equity base. What is the main reason?
options: Profit is small relative to equity, much of which is idle cash and goodwill
quiz.why: Equity includes a very large cash pile and acquisition goodwill that do not yet earn operating returns.

lessons.summary: With EPS of ₹0.40, a P/E is almost meaningless. Instead we ask what profit a given price demands years from now.

blocks.x: At these multiples, the market is not paying for today's profit. It is paying for profit years from now. The question is **how much profit** the price requires.
Reverse thinking: what profit does the price imply?

head: Price

blocks.label: How the reverse calculation works
blocks.expr:
Profit needed = Market cap ÷ 25
Growth needed = (Profit needed ÷ 366)^(1/8) − 1
blocks.note: Example at ₹300: 275,700 ÷ 25 = 11,028. 11,028 ÷ 366 = 30. 30^(1/8) − 1 = 53% a year, to simply earn back today's price over eight years.

blocks.x: What you must believe

items: **Food delivery stays strong** while competition continues, because it funds everything else.
**Quick commerce profit scales** from ₹430 crore to a size that can justify the price.
**Losses in going-out and new initiatives shrink** or become profitable.
**Stock-based pay and leases grow slower than profit,** so operating profit finally exceeds depreciation and rent.

blocks.title: A tool, not a target
blocks.x: Pick today's price from FinSight and run the reverse calculation. If the profit growth required is far above anything the company or its sector has achieved, the price is demanding. That does not mean it must fall, only that expectations are high.

blocks.title: Estimates, not forecasts
blocks.x: The prices here are placeholders. The calculation assumes a 25x multiple in year eight, no dilution and no change in cash. Real outcomes can differ widely.

quiz.q: Market cap is ₹275,700 crore. At a 25x P/E in year eight, what profit is needed?
quiz.why: Profit needed = market cap ÷ P/E = 275,700 ÷ 25 = ₹11,028 crore.

quiz.q: Why is P/E not useful for Eternal today?
options: EPS is tiny, so the ratio is huge and says little about value
quiz.why: With EPS of ₹0.40, even a modest price gives a P/E in the hundreds, so a forward-looking approach is more informative.

lessons.title: The verdict, and what Eternal teaches about platform businesses
lessons.summary: A fortress balance sheet and a powerful profit engine, funding a large and still-loss-making build-out.

blocks.x: The thesis in plain words

Eternal is a strong, debt-free consumer platform. Food delivery earns ₹2,079 crore a year and funds a quick commerce business that has just turned profitable, a going-out business losing ₹292 crore, and new initiatives losing ₹206 crore. Headline revenue growth of 169% is an accounting effect. The honest picture: EBITDA doubled, profit fell 31%, treasury income carries the bottom line, and free cash flow after leases was −₹1,957 crore.

blocks.x: Eternal alongside other growth-phase companies

All three burned cash while growing, but Eternal alone funded it entirely from a cash pile built by issuing shares, and it has by far the lowest return on equity. Solar earns 27% on equity while burning similar cash. **The same cash burn can mean very different things depending on what each rupee invested earns.**
What to monitor each quarter

items: Quick commerce segment profit and the take rate.
Losses in going-out and new initiatives.
Core operating profit after stock-based pay and depreciation.
Operating cash flow, capex and lease payments.
The size and yield of the treasury.

blocks.title: The real skill
blocks.x: For platform businesses, ask three things: what is recorded as revenue, which segments make or lose money, and where profit comes from. Those answers matter more than the headline growth rate.

blocks.title: Education, not advice
blocks.x: This case study illustrates a method on a real filing. It does not recommend any investment. Check the latest filings and consider your own goals, or speak to a qualified adviser, before investing.

quiz.q: Which pair of questions matters most when analysing a platform business?
options: How revenue is recorded, and which segments make the profit
quiz.why: Revenue recognition and segment profit show the real economics beneath a headline growth number.

quiz.q: Why can similar cash burn mean different things for Eternal and Solar?
options: Returns on the capital invested differ greatly (1.2% vs 26.7% ROE)
quiz.why: Spending cash is justified only if it earns attractive returns. The two companies differ sharply on that.
