Current operating assets minus current operating liabilities.
Year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter comparisons.
Large investors gradually buying a stock, often during quiet bases, visible as up-day volume and strong closes.
A volatility measure: the average of the true range (the largest of high−low, |high−previous close| and |low−previous close|) over, typically, 14 periods.
A multi-week consolidation where supply is absorbed before a possible next advance, such as a cup and handle or flat base.
A close below the last higher low (in an uptrend) or above the last lower high (in a downtrend), the first hard evidence that the trend’s pattern has failed.
A move above resistance (or a pivot) that ends a consolidation, ideally on strong volume.
The area from the pivot to a few percent above it (commonly up to 3% to 5%) where entry still offers acceptable reward/risk.
A chart symbol showing a period’s open, high, low and close, with a body between open and close and wicks to the extremes.
Heavy volume with little price progress, which can indicate supply meeting demand at a level.
Large holders selling into strength, often near highs, seen as heavy volume with weak closes and stalling price.
An index day that falls meaningfully on higher volume than the previous session, a sign of institutional selling.
The decline from a peak in account equity to a subsequent trough, usually quoted as a percentage.
Exponential moving average: an average that gives more weight to recent prices, so it reacts faster than an SMA.
The average result per trade: (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss).
A strong up day on higher volume, typically on day four or later of a rally attempt after a correction, suggesting buyers are returning.
The 50-day average crossing above (golden) or below (death) the 200-day average. Both are lagging trend confirmations.
A swing high above the previous one, and a pullback low above the previous low. Together they define an uptrend.
A rare pattern where a stock roughly doubles in a few weeks, then consolidates in a very tight range before continuing.
A backtesting error where information not available at the time of the decision is used.
Moving Average Convergence Divergence: the gap between a 12 and 26-period EMA, with a 9-period signal line and histogram.
A relative strength measure that normalises a stock-to-index ratio around a zero line, using its 52-week average.
How many stocks participate in a market move, measured by advance/decline, new highs and lows, and the share of stocks above key averages.
On-Balance Volume: a running total that adds volume on up days and subtracts it on down days.
Tuning a strategy so closely to past data that it captures noise and fails on new data.
The price level that completes a base and triggers a buy, such as the handle high of a cup and handle.
Choosing the number of shares so that a stop-out costs a fixed percentage of capital: capital at risk ÷ risk per share.
A trade’s result expressed in units of initial risk. +3R means a profit three times the amount risked.
A comparison of a stock’s performance with a benchmark or with other stocks. Not the same as RSI.
A percentile-style rank of a stock’s weighted past performance versus all other stocks, from low (weak) to high (strong).
Relative Strength Index: a 0 to 100 momentum oscillator based on average gains versus average losses over, typically, 14 periods.
A brief break below support or a base low that quickly reverses, flushing out weak holders and stop orders.
Simple moving average: the arithmetic mean of the last N closing prices.
Stan Weinstein’s framework of four stages: basing (1), advancing (2), topping (3) and declining (4), using the 30-week average.
A 0 to 100 oscillator showing where the close sits within the recent high-low range.
Price zones where demand (support) or supply (resistance) has previously stopped a decline or an advance.
A testing error where only stocks that still exist are included, hiding failures and overstating results.
Mark Minervini’s eight-condition filter for stocks in a confirmed Stage 2 uptrend.
Volatility Contraction Pattern: a base whose pullbacks get progressively smaller while volume dries up, showing supply is running out.
A period of unusually low volume, typically in the last stage of a base, showing sellers have largely finished.
